1.0.oldText: After clear and unmistakable evidence that the existing federal government does not work, you are now called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America. The subject speaks for its own importance. Its consequences amount to nothing less than the survival of the UNION, the safety and welfare of its component parts, and the fate of an empire that is, in many respects, the most consequential in the world. It has often been said that the people of this country seem to have been chosen, by their conduct and example, to settle a critical question: whether human societies are truly capable of building good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever doomed to depend on accident and force for their political constitutions. If there is any truth to that observation, the present crisis can rightly be regarded as the era when that decision must be made. A wrong choice on our part would, in this view, count as a general misfortune for all of humanity.

1.1.oldText: This idea adds the motives of philanthropy to those of patriotism, sharpening the concern that all thoughtful and decent people must feel about the outcome. We will be fortunate if our choice is guided by a sound judgment of our true interests, undisturbed and unbiased by considerations unrelated to the public good. But this is more to be hoped for than realistically expected. The plan put before us touches too many particular interests and disturbs too many local institutions not to draw in many issues unrelated to its merits, along with views, passions, and prejudices that are unfriendly to the discovery of truth.

1.2.oldText: Among the most formidable obstacles the new Constitution will face are two clearly visible ones. First, there is the obvious self-interest of a certain class of men in every State who will resist any change that might reduce the power, salary, and importance of the offices they hold under the State governments. Second, there is the perverted ambition of another class who either hope to enrich themselves through the confusion of their country, or flatter themselves with better prospects for advancement if the empire is broken into several partial confederacies rather than united under one government.

1.3.oldText: It is not, however, my plan to dwell on observations of this kind. I am well aware that it would be unfair to dismiss the opposition of any group simply because their position might invite suspicion, treating them all as motivated by self-interest or ambition. Honesty requires us to admit that even such men may act with upright intentions. There is no doubt that much of the opposition that has appeared, or may yet appear, will spring from sources that are at least blameless if not respectable—the honest mistakes of minds led astray by preconceived suspicions and fears. Indeed, the causes that bias judgment are so numerous and so powerful that on many occasions we see wise and good people on the wrong as well as the right side of questions of the highest importance to society. This fact, properly considered, would teach moderation to those who are utterly convinced they are right in any controversy. Another reason for caution is that we are not always sure that the defenders of truth are guided by purer motives than their opponents. Ambition, greed, personal hostility, party loyalty, and other motives no nobler than these are just as apt to operate in those who support the right side of a question as in those who oppose it. Even without these reasons for moderation, nothing could be more wrongheaded than the intolerant spirit that has always marked political parties. In politics, as in religion, it is equally absurd to try to make converts by fire and sword. Heresies in either field can rarely be cured by persecution.

1.4.oldText: And yet, however just these sentiments may be, we already have ample signs that this debate will follow the pattern of every great national discussion. A torrent of angry and malignant passions will be unleashed. Judging by the conduct of opposing parties, we can expect both sides to try to prove the rightness of their views, and to win converts, through the loudness of their declamations and the bitterness of their attacks. An enlightened concern for the energy and effectiveness of government will be branded as the offspring of a temperament that loves despotic power and hates liberty. Excessive anxiety about danger to the rights of the people—which is more often a fault of the head than of the heart—will be portrayed as mere pretense and trickery, the stale bait of popularity at the expense of the public good. On one hand, it will be forgotten that suspicion is the usual companion of love, and that a noble enthusiasm for liberty is liable to be infected with a narrow and illiberal distrust. On the other hand, it will be equally forgotten that the vigor of government is essential to the security of liberty; that, in the eyes of sound and well-informed judgment, their interests can never be separated; and that a dangerous ambition more often hides behind the plausible mask of zeal for the rights of the people than under the suspect appearance of zeal for firm and effective government. History will teach us that the first has been a far surer road to despotism than the second, and that of those who have overturned the liberties of republics, most began their careers by paying obsequious court to the people—starting as demagogues and ending as tyrants.

1.5.oldText: In the course of the preceding remarks, my fellow citizens, I have aimed to put you on guard against any attempts, from any quarter, to influence your decision on a matter of the utmost importance to your welfare by anything other than the evidence of truth. You will, no doubt, also have gathered from the general drift of these remarks that they come from a source not unfriendly to the new Constitution. Yes, my countrymen, I admit to you that, after careful consideration, I am clearly of the opinion that it is in your interest to adopt it. I am convinced that this is the safest course for your liberty, your dignity, and your happiness. I do not pretend to reservations I do not feel. I will not entertain you with the appearance of weighing the matter when I have already decided. I frankly tell you my convictions, and I will openly lay before you the reasons they rest on. The consciousness of good intentions disdains ambiguity. I will not, however, multiply professions on this point. My motives must remain locked in my own breast. My arguments will be open to all and may be judged by all. They will at least be offered in a spirit that will not disgrace the cause of truth.

1.6.oldText: I propose, in a series of papers, to discuss the following important particulars:

1.7.oldText: THE USEFULNESS OF THE UNION TO YOUR POLITICAL PROSPERITY; THE INADEQUACY OF THE PRESENT CONFEDERATION TO PRESERVE THAT UNION; THE NECESSITY OF A GOVERNMENT AT LEAST AS ENERGETIC AS THE ONE PROPOSED, IN ORDER TO ACHIEVE THIS OBJECT; THE CONFORMITY OF THE PROPOSED CONSTITUTION TO THE TRUE PRINCIPLES OF REPUBLICAN GOVERNMENT; ITS ANALOGY TO YOUR OWN STATE CONSTITUTION; and lastly, THE ADDITIONAL SECURITY THAT ITS ADOPTION WILL PROVIDE FOR THIS FORM OF GOVERNMENT, FOR LIBERTY, AND FOR PROPERTY.

1.8.oldText: As this discussion proceeds, I will try to give a satisfactory answer to all the objections that have appeared and that seem to merit your attention.

1.9.oldText: It may seem unnecessary to argue for the usefulness of the UNION, a point no doubt deeply engraved on the hearts of the great body of people in every State, and one that may be imagined to have no opponents. But the fact is that we already hear it whispered in the private circles of those who oppose the new Constitution: that the thirteen States cover too great an area for any single general system, and that we must inevitably resort to separate confederacies for distinct portions of the whole.(1) This doctrine will, in all probability, be gradually spread until it has enough adherents to support an open declaration of it. For nothing can be clearer, to those who are able to take a broad view of the subject, than the choice between adopting the new Constitution and dismembering the Union. It will therefore be useful to begin by examining the advantages of that Union, the certain evils, and the probable dangers, to which every State will be exposed if it is dissolved. That, accordingly, will be the subject of my next paper.

1.10.oldText: 1. The same idea, traced to its consequences, is put forward in several of the recent publications against the new Constitution.

2.0.oldText: When the people of America reflect that they are now called upon to decide a question whose consequences must prove one of the most important ever to engage their attention, the wisdom of taking a comprehensive and serious view of it will be obvious.

2.1.oldText: Nothing is more certain than the indispensable necessity of government, and it is equally undeniable that whenever and however government is created, the people must give up some of their natural rights in order to vest it with the powers it needs. It is therefore well worth considering whether it would serve the interests of the American people more for them to be, for all general purposes, one nation under one federal government, or to divide themselves into separate confederacies and grant the head of each the same kinds of powers proposed for one national government.

2.2.oldText: Until recently, it has been an accepted and unchallenged opinion that the prosperity of the American people depended on their continuing firmly united, and the wishes, prayers, and efforts of our best and wisest citizens have been steadily directed to that goal. But politicians have now appeared who insist this opinion is mistaken, and that instead of looking for safety and happiness in union, we ought to seek it by dividing the States into separate confederacies or sovereignties. However extraordinary this new doctrine may seem, it has its advocates—and certain figures who once opposed it strongly are now among them. Whatever arguments or inducements have produced this change in the views and statements of these gentlemen, it would not be wise for the people at large to adopt these new political tenets without being fully convinced that they rest on truth and sound policy.

2.3.oldText: It has often given me pleasure to observe that independent America was not made up of detached and distant territories, but that one connected, fertile, wide-spreading country was the inheritance of our western sons of liberty. Providence has, in a special way, blessed it with a variety of soils and products and watered it with countless streams for the delight and convenience of its inhabitants. A succession of navigable waters forms a kind of chain around its borders, as if to bind it together, while the noblest rivers in the world, running at convenient distances, give them highways for the easy exchange of friendly aid and the mutual transport and trade of their various commodities.

2.4.oldText: With equal pleasure I have often noted that Providence has chosen to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs, who, by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war, have nobly established general liberty and independence.

2.5.oldText: This country and this people seem made for each other, and it appears that Providence intended an inheritance so fitting and convenient for a band of brothers, joined by the strongest ties, never to be split into a number of unsocial, jealous, and alien sovereignties.

2.6.oldText: Similar sentiments have until now prevailed among all classes and groups of people among us. For all general purposes we have consistently been one people, each individual citizen everywhere enjoying the same national rights, privileges, and protection. As a nation we have made peace and war; as a nation we have defeated our common enemies; as a nation we have formed alliances, made treaties, and entered into various compacts and conventions with foreign states.

2.7.oldText: A strong sense of the value and blessings of union led the people, very early on, to set up a federal government to preserve and perpetuate it. They formed it almost as soon as they had a political existence—indeed, at a time when their homes were in flames, when many of their citizens were bleeding, and when the progress of war and devastation left little room for the calm and mature inquiry and reflection that must always precede the formation of a wise and well-balanced government for a free people. It is no surprise that a government created in such unfavorable times should, on trial, prove greatly deficient and inadequate to the purpose it was meant to serve.

2.8.oldText: This intelligent people perceived these defects and regretted them. Still as attached to union as they were enamored of liberty, they observed the danger immediately threatening the former and more remotely threatening the latter. Persuaded that ample security for both could only be found in a national government more wisely framed, they, as with one voice, called the recent convention at Philadelphia to take that important subject under consideration.

2.9.oldText: This convention was made up of men who possessed the confidence of the people, many of whom had become highly distinguished by their patriotism, virtue, and wisdom in times that tried the minds and hearts of men. They undertook the difficult task. In the mild season of peace, with minds free of other concerns, they spent many months in cool, uninterrupted, daily consultation. Finally, without being intimidated by power or moved by any passions except love for their country, they presented and recommended to the people the plan produced by their joint and very unanimous deliberations.

2.10.oldText: Admit, as is the fact, that this plan is only RECOMMENDED, not imposed. Yet remember that it is recommended neither for BLIND approval nor for BLIND rejection, but for the calm and candid consideration that the size and importance of the subject demand and ought to receive. But this (as was noted in the previous paper of this series) is more to be wished than expected—that it will actually be considered and examined that way. Past experience teaches us not to be too hopeful in such expectations. It is not yet forgotten that well-grounded fears of imminent danger led the American people to form the memorable Congress of 1774. That body recommended certain measures to its constituents, and events proved their wisdom; yet it is fresh in our memories how soon the press began to teem with pamphlets and weekly papers attacking those very measures. Not only did many government officials, who obeyed personal interest, work tirelessly against them, but so did others—from a mistaken sense of consequences, from undue influence of old loyalties, or from ambition aimed at goals not aligned with the public good. Many were indeed deceived and misled, but the great majority of the people reasoned and decided wisely; and they are happy now to reflect that they did so.

2.11.oldText: They considered that the Congress was made up of many wise and experienced men. That, gathered from different parts of the country, they brought with them and shared a variety of useful information. That, during the time they spent together inquiring into and discussing the true interests of their country, they must have acquired very accurate knowledge on that score. That they personally had a stake in the public liberty and prosperity, and that it was therefore as much their inclination as their duty to recommend only such measures as they truly thought prudent and advisable, after the most mature deliberation.

2.12.oldText: These and similar considerations led the people to rely heavily on the judgment and integrity of the Congress, and they took its advice in spite of the various tricks and efforts used to discourage them. But if the people at large had reason to trust the men of that Congress—few of whom had been fully tested or generally known—they have still greater reason now to respect the judgment and advice of the convention. For it is well known that some of the most distinguished members of that earlier Congress, since tested and justly approved for their patriotism and abilities, who have grown old in the gathering of political experience, were also members of this convention and brought into it their accumulated knowledge and experience.

2.13.oldText: It is worth remarking that not only the first, but every subsequent Congress, as well as the recent convention, has invariably joined with the people in believing that the prosperity of America depended on its Union. To preserve and perpetuate it was the great object of the people in forming that convention, and it is also the great object of the plan the convention has recommended for adoption. With what justification, then, or for what good purpose, are some men at this particular moment trying to belittle the importance of the Union? Or why is it suggested that three or four confederacies would be better than one? I am persuaded in my own mind that the people have always thought rightly on this subject, and that their universal and uniform attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I will try to develop and explain in some of the papers to follow. Those who promote the idea of substituting a number of separate confederacies for the plan of the convention seem clearly to foresee that rejecting it would put the continuance of the Union in the utmost jeopardy. That would certainly be the case, and I sincerely wish every good citizen could see just as clearly that, whenever the dissolution of the Union arrives, America will have reason to exclaim, in the words of the poet: "FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS."

3.0.oldText: It is not a new observation that the people of any country—if, like the Americans, they are intelligent and well-informed—rarely adopt and steadily hold an erroneous opinion about their interests for many years. That fact naturally creates great respect for the high regard the American people have so long and uniformly held for the importance of remaining firmly united under one federal government, equipped with sufficient powers for all general and national purposes.

3.1.oldText: The more carefully I consider and investigate the reasons that seem to have given rise to this opinion, the more convinced I become that they are sound and conclusive.

3.2.oldText: Among the many concerns to which a wise and free people must direct their attention, providing for their SAFETY seems to be the first. The SAFETY of the people relates to a great variety of circumstances and considerations, and therefore allows great latitude to those who wish to define it precisely and comprehensively.

3.3.oldText: For the moment, I mean to consider it only as it relates to the preservation of peace and tranquility, both against dangers from FOREIGN ARMS AND INFLUENCE and against dangers of the LIKE KIND arising from domestic causes. Since the former comes first in order, it is fitting to discuss it first. Let us therefore examine whether the people are not right in their opinion that a cordial Union, under an effective national government, gives them the best security that can be devised against HOSTILITIES from abroad.

3.4.oldText: The number of wars that have happened or will happen in the world will always be in proportion to the number and weight of the causes—whether REAL or PRETENDED—that PROVOKE or INVITE them. If this remark is correct, it becomes useful to ask whether so many JUST causes of war are likely to be given by UNITED AMERICA as by DISUNITED America. For if it turns out that United America will probably give the fewest, then in this respect Union most tends to keep the people at peace with other nations.

3.5.oldText: JUST causes of war, for the most part, arise either from violations of treaties or from direct violence. America has already formed treaties with no fewer than six foreign nations, and all of them, except Prussia, are maritime powers and therefore able to harass and injure us. She also has extensive commerce with Portugal, Spain, and Britain, and with the latter two we must additionally take into account the fact that they are neighbors.

3.6.oldText: It is of high importance to the peace of America that she observe the laws of nations toward all these powers, and to me it seems clear this will be more perfectly and punctually done by one national government than it could be either by thirteen separate States or by three or four distinct confederacies.

3.7.oldText: Because once an effective national government is established, the best men in the country will not only consent to serve, but will generally be appointed to manage it. For although town, county, or other narrow influence may place men in State assemblies, senates, courts, or executive offices, a more general and extensive reputation for talent and other qualifications will be necessary to recommend men to offices under the national government—especially as it will have the widest field for choice and never face that shortage of suitable people which is not uncommon in some of the States. Hence the administration, the political counsels, and the judicial decisions of the national government will be wiser, more systematic, and more judicious than those of individual States, and consequently more satisfactory in dealings with other nations, as well as more SAFE for us.

3.8.oldText: Because, under the national government, treaties and articles of treaties, as well as the laws of nations, will always be interpreted in one sense and executed in the same way—whereas rulings on the same points and questions, in thirteen States or in three or four confederacies, will not always agree or be consistent. This will follow both from the variety of independent courts and judges appointed by different and independent governments, and from the different local laws and interests that may affect and influence them. The wisdom of the convention, in committing such questions to the jurisdiction and judgment of courts appointed by, and answerable only to, one national government, cannot be too highly praised.

3.9.oldText: Because the prospect of immediate loss or gain may often tempt the governing party in one or two States to depart from good faith and justice. But those temptations, not reaching the other States and therefore having little or no influence on the national government, will fail, and good faith and justice will be preserved. The case of the treaty of peace with Britain adds great weight to this reasoning.

3.10.oldText: Because, even if the governing party in a State should be willing to resist such temptations, those temptations may, and commonly do, result from circumstances peculiar to the State and may affect a great number of its inhabitants. The governing party may not always be able, even if willing, to prevent the planned injustice or to punish the offenders. But the national government, not being affected by such local circumstances, will neither be tempted to commit the wrong itself, nor lack the power or willingness to prevent or punish its commission by others.

3.11.oldText: So far, then, as either deliberate or accidental violations of treaties and the laws of nations provide JUST causes of war, they are less to be feared under one general government than under several smaller ones, and in that respect the former most favors the SAFETY of the people.

3.12.oldText: As for those just causes of war that arise from direct and unlawful violence, it seems equally clear to me that one good national government provides far more security against dangers of that kind than can come from any other source.

3.13.oldText: Because such acts of violence are more often caused by the passions and interests of a part than of the whole; of one or two States than of the Union. Not a single Indian war has yet been caused by the aggressions of the present federal government, weak as it is. But there are several instances of Indian hostilities provoked by the improper conduct of individual States, who—either unable or unwilling to restrain or punish offenses—have given occasion for the slaughter of many innocent inhabitants.

3.14.oldText: The proximity of Spanish and British territories, bordering some States and not others, naturally confines the causes of quarrel more directly to the borderers. The bordering States, if any, will be the ones who, under the impulse of sudden irritation and a quick sense of apparent interest or injury, will be most likely to provoke war with these nations through direct violence. Nothing can so effectively prevent that danger as a national government, whose wisdom and prudence will not be diminished by the passions that drive the parties immediately involved.

3.15.oldText: But the national government will not only give fewer just causes of war; it will also be better able to settle them amicably. It will be more temperate and cool, and in that respect, as well as in others, will be more capable of acting deliberately than the offending State. The pride of states, like that of men, naturally disposes them to justify all their actions and resists their acknowledging, correcting, or repairing their errors and offenses. The national government, in such cases, will not be affected by this pride, but will proceed with moderation and candor to consider and decide on the means most fitting to extricate them from the difficulties that threaten them.

3.16.oldText: Besides, it is well known that acknowledgments, explanations, and compensations are often accepted as satisfactory from a strong, united nation, while they would be rejected as unsatisfactory if offered by a State or confederacy of little weight or power.

3.17.oldText: In 1685, the state of Genoa, having offended Louis XIV, tried to appease him. He demanded that they send their Doge, or chief magistrate, accompanied by four of their senators, to FRANCE to ask his pardon and receive his terms. They were forced to comply for the sake of peace. Would he, on any occasion, either have demanded or have accepted such humiliation from Spain, Britain, or any other POWERFUL nation?

4.0.oldText: My last paper gave several reasons why the safety of the people would be best secured by union against the danger that may come from JUST causes of war given to other nations. Those reasons show that such causes would not only be given more rarely, but would also be more easily settled, by a national government than by either the State governments or the proposed small confederacies.

4.1.oldText: But the safety of the people of America against dangers from FOREIGN force depends not only on their refraining from giving JUST causes of war to other nations, but also on placing and keeping themselves in a position that does not INVITE hostility or insult. For it hardly needs to be said that there are PRETENDED as well as just causes of war.

4.2.oldText: It is too true, however shameful to human nature, that nations in general will make war whenever they see a prospect of gaining anything by it. Indeed, absolute monarchs will often make war when their nations stand to gain nothing—pursuing purely personal aims such as thirst for military glory, revenge for personal insults, ambition, or private agreements to enrich or support their particular families or partisans. These and various other motives, which affect only the mind of the sovereign, often lead him into wars not justified by justice or by the voice and interests of his people. But, apart from these inducements to war—which are more common in absolute monarchies, though they well deserve our attention—there are others that affect nations as often as kings, and some of them, on examination, will be found to grow out of our particular situation and circumstances.

4.3.oldText: With France and Britain we are rivals in the fisheries, and we can supply their markets more cheaply than they can themselves, despite any efforts to prevent it through bounties on their own fish or duties on foreign fish.

4.4.oldText: With them and with most other European nations we are rivals in shipping and the carrying trade. We will deceive ourselves if we suppose any of them will rejoice to see it flourish. For since our carrying trade cannot grow without to some degree shrinking theirs, it is more in their interest, and will be more their policy, to restrict it than to promote it.

4.5.oldText: In the trade with China and India, we interfere with more than one nation, since it allows us to share advantages they had largely monopolized, and since we thereby supply ourselves with goods we used to buy from them.

4.6.oldText: The expansion of our own commerce in our own ships cannot please any nations that hold territories on or near this continent. The cheapness and excellence of our products, combined with our nearness, the enterprise and skill of our merchants and navigators, will give us a greater share in the advantages those territories afford than the wishes or policies of their respective sovereigns will allow.

4.7.oldText: Spain finds it convenient to close the Mississippi against us on one side, and Britain shuts us out from the Saint Lawrence on the other. Neither will permit the other waters between them and us to become channels for mutual exchange and trade.

4.8.oldText: The people of America are aware that motives for war may arise from these circumstances, as well as from others not yet so obvious; and that whenever such motives find the right time and opportunity, pretexts to color and justify them will not be lacking. Wisely, therefore, do they consider union and a good national government as necessary to put and keep them in SUCH A SITUATION as will tend to repress and discourage war rather than INVITE it. That situation consists in the best possible state of defense, and necessarily depends on the government, the arms, and the resources of the country.

4.9.oldText: Since the safety of the whole is the interest of the whole, and cannot be provided for without government, whether one or several or many, let us inquire whether one good government is not, with respect to the matter at hand, more capable than any other given number whatever.

4.10.oldText: One government can collect and use the talents and experience of the ablest men, wherever in the Union they may be found. It can act on uniform principles of policy. It can harmonize, integrate, and protect its various parts and members, and extend the benefit of its foresight and precautions to each. In forming treaties, it will consider the interest of the whole and the particular interests of the parts as connected with that of the whole. It can apply the resources and power of the whole to the defense of any particular part, and do so more easily and quickly than State governments or separate confederacies could possibly do, given their lack of coordination and unity. It can place the militia under one plan of discipline, and by putting their officers in proper subordination to the Chief Magistrate, will, in effect, consolidate them into one corps, making them more effective than if divided into thirteen, or into three or four distinct, independent companies.

4.11.oldText: What would the militia of Britain be if the English militia obeyed the government of England, the Scottish militia obeyed the government of Scotland, and the Welsh militia obeyed the government of Wales? Suppose an invasion: would those three governments, even if they agreed at all, be able with all their forces to act against the enemy as effectively as the single government of Great Britain?

4.12.oldText: We have heard much of the fleets of Britain, and the time may come, if we are wise, when the fleets of America may attract attention. But if one national government had not so regulated the navigation of Britain as to make it a nursery for seamen—if one national government had not summoned all the national means and materials for forming fleets—their power and their thunder would never have been celebrated. Let England have its navigation and fleet; let Scotland have its navigation and fleet; let Wales have its navigation and fleet; let Ireland have its navigation and fleet; let those four constituent parts of the British empire be under four independent governments, and it is easy to see how soon each would shrink into comparative insignificance.

4.13.oldText: Apply these facts to our own case. Leave America divided into thirteen, or, if you prefer, into three or four independent governments—what armies could they raise and pay? What fleets could they ever hope to have? If one were attacked, would the others fly to its rescue and spend their blood and money in its defense? Would there be no danger of their being flattered into neutrality by its plausible promises, or seduced by too great a love of peace into refusing to risk their tranquility and present safety for the sake of neighbors of whom they have perhaps been jealous, and whose importance they are content to see diminished? Such conduct would not be wise, but it would be natural. The history of the states of Greece, and of other countries, abounds with such examples, and it is not unlikely that what has so often happened would, under similar circumstances, happen again.

4.14.oldText: But suppose they were willing to help the invaded State or confederacy. How, when, and in what proportion would aid in men and money be provided? Who would command the allied armies, and from which of them would he take his orders? Who would settle the terms of peace, and in case of disputes what umpire would decide between them and force compliance? Various difficulties and inconveniences would be inseparable from such a situation; whereas one government, watching over the general and common interests, and combining and directing the powers and resources of the whole, would be free of all these embarrassments and would do far more for the safety of the people.

4.15.oldText: But whatever our situation—whether firmly united under one national government, or split into a number of confederacies—it is certain that foreign nations will know and view it exactly as it is, and will act toward us accordingly. If they see that our national government is effective and well administered, our trade prudently regulated, our militia properly organized and disciplined, our resources and finances discreetly managed, our credit re-established, our people free, content, and united, they will be far more inclined to cultivate our friendship than to provoke our resentment. If, on the other hand, they find us either lacking an effective government (each State doing right or wrong as its rulers find convenient), or split into three or four independent and probably discordant republics or confederacies—one inclining to Britain, another to France, and a third to Spain, and perhaps played off against one another by all three—what a poor, pitiful figure will America cut in their eyes! How exposed she would become not only to their contempt but to their abuse, and how soon would dear-bought experience proclaim that when a people or family so divides, it never fails to be against itself.

5.0.oldText: Queen Anne, in her letter of July 1, 1706, to the Scottish Parliament, makes some observations on the importance of the UNION then being formed between England and Scotland that deserve our attention. I will share with the public one or two extracts: "An entire and perfect union will be the solid foundation of lasting peace: It will secure your religion, liberty, and property; remove the animosities among yourselves, and the jealousies and differences between our two kingdoms. It must increase your strength, riches, and trade; and by this union the whole island, being joined in affection and free from all apprehensions of different interest, will be ENABLED TO RESIST ALL ITS ENEMIES." "We most earnestly recommend to you calmness and unanimity in this great and weighty affair, that the union may be brought to a happy conclusion, being the only EFFECTUAL way to secure our present and future happiness, and disappoint the designs of our and your enemies, who will doubtless, on this occasion, USE THEIR UTMOST ENDEAVORS TO PREVENT OR DELAY THIS UNION."

5.1.oldText: It was noted in the previous paper that weakness and divisions at home would invite dangers from abroad, and that nothing would do more to secure us from them than union, strength, and good government within ourselves. This subject is rich and cannot easily be exhausted.

5.2.oldText: The history of Great Britain is the one with which we are generally best acquainted, and it offers us many useful lessons. We may profit from their experience without paying the price it cost them. Although it seems obvious to common sense that the people of such an island should be only one nation, we find that they were for ages divided into three, and that those three were almost constantly embroiled in quarrels and wars with one another. Despite the fact that their true interests with respect to the continental nations were really the same, the arts, policies, and practices of those nations kept their mutual jealousies perpetually inflamed, and for a long series of years they were far more inconvenient and troublesome than they were useful or helpful to each other.

5.3.oldText: Should the people of America divide themselves into three or four nations, would not the same thing happen? Would not similar jealousies arise and be likewise nurtured? Instead of being "joined in affection" and free from all apprehension of different "interests," envy and jealousy would soon extinguish confidence and affection, and the partial interests of each confederacy, rather than the general interests of all America, would be the only objects of their policies and pursuits. Hence, like most other BORDERING nations, they would always be either embroiled in disputes and war, or living in constant fear of them.

5.4.oldText: The most enthusiastic advocates of three or four confederacies cannot reasonably suppose they would long remain on equal footing in strength, even if it were possible to form them so at first. But, granting that this were practicable, what human contrivance can secure the continuance of such equality? Apart from local circumstances that tend to generate and increase power in one part and to impede its progress in another, we must consider the effects of that superior policy and good management which would probably distinguish the government of one above the rest, and by which their relative equality in strength and standing would be destroyed. For it cannot be assumed that the same degree of sound policy, prudence, and foresight would uniformly be observed by each of these confederacies for a long succession of years.

5.5.oldText: Whenever, and from whatever causes, it might happen—and happen it would—that one of these nations or confederacies should rise on the scale of political importance well above her neighbors, that moment those neighbors would view her with envy and fear. Both passions would lead them to encourage, if not actively promote, whatever might reduce her importance, and would also restrain them from measures intended to advance or even to secure her prosperity. It would not take much time for her to discern these unfriendly attitudes. She would soon begin not only to lose confidence in her neighbors, but also to feel a disposition equally unfavorable toward them. Distrust naturally creates distrust, and nothing more quickly turns goodwill and kind conduct into hostility than invidious jealousies and unfair imputations, whether spoken or implied.

5.6.oldText: The North is generally the region of strength, and many local circumstances make it likely that the most Northern of the proposed confederacies would, at no distant time, be unquestionably more formidable than any of the others. No sooner would this become evident than the NORTHERN HIVE would arouse the same ideas and feelings in the more southern parts of America that it formerly did in the southern parts of Europe. Nor is it a rash conjecture that its young swarms might often be tempted to gather honey in the more blooming fields and milder air of their luxurious and more delicate neighbors.

5.7.oldText: Those who carefully study the history of similar divisions and confederacies will find ample reason to fear that the ones being contemplated would be neighbors only in the sense that they would border one another; that they would neither love nor trust each other, but on the contrary would be a prey to discord, jealousy, and mutual injuries. In short, they would place us exactly in the position in which some nations doubtless wish to see us—FORMIDABLE ONLY TO EACH OTHER.

5.8.oldText: When did the independent states into which Britain and Spain were formerly divided ever combine in such alliance, or unite their forces against a foreign enemy? The proposed confederacies will be DISTINCT NATIONS. Each would have to regulate its commerce with foreigners through separate treaties; and since their products and commodities are different and suited to different markets, those treaties would be essentially different. Different commercial concerns must create different interests, and so different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations. Hence it might, and probably would, happen that the foreign nation with whom the SOUTHERN confederacy was at war would be the one with whom the NORTHERN confederacy most wished to preserve peace and friendship. An alliance so contrary to their immediate interest would not therefore be easy to form, nor, if formed, would it be observed and fulfilled with perfect good faith.

5.9.oldText: Indeed, it is far more probable that in America, as in Europe, neighboring nations, acting under the impulse of opposite interests and unfriendly passions, would frequently take different sides. Considering our distance from Europe, it would be more natural for these confederacies to fear danger from one another than from distant nations, and therefore that each of them would be more eager to guard against the others through foreign alliances than to guard against foreign dangers through alliances among themselves. And here let us not forget how much easier it is to receive foreign fleets into our ports and foreign armies into our country than it is to persuade or compel them to leave. How many conquests did the Romans and others make in the role of allies, and what changes did they introduce, under that same role, into the governments of those they pretended to protect.

5.10.oldText: Let candid men judge, then, whether dividing America into any given number of independent sovereignties would tend to secure us against the hostilities and improper interference of foreign nations.

6.0.oldText: The three previous papers have been devoted to enumerating the dangers we would face, in a state of disunion, from the arms and arts of foreign nations. I will now turn to dangers of a different and perhaps still more alarming kind—those that will in all probability flow from disputes between the States themselves, and from domestic factions and upheavals. These have already been touched on in some places; but they deserve fuller and more particular investigation.

6.1.oldText: A man must be far gone in utopian speculations who can seriously doubt that, if these States were either wholly disunited or only united in partial confederacies, the subdivisions into which they might be thrown would have frequent and violent conflicts with one another. To assume there are no motives for such conflicts, and to use that as an argument against their occurrence, would be to forget that men are ambitious, vindictive, and rapacious. To expect continued harmony among a number of independent, unconnected sovereignties in the same neighborhood would be to ignore the uniform course of human events and defy the accumulated experience of the ages.

6.2.oldText: The causes of hostility among nations are countless. Some operate broadly and almost constantly on the collective bodies of society. Of this kind are the love of power, or the desire of pre-eminence and dominion; and the jealousy of power, or the desire of equality and safety. Others have a more limited but equally active influence within their spheres. Such are the rivalries and competitions of commerce among commercial nations. And still others, no less numerous than the former, originate entirely in private passions—in the attachments, enmities, interests, hopes, and fears of leading individuals in the communities they belong to. Men of this class, whether favorites of a king or of a people, have in too many instances abused the confidence placed in them, and, claiming some public motive as a pretext, have not hesitated to sacrifice national tranquility to personal advantage or personal gratification.

6.3.oldText: The famous Pericles, in deference to the resentment of a prostitute,(1) attacked, defeated, and destroyed the city of the SAMIANS at the cost of much blood and treasure of his countrymen. The same man, driven by private spite against the MEGARIANS,(2) another nation of Greece—or to escape a prosecution with which he was threatened as accomplice in a supposed theft by the sculptor Phidias,(3) or to dodge accusations being prepared against him for squandering state funds in the purchase of popularity,(4) or by some combination of all these causes—was the original author of that famous and fatal war known in Grecian annals as the PELOPONNESIAN war, which, after various reverses, pauses, and renewals, ended in the ruin of the Athenian commonwealth.

6.4.oldText: The ambitious cardinal who was prime minister to Henry VIII, allowing his vanity to aspire to the triple crown,(5) hoped to win that splendid prize through the influence of the Emperor Charles V. To secure the favor and interest of this enterprising and powerful monarch, he plunged England into a war with France, contrary to the plainest dictates of policy and at the risk of the safety and independence not only of the kingdom he ruled by his counsels but of Europe in general. For if there ever was a sovereign who came near to realizing the project of universal monarchy, it was the Emperor Charles V, of whose intrigues Wolsey was at once the instrument and the dupe.

6.5.oldText: The influence which the bigotry of one woman,(6) the petulance of another,(7) and the cabals of a third(8) had on the contemporary policy, ferments, and pacifications of a considerable part of Europe are subjects too often discussed not to be generally known.

6.6.oldText: To multiply examples of the agency of personal considerations in producing great national events—whether foreign or domestic, depending on their direction—would be a needless waste of time. Those who have even a superficial acquaintance with the sources from which they may be drawn will themselves recall a variety of instances; and those who have a tolerable knowledge of human nature will not need such evidence to form their opinion either of the reality or the extent of that agency. Still, a reference illustrating the general principle may fittingly be made to a case that has lately occurred among ourselves. If Shays had not been a DESPERATE DEBTOR, it is much to be doubted whether Massachusetts would have been plunged into a civil war.

6.7.oldText: But notwithstanding the concurring testimony of experience on this point, there are still to be found visionary or designing men ready to advocate the paradox of perpetual peace among the States, even though dismembered and alienated from each other. The genius of republics (they say) is peaceful; the spirit of commerce tends to soften men's manners and to extinguish those inflammable humors that have so often kindled into wars. Commercial republics, like ours, will never be inclined to waste themselves in ruinous quarrels with each other. They will be governed by mutual interest and will cultivate a spirit of mutual amity and concord.

6.8.oldText: Is it not (we may ask these political projectors) the true interest of all nations to cultivate the same benevolent and philosophic spirit? If this is their true interest, have they in fact pursued it? Has it not, on the contrary, invariably been found that momentary passions and immediate interest exercise a more active and imperious control over human conduct than general or remote considerations of policy, utility, or justice? Have republics in practice been less addicted to war than monarchies? Are the former not administered by MEN as well as the latter? Are there not aversions, preferences, rivalries, and desires for unjust acquisitions that affect nations as well as kings? Are popular assemblies not frequently subject to impulses of rage, resentment, jealousy, greed, and other irregular and violent propensities? Is it not well known that their decisions are often governed by a few individuals in whom they place confidence, and are therefore liable to be tinged by the passions and views of those individuals? Has commerce so far done anything more than change the objects of war? Is the love of wealth not as domineering and enterprising a passion as that of power or glory? Have there not been as many wars founded upon commercial motives, since commerce became the prevailing system of nations, as were before caused by the lust for territory or dominion? Has the spirit of commerce not, in many instances, supplied new incentives to both these appetites? Let experience, the least fallible guide of human opinion, be appealed to for an answer to these questions.

6.9.oldText: Sparta, Athens, Rome, and Carthage were all republics; two of them, Athens and Carthage, were of the commercial kind. Yet they were as often engaged in wars, offensive and defensive, as the neighboring monarchies of the same times. Sparta was little more than a well-regulated camp; and Rome was never sated of carnage and conquest.

6.10.oldText: Carthage, though a commercial republic, was the aggressor in the very war that ended in her destruction. Hannibal had carried her arms into the heart of Italy and to the gates of Rome before Scipio, in turn, defeated him in the territories of Carthage and made a conquest of the commonwealth.

6.11.oldText: Venice, in later times, figured more than once in wars of ambition, until, becoming a target for the other Italian states, Pope Julius II found means to forge that formidable league(9) which dealt a deadly blow to the power and pride of this haughty republic.

6.12.oldText: The provinces of Holland, until they were overwhelmed by debt and taxes, took a leading and conspicuous part in the wars of Europe. They had furious contests with England for dominion of the sea, and were among the most persistent and implacable opponents of Louis XIV.

6.13.oldText: In the government of Britain, the representatives of the people make up one branch of the national legislature. Commerce has for ages been the predominant pursuit of that country. Yet few nations have been more frequently engaged in war, and many of the wars in which that kingdom has been engaged have proceeded from the people.

6.14.oldText: There have been, if I may put it this way, almost as many popular as royal wars. The cries of the nation and the demands of their representatives have, on various occasions, dragged their monarchs into war or kept them in it, contrary to their inclinations and sometimes contrary to the real interests of the State. In that memorable struggle for supremacy between the rival houses of AUSTRIA and BOURBON, which so long kept Europe in flames, it is well known that the antipathies of the English against the French, supporting the ambition—or rather the avarice—of a favorite leader,(10) prolonged the war beyond the limits set by sound policy, and for a considerable time in opposition to the views of the court.

6.15.oldText: The wars of these two last-mentioned nations have largely grown out of commercial concerns: the desire to supplant and the fear of being supplanted, either in particular branches of trade or in the general advantages of trade and navigation, and sometimes even the more culpable desire of sharing in the commerce of other nations without their consent.

6.16.oldText: The most recent war between Britain and Spain sprang from the British merchants' attempts to carry on illicit trade with the Spanish main. These unjustifiable practices on their side produced harshness on the Spanish side toward British subjects—harshness no more justifiable, since it exceeded the bounds of just retaliation and was chargeable with inhumanity and cruelty. Many of the English who were captured on the Spanish coast were sent to dig in the mines of Potosi; and by the usual progress of a spirit of resentment, the innocent were after a while lumped in with the guilty in indiscriminate punishment. The complaints of the merchants kindled a violent flame throughout the nation, which soon broke out in the House of Commons and was passed from there to the ministry. Letters of reprisal were issued, and a war ensued that, in its consequences, overthrew all the alliances which only twenty years before had been formed with sanguine expectations of the most beneficial fruits.

6.17.oldText: From this summary of what has happened in other countries whose situations have most closely resembled our own, what reason can we have to trust those reveries that would seduce us into expecting peace and cordiality between the members of the present confederacy in a state of separation? Have we not already seen enough of the falsity and extravagance of those idle theories that have amused us with promises of exemption from the imperfections, weaknesses, and evils inherent in society in every form? Is it not time to wake from the deceitful dream of a golden age and to adopt as a practical maxim, for the direction of our political conduct, that we, like the other inhabitants of the globe, are still far from the happy realm of perfect wisdom and perfect virtue?

6.18.oldText: Let the extreme low point to which our national dignity and credit have sunk, the inconveniences felt everywhere from a lax and ill administration of government, the revolt of part of the State of North Carolina, the recent menacing disturbances in Pennsylvania, and the actual insurrections and rebellions in Massachusetts—let all these declare!

6.19.oldText: So far is the general sense of mankind from agreeing with the doctrines of those who try to lull our fears of discord and hostility between the States, in the event of disunion, that long observation of the progress of society has made it a sort of political axiom that proximity, or nearness of situation, makes nations natural enemies. An intelligent writer expresses himself on this subject to the following effect: "NEIGHBORING NATIONS (says he) are naturally enemies of each other unless their common weakness forces them to league in a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC, and their constitution prevents the differences that neighborhood occasions, extinguishing that secret jealousy which disposes all states to aggrandize themselves at the expense of their neighbors."(11) This passage at once points out the EVIL and suggests the REMEDY.

6.26.oldText: 9. The League of Cambray, comprising the Emperor, the King of France, the King of Aragon, and most of the Italian princes and states.

6.28.oldText: 11. See "Principes des Negociations" by l'Abbé de Mably.

7.0.oldText: People sometimes ask, with an air of triumph, what reasons the States would have to make war on each other if they were disunited. A complete answer would be: precisely the same reasons that have, at various times, drowned all the nations of the world in blood. But unfortunately for us, the question allows a more specific answer. There are causes of conflict already in plain view, and we have enough experience—even under the restraints of a federal constitution—to judge what we could expect if those restraints were removed.

7.1.oldText: Territorial disputes have always been one of the most fertile sources of hostility among nations. Probably the largest share of wars that have devastated the earth have sprung from this cause. The same cause would exist among us in full force. We have a vast tract of unsettled territory within the boundaries of the United States. Several States already have rival, unresolved claims, and dissolving the Union would lay the foundation for similar claims among all of them. They have already had serious and heated arguments about the rights to lands that were ungranted at the time of the Revolution—usually called the crown lands. The States within whose colonial governments those lands fell have claimed them as their property. The other States have argued that the rights of the crown in this matter passed to the Union—especially as to all the western territory which, by actual possession or by submission of the Indian proprietors, fell under the jurisdiction of the king of Great Britain until it was surrendered in the peace treaty. That, it has been said, was in any case an acquisition by the Confederacy through compact with a foreign power. Congress has prudently tried to defuse this controversy by persuading the States to cede such lands to the United States for the benefit of all. Under a continuing Union, this approach has gone far enough to make a peaceful end of the dispute likely. But breaking up the Confederacy would revive this dispute and create others on the same subject. At present, much of the vacant western territory is, by cession at least—if not by any prior right—the common property of the Union. If the Union ended, the States that made the cessions on a federal compromise would likely reclaim those lands as a reversion, since the reason for the grant would have ceased. The other States would surely insist on a share, by right of representation. Their argument would be that a grant once made cannot be revoked, and that the justice of sharing in territory acquired or secured by the joint efforts of the Confederacy remained intact. Even if every State improbably agreed that each had a right to a share of this common stock, the question of a fair rule of apportionment would still be a hurdle. Different States would propose different principles, and since these would clash with the opposing interests of the parties, peaceful adjustment might not come easily.

7.2.oldText: In the broad field of western territory, then, we see plenty of room for hostile claims, with no umpire or common judge to step between the contending parties. Reasoning from the past to the future, we have good reason to fear that the sword would sometimes be appealed to as the arbiter of their differences. The dispute between Connecticut and Pennsylvania over the land at Wyoming warns us not to be optimistic about easy settlements of such disagreements. The Articles of Confederation required the parties to submit the matter to a federal court. The submission was made, and the court ruled in favor of Pennsylvania. But Connecticut showed strong signs of dissatisfaction with that ruling, and she did not seem fully reconciled to it until something like compensation for her supposed loss was found through negotiation. Nothing here is meant to cast even the slightest blame on that State. She no doubt sincerely believed she had been wronged by the decision, and States, like individuals, accept rulings against their own interests only with great reluctance.

7.3.oldText: Those who saw the inside of the controversy between this State and the district of Vermont can confirm the opposition we faced—from States with no stake in the claim as well as those that had one—and can testify to the danger our Confederacy's peace might have run if this State had tried to assert its rights by force. Two motives drove that opposition. One was a wariness of our future power. The other was the interest of certain influential individuals in the neighboring States, who had obtained land grants under the actual government of that district. Even the States that brought forward their own claims against ours seemed more eager to dismember this State than to make good their own pretensions. These were New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. New Jersey and Rhode Island, on every occasion, showed warm zeal for Vermont's independence. Maryland did the same, until alarmed by signs of a connection between Canada and that State. As small States, they viewed the prospect of our growing greatness with an unfriendly eye. Reviewing these episodes, we can trace some of the causes that would likely embroil the States with each other if they had the misfortune to become disunited.

7.4.oldText: Commercial competition would be another fertile source of conflict. The States with less favorable circumstances would seek to escape the disadvantages of their location and share in the advantages of their luckier neighbors. Each State, or separate confederacy, would pursue its own commercial policy. This would create distinctions, preferences, and exclusions, and these would breed discontent. The habits of trade on equal terms, which we have known since the country was first settled, would sharpen these grievances even more than they would have on their own. WE WOULD BE QUICK TO LABEL AS INJURIES WHAT WERE REALLY THE LEGITIMATE ACTS OF INDEPENDENT SOVEREIGNTIES PURSUING THEIR OWN INTERESTS. The spirit of enterprise that marks America's commercial class has never let an opportunity go unused. It is unlikely that this unbridled spirit would respect the trade regulations by which particular States might try to secure exclusive benefits for their own citizens. Violations of these regulations on one side, and the efforts to prevent and punish them on the other, would naturally lead to outrages, then to reprisals, then to wars.

7.5.oldText: The chances some States would have to make others tributary through commercial regulations would be borne with impatience by the tributary States. The relative situation of New York, Connecticut, and New Jersey would be a clear example. New York, needing revenue, must impose duties on her imports. A large share of those duties must be paid by the inhabitants of the two other States as consumers of what we import. New York would not be willing or able to give up this advantage. Her citizens would not agree to refund a duty they had paid in favor of the citizens of her neighbors. Even if they wanted to, it would be impractical to distinguish those customers in our own markets. Would Connecticut and New Jersey long submit to being taxed by New York for her exclusive benefit? Should we be allowed to keep undisturbed possession of a metropolis whose advantage was so odious to our neighbors and, in their view, so oppressive? Could we hold it against the weight of Connecticut on one side and the cooperating pressure of New Jersey on the other? Only recklessness would answer these questions yes.

7.6.oldText: The Union's public debt would be another cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies. Both the initial apportionment and the gradual paying-off afterward would breed ill humor and resentment. How could the States ever agree on a rule of apportionment that satisfied everyone? Hardly any rule that could be proposed is entirely free of real objections. As usual, those objections would be magnified by the opposing interests of the parties. The States even disagree on the general principle of paying off the public debt. Some, either less impressed by the importance of national credit or because their citizens have little immediate stake in the question, feel indifference—if not outright reluctance—to paying the domestic debt at any rate. These States would be inclined to magnify the difficulties of distribution. Others, with many citizens who hold a disproportionate share of the national debt as creditors, would push hard for some fair and effective provision. The procrastinations of the first group would stir resentment in the second. Meanwhile, the settlement of a rule would be delayed by real disagreement and deliberate stalling. The citizens of the interested States would clamor. Foreign powers would press for satisfaction of their just demands. And the peace of the States would be put at risk by the double threat of foreign invasion and internal conflict.

7.7.oldText: Suppose the difficulty of agreeing on a rule were overcome and the apportionment made. There would still be plenty of reason to expect that the rule, in practice, would bear harder on some States than on others. Those who suffered would naturally seek to ease the burden. The others would just as naturally resist a revision likely to increase their own load. Their refusal would be too convenient an excuse for the complaining States to withhold their contributions—they would seize on it eagerly. And those States' non-compliance with their obligations would be a ground for bitter argument and quarrel. Even if the rule adopted in practice lived up to its principle of equality, delinquencies in payment from some States would still result from various other causes: real lack of resources, mismanagement of finances, accidental disorders in government, and—on top of all that—the reluctance people generally feel to part with money for purposes that have outlived the urgent needs that produced them and that interfere with the supply of immediate wants. Delinquencies, from whatever causes, would breed complaints, accusations, and quarrels. Perhaps nothing is more likely to disturb the tranquility of nations than being bound to mutual contributions for some common purpose that does not yield an equal and matching benefit. For it is an observation as true as it is well-worn, that there is nothing people are quicker to fight about than the payment of money.

7.8.oldText: Laws that violate private contracts, since they amount to aggressions on the rights of those States whose citizens are injured by them, may be considered another probable source of hostility. We have no reason to expect that a more liberal or fairer spirit will preside over the laws of the individual States in the future—if unrestrained by additional checks—than we have already seen in too many cases disgracing their codes. We have noticed the disposition to retaliation aroused in Connecticut as a result of the outrages committed by the Legislature of Rhode Island. We can reasonably infer that in similar cases, under other circumstances, a war—not of PARCHMENT, but of the sword—would punish such atrocious breaches of moral obligation and social justice.

7.9.oldText: The probability of incompatible alliances between the different States or confederacies and different foreign nations, and the effects of that on the peace of the whole, have been laid out fully enough in earlier papers. From the view they have given of this part of the subject, the conclusion is this: America, if not connected at all, or connected only by the weak tie of a simple offensive and defensive league, would—through the operation of such clashing alliances—be gradually drawn into all the destructive mazes of European politics and wars. And through the destructive disputes among the parts into which she had been divided, she would likely fall prey to the schemes and machinations of powers that were equally enemies of them all. Divide et impera(1) must be the motto of every nation that either hates or fears us.(2)

7.11.oldText: 2. So that the entire subject of these papers may be laid before the public as soon as possible, it is proposed to publish them four times a week—on Tuesday in the New York Packet and on Thursday in the Daily Advertiser.

8.0.oldText: Taking it as established, then, that the several States—if disunited, or thrown into whatever combinations might emerge from the wreck of the general Confederacy—would be subject to the same alternations of peace and war, friendship and hostility with each other that have been the lot of all neighboring nations not united under one government, let us briefly examine some of the consequences such a situation would bring.

8.1.oldText: War between the States, in the early period of their separate existence, would bring far greater suffering than it usually does in countries that have long had regular military establishments. The disciplined armies always kept up on the European continent, while bearing a malign aspect to liberty and economy, have nonetheless produced the considerable benefit of making sudden conquests impractical and preventing the rapid devastation that used to mark the progress of war before such armies existed. The art of fortification has contributed to the same ends. The nations of Europe are ringed with chains of fortified places that mutually obstruct invasion. Campaigns are spent reducing two or three frontier garrisons just to gain entrance into an enemy's country. Similar obstacles arise at every step to wear down the strength and slow the advance of an invader. Once, an invading army would penetrate to the heart of a neighboring country almost as quickly as news of its approach could be received. Now a comparatively small force of disciplined troops, acting on the defensive with the help of fortifications, can impede and ultimately frustrate the efforts of a much larger one. The history of war in that part of the globe is no longer a history of nations subdued and empires overturned, but of towns taken and retaken; of battles that decide nothing; of retreats more useful than victories; of much effort and little gain.

8.2.oldText: In this country the picture would be entirely reversed. Suspicion of military establishments would put them off as long as possible. The lack of fortifications, leaving the frontiers of one State open to another, would invite incursions. The populous States would, with little trouble, overrun their less populous neighbors. Conquests would be as easy to make as they would be hard to keep. War, therefore, would be erratic and predatory. PLUNDER and devastation always march in the train of irregular forces. The sufferings of individuals would be the leading feature of the events that defined our military exploits.

8.3.oldText: This picture is not overdrawn—though I admit it would not long remain accurate. Safety from external danger is the most powerful guide of national conduct. Even the ardent love of liberty will, after a while, give way to its demands. The violent destruction of life and property that goes with war, and the constant strain and alarm of a state of continual danger, will compel even the nations most attached to liberty to turn for repose and security to institutions that tend to destroy their civil and political rights. To be safer, they eventually become willing to risk being less free.

8.4.oldText: The institutions chiefly meant here are STANDING ARMIES and the related apparatus of military establishments. Standing armies, it is said, are not provided against in the new Constitution, and so it is inferred that they may exist under it.(1) Their existence, however, by the very terms of the proposition, is at most uncertain and conditional. But standing armies, one may reply, must inevitably follow from a dissolution of the Confederacy. Frequent war and constant apprehension, which require an equally constant state of preparation, will reliably produce them. The weaker States or confederacies would resort to them first, to put themselves on a level with their more powerful neighbors. They would try to make up for inferior population and resources by a more regular and effective system of defense, by disciplined troops, and by fortifications. At the same time, they would be forced to strengthen the executive arm of government, and in doing so their constitutions would gradually drift toward monarchy. It is in the nature of war to enlarge the executive at the expense of legislative authority.

8.5.oldText: The measures just described would soon give the States or confederacies that adopted them a superiority over their neighbors. Small states, or states of less natural strength, with vigorous governments and the help of disciplined armies, have often triumphed over large states, or states of greater natural strength, that lacked these advantages. Neither the pride nor the safety of the more important States or confederacies would let them long submit to this humiliating and accidental superiority. They would quickly take up means similar to those by which it had been achieved, to recover their lost preeminence. So in a short time we would see established in every part of this country the same engines of despotism that have been the scourge of the Old World. This, at any rate, would be the natural course of things, and our reasoning will be the more sound the more it is fitted to that standard.

8.6.oldText: These are not vague inferences drawn from supposed or speculative defects in a Constitution whose entire power is lodged in the hands of a people, or their representatives and delegates. They are solid conclusions, drawn from the natural and necessary progress of human affairs.

8.7.oldText: It may perhaps be asked, by way of objection, why standing armies did not arise out of the disputes that so often distracted the ancient republics of Greece. Several answers, all equally satisfactory, can be given. The industrious habits of people today—absorbed in the pursuit of gain and devoted to the advancement of agriculture and commerce—are incompatible with the condition of a nation of soldiers, which was the actual condition of the people of those republics. The means of revenue, vastly multiplied by the increase of gold and silver and of industry, and the science of finance—an offspring of modern times—together with the habits of nations, have produced a complete revolution in the system of war and have made disciplined armies, distinct from the body of the citizens, the inseparable companions of frequent hostility.

8.8.oldText: There is also a wide difference between military establishments in a country rarely exposed by its situation to internal invasion, and in one that is often subject to such invasion and always afraid of it. The rulers of the first kind have no plausible pretext—even if they were inclined—to keep up armies as numerous as must necessarily be maintained in the second. Since these armies are seldom if ever called into activity for internal defense, the people are in no danger of being broken to military subordination. The laws are not accustomed to relaxing for military emergencies. The civil state remains in full vigor, neither corrupted nor confused by the principles or tendencies of the military state. The smallness of the army means the natural strength of the community more than matches it. And the citizens, not used to looking up to military power for protection or submitting to its oppressions, neither love nor fear the soldiery. They view them with a spirit of wary acquiescence as a necessary evil, and stand ready to resist a power they suspect may be turned against their rights.

8.9.oldText: An army under such conditions can usefully help the magistrate suppress a small faction, an occasional mob, or an insurrection. But it will be unable to enforce encroachments against the united efforts of the great body of the people.

8.10.oldText: In a country in the second predicament described above, the opposite of all this happens. The constant threat of danger forces the government to be always ready to repel it. Its armies must be numerous enough for immediate defense. The continual need for their services raises the importance of the soldier and proportionally lowers the condition of the citizen. The military state becomes elevated above the civil. The inhabitants of territories that are often the theater of war are unavoidably subjected to frequent infringements on their rights, which weaken their sense of those rights. By degrees, the people are brought to consider the soldiery not only as their protectors but as their superiors. The transition from this attitude to regarding them as masters is neither remote nor difficult. But it is very difficult to get a people in such a frame of mind to mount a bold or effective resistance to usurpations backed by military power.

8.11.oldText: The kingdom of Great Britain falls within the first description. An island situation and a powerful navy, guarding it largely against the possibility of foreign invasion, remove the need for a large army within the kingdom. Enough force to hold off a sudden landing until the militia could rally and form up has been all that was deemed necessary. No motive of national policy has demanded, nor would public opinion have tolerated, a larger number of troops on its home establishment. For a long time there has been little room for the operation of the other causes mentioned as the consequences of internal war. This peculiar good fortune of situation has gone a long way toward preserving the liberty that country still enjoys today, despite the prevailing venality and corruption. If, on the contrary, Britain had been situated on the continent and had been forced—as she would have been by that situation—to make her military establishments at home as large as those of the other great powers of Europe, she, like them, would in all probability today be a victim to the absolute power of a single man. It is possible, though not easy, that the people of that island may yet be enslaved from other causes; but it cannot be by the prowess of an army as small as the one usually kept up within the kingdom.

8.12.oldText: If we are wise enough to preserve the Union, we may for ages enjoy an advantage similar to that of an island situation. Europe is far from us. Her colonies in our vicinity are likely to remain too disproportioned in strength to threaten us seriously. Extensive military establishments cannot, in this position, be necessary to our security. But if we should be disunited, and the parts either stayed separated or—what is more likely—were thrown together into two or three confederacies, we would in a short time be in the predicament of the continental powers of Europe. Our liberties would fall prey to the means of defending ourselves against each other's ambition and jealousy.

8.13.oldText: This is no shallow or trivial idea, but a solid and weighty one. It deserves the most serious and careful consideration of every prudent and honest man, of whatever party. If such men will make a firm and solemn pause and reflect calmly on the importance of this idea; if they contemplate it in all its bearings and trace it to all its consequences, they will not hesitate to part with trivial objections to a Constitution whose rejection would in all likelihood put a final end to the Union. The airy phantoms that flit before the disordered imaginations of some of its opponents would quickly give way to the more substantial forms of dangers that are real, certain, and formidable.

8.14.oldText: 1.
