That language now seems as wild as much of what we hear today from the same quarter will seem once experience, the best oracle of wisdom, has given us further lessons. Such language always betrayed ignorance of the true springs of human conduct and ignored the original reasons for establishing civil power. Why was government instituted at all? Because the passions of men will not yield to the dictates of reason and justice without restraint. Has it ever been found that bodies of men act with more uprightness or greater disinterestedness than individuals? The opposite has been observed by every careful student of human conduct, and the inference rests on obvious reasons. Concern for reputation has less force when the disgrace of a bad action is divided among many than when it falls on one person alone. A spirit of faction, which tends to mix its poison into the deliberations of all bodies of men, will often drive the people in those bodies into improprieties and excesses they would blush to commit as private individuals.

15.12.oldText: Beyond all this, there is in the nature of sovereign power an impatience of control, which makes those who exercise it look with hostility on any external attempt to restrain or direct its operations. From this spirit it follows that in every political association formed to unite a number of lesser sovereignties in a common interest, there is a kind of eccentric tendency in the subordinate bodies—a constant effort in each to fly off from the common center. This tendency is not hard to explain. It originates in the love of power. Power that is controlled or limited is almost always the rival and enemy of the power that controls or limits it. This simple proposition shows how little reason there is to expect that the people running the affairs of the particular members of a confederacy will at all times be ready, with perfect good humor and unbiased regard for the public good, to carry out the resolutions or decrees of the general authority. The opposite is the natural result of human nature.

15.13.oldText: Therefore, if the measures of the Confederacy cannot be carried out without the intervention of the particular State administrations, there is little chance they will be carried out at all. The rulers of the respective members, whether they have a constitutional right to do so or not, will judge the propriety of the measures themselves. They will weigh how the proposal fits their immediate interests or aims, and the momentary conveniences or inconveniences of adopting it. All of this will be done in a spirit of self-interested and suspicious scrutiny, without the knowledge of national circumstances and reasons of state that sound judgment requires, and with such a strong bias toward local objects that it can hardly fail to mislead the decision. The same process must be repeated in every member of the body, and the execution of plans framed by the councils of the whole will always depend on the discretion of the ill-informed and prejudiced opinion of every part. Anyone familiar with the proceedings of popular assemblies—who has seen how hard it often is to bring them to harmonious resolutions on important points without outside pressure—will easily grasp how impossible it must be to induce a number of such assemblies, deliberating at a distance from one another, at different times, and under different impressions, to cooperate long in the same views and pursuits.

15.14.oldText: In our case, the agreement of thirteen distinct sovereign wills is required, under the Confederation, for the complete execution of every important measure of the Union. The result has been what should have been foreseen. The measures of the Union have not been carried out. The delinquencies of the States have, step by step, grown to such an extreme that they have stopped all the wheels of national government and brought them to a dead halt. Congress at this point barely has the means to keep up the forms of administration until the States can agree on a more substantial replacement for the present shadow of a federal government. Things did not reach this desperate extremity all at once. The causes I have specified at first produced only unequal and disproportionate degrees of compliance with the Union's requisitions. The greater deficiencies of some States gave the complying or least delinquent States both an excuse of example and a temptation of self-interest. Why should we do more proportionally than those traveling with us in the same political voyage? Why should we agree to bear more than our fair share of the common burden? These suggestions human selfishness could not resist, and even speculative men looking ahead to remote consequences could not, without hesitation, oppose them. Each State, yielding to the persuasive voice of immediate interest or convenience, has successively withdrawn its support, until the frail and tottering edifice seems ready to fall on our heads and crush us beneath its ruins.

16.0.oldText: The tendency of the principle of legislating for States or communities in their political capacities, as shown by the experiment we have made of it, is equally confirmed by the events that have befallen all other confederate governments we know of, in exact proportion to the prevalence of that principle in those systems. The confirmation of this fact deserves a separate, detailed examination. I will only note here that of all the confederacies of antiquity that history has handed down to us, the Lycian and Achaean leagues, so far as their remains can be traced, appear to have been most free from the chains of that mistaken principle. They were accordingly the ones that have most deserved—and most generously received—the praise of political writers.

16.1.oldText: This objectionable principle may, with truth and emphasis, be called the parent of anarchy. We have seen that delinquencies on the part of the members of the Union are its natural and necessary offspring, and that whenever they happen, the only constitutional remedy is force, and the immediate effect of using force is civil war.

16.2.oldText: It remains to ask how far so hateful an instrument of government, applied to us, would even be capable of achieving its purpose. Unless a large army were constantly at the disposal of the national government, it would either not be able to use force at all or, when it could, the use would amount to a war between parts of the Confederacy over the violations of a league. In such a war, the strongest combination would most likely prevail, whether it consisted of those upholding or those resisting the general authority. It would rarely happen that the delinquency to be redressed was confined to a single member. If more than one had neglected its duty, similarity of situation would lead them to unite for common defense. Beyond this motive of sympathy, if a large and influential State happened to be the offending member, it would usually have enough weight with its neighbors to win some of them as allies. Specious arguments about danger to the common liberty could easily be devised. Plausible excuses for the offenders' deficiencies could without difficulty be invented to alarm the apprehensions, inflame the passions, and conciliate the goodwill even of States not chargeable with any violation or omission of duty. This would be all the more likely because the delinquencies of the larger members might be expected sometimes to spring from ambitious premeditation in their rulers, who hoped to throw off all external control on their schemes of personal aggrandizement. To accomplish this, they would presumably tamper beforehand with leading individuals in nearby States. If allies could not be found at home, they would turn to foreign powers, which would seldom be unwilling to encourage dissensions in a Confederacy whose firm union they had so much to fear. Once the sword is drawn, the passions of men respect no limits of moderation. The promptings of wounded pride and the urgings of irritated resentment would carry the States against which the arms of the Union were exerted to any extreme needed to avenge the affront or avoid the disgrace of submission. The first war of this kind would probably end in dissolving the Union.

16.3.oldText: This may be considered the violent death of the Confederacy. Its more natural death is what we now seem on the point of experiencing, if the federal system is not soon rebuilt in a more substantial form. Given the genius of this country, it is unlikely the complying States would often be inclined to support the authority of the Union by going to war against the non-complying States. They would always be more ready to take the milder course of putting themselves on equal footing with the delinquent members by following their example. The guilt of all would thus become the security of all. Our past experience has shown this spirit at full strength. There would in fact be an insurmountable difficulty in determining when force could properly be used. In the matter of monetary contributions, which would be the most common source of delinquency, it would often be impossible to tell whether the failure came from unwillingness or inability. The pretense of inability would always be at hand. The case would have to be very flagrant for its falseness to be detected with enough certainty to justify the harsh expedient of compulsion. It is easy to see that this problem alone, every time it arose, would open a wide field for factional motives, partiality, and oppression in whatever majority happened to prevail in the national council.

16.4.oldText: It seems to need no proof that the States ought not to prefer a national Constitution that could only be kept running through a large standing army constantly executing the ordinary requisitions or decrees of the government. Yet that is the plain alternative implied by those who deny the government the power of extending its operations to individuals. Such a scheme, if it were practical at all, would instantly degenerate into a military despotism. But in every light it will be found impractical. The resources of the Union would not suffice to maintain an army large enough to keep the larger States within the bounds of duty, nor would the means ever be available to form such an army in the first place. Anyone who considers the population and strength of several of these States singly today, and looks ahead to what they will become even half a century from now, will at once dismiss as idle and visionary any scheme aimed at regulating their movements by laws operating on them in their collective capacities and enforced by coercion applied to them in those same capacities. A project of this kind is little less fantastic than the monster-taming spirit attributed to the legendary heroes and demigods of antiquity.

16.5.oldText: Even in confederacies whose members were smaller than many of our counties, the principle of legislating for sovereign States, backed by military coercion, has never been effective. It has rarely even been attempted except against the weaker members, and in most cases attempts to coerce the refractory and disobedient have been the signals of bloody wars in which one half of the confederacy raised its banners against the other half.

16.6.oldText: The conclusion these observations must lead a thoughtful mind to is this: if it is at all possible to construct a federal government capable of regulating the common concerns and preserving the general peace, it must be founded, with regard to the objects placed under its care, on the reverse of the principle pushed by the opponents of the proposed Constitution. It must extend its action to the persons of the citizens. It must require no intermediate legislatures, but must itself be empowered to use the arm of the ordinary magistrate to enforce its own resolutions. The majesty of the national authority must be made manifest through the courts of justice. The government of the Union, like that of each State, must be able to address itself directly to the hopes and fears of individuals and to attract to its support those passions which have the strongest influence on the human heart. In short, it must possess all the means—and have the right to use all the methods—of executing the powers entrusted to it that are possessed and used by the government of the particular States.

16.7.oldText: To this reasoning it may perhaps be objected that if any State were disaffected from the authority of the Union, it could at any time obstruct the execution of its laws and bring matters to the same point of force with which the opposite scheme is reproached.

16.8.oldText: The plausibility of this objection vanishes the moment we notice the essential difference between mere NON-COMPLIANCE and DIRECT and ACTIVE RESISTANCE. If the intervention of the State legislatures is necessary to give effect to a measure of the Union, they have only NOT TO ACT, or TO ACT EVASIVELY, and the measure is defeated. This neglect of duty can be disguised under feigned but flimsy provisions, so as not to appear, and so not to alarm the people about the safety of the Constitution. State leaders may even take credit for their stealthy invasions of it on the ground of some temporary convenience, exemption, or advantage.

16.9.oldText: But if the execution of the laws of the national government did not require the intervention of the State legislatures—if those laws operated immediately on the citizens themselves—the particular governments could not interrupt their progress without an open and violent exertion of an unconstitutional power. No omissions or evasions would suffice. They would be obliged to act, and to act in a way that would leave no doubt that they had encroached on national rights. An experiment of this nature would always be hazardous in the face of a constitution at all capable of defending itself, and of a people enlightened enough to distinguish between a legal exercise and an illegal usurpation of authority. Success would require not merely a factious majority in the legislature, but the cooperation of the courts of justice and of the body of the people. If the judges were not in conspiracy with the legislature, they would declare the resolutions of such a majority contrary to the supreme law of the land, unconstitutional, and void. If the people were not infected with the spirit of their State representatives, they—as the natural guardians of the Constitution—would throw their weight onto the national side and give it a decided edge in the contest. Attempts of this kind would not often be made lightly or rashly, because they could seldom be made without danger to those who made them, except in cases of tyrannical exercise of federal authority.

16.10.oldText: If opposition to the national government were to arise from the disorderly conduct of refractory or seditious individuals, it could be put down by the same means used daily against the same evil under the State governments. The magistracy, being equally the ministers of the law of the land—whatever its source—would no doubt be as ready to guard national regulations as local ones from the inroads of private lawlessness. As for the partial commotions and insurrections that sometimes disturb society, springing from the intrigues of a small faction or from sudden or occasional ill-humors that do not infect the body of the community, the general government could draw on more extensive resources to suppress them than any single member could. As for those mortal feuds that, in certain circumstances, spread a conflagration through a whole nation or a very large portion of it—proceeding either from weighty grievances created by the government or from the contagion of some violent popular paroxysm—they fall outside any ordinary calculation. When they happen, they usually amount to revolutions and dismemberments of empire. No form of government can always avoid or control them. It is vain to hope to guard against events too mighty for human foresight or precaution, and idle to object to a government because it cannot perform impossibilities.

17.0.oldText: An objection different from the one stated and answered in my last paper may also be urged against the principle of legislating for individual citizens of America. It may be said that this would tend to make the government of the Union too powerful and to enable it to absorb those residual authorities that ought to be left with the States for local purposes. Granting the love of power its widest reasonable scope, I confess I am at a loss to see what temptation those entrusted with the administration of the general government could ever feel to strip the States of authorities of that kind. The regulation of the merely domestic affairs of a State seems to me to offer little allurement to ambition. Commerce, finance, negotiation, and war seem to take in all the objects that have charms for minds governed by that passion, and all the powers necessary for those objects ought, in the first instance, to be lodged in the national depository. The administration of private justice between citizens of the same State, the supervision of agriculture and similar concerns—in short, all the matters proper for local legislation—can never be desirable charges of a general jurisdiction. It is therefore unlikely that the federal councils would be inclined to usurp such powers. The attempt to exercise them would be as troublesome as it would be useless, and the possession of them would for that reason add nothing to the dignity, importance, or splendor of the national government.

17.1.oldText: But suppose, for argument's sake, that mere wantonness and lust of domination would be enough to produce that disposition. Even then it can be safely affirmed that the sense of the constituent body of the national representatives—in other words, the people of the several States—would check the indulgence of so extravagant an appetite. It will always be far easier for the State governments to encroach on the national authorities than for the national government to encroach on the State authorities. The proof of this turns on the greater degree of influence the State governments will generally have over the people, provided they administer their affairs with uprightness and prudence. This same fact also teaches us that there is an inherent and intrinsic weakness in all federal constitutions, and that no pains can be too great in their organization to give them all the force compatible with the principles of liberty.

17.2.oldText: The superior influence of the particular governments would result partly from the diffuse construction of the national government, but mainly from the nature of the objects to which the State administrations would devote their attention.

17.3.oldText: It is a known fact about human nature that its affections are commonly weaker the more distant or diffuse the object. By the same principle that a man is more attached to his family than to his neighborhood, and to his neighborhood than to the community at large, the people of each State would tend to feel a stronger bias toward their local governments than toward the government of the Union—unless the force of that principle were destroyed by a much better administration of the latter.

17.4.oldText: This strong inclination of the human heart would find powerful reinforcements in the objects of State regulation.

17.5.oldText: The variety of more minute interests that will necessarily fall under the supervision of the local administrations, and which will form so many small streams of influence running through every part of society, cannot be specified without involving a level of detail too tedious and uninteresting to be worth the instruction it might give.

17.6.oldText: There is one transcendent advantage belonging to the province of the State governments, and it alone is enough to settle the matter clearly: I mean the ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice. This, more than anything else, is the most powerful, most universal, and most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment. As the immediate and visible guardian of life and property—its benefits and its terrors constantly active before the public eye, regulating all those personal interests and familiar concerns to which individual sensitivity is most awake—it does more than any other circumstance to imprint on the people's minds affection, esteem, and reverence toward the government. This great cement of society, which will spread almost wholly through the channels of the particular governments, would by itself give them so decisive a hold over their respective citizens as to make them at all times a complete counterweight—and, not infrequently, a dangerous rival—to the power of the Union.

17.7.oldText: The operations of the national government, on the other hand, fall less immediately under the observation of the mass of citizens. The benefits derived from it will mainly be perceived and attended to by speculative thinkers. Relating to more general interests, they will be less likely to come home to the feelings of the people, and so less likely to inspire a habitual sense of obligation and an active sentiment of attachment.

17.8.oldText: The reasoning here has been abundantly illustrated by the experience of all federal constitutions we are acquainted with, and of all others that have borne the slightest analogy to them.

17.9.oldText: Although the ancient feudal systems were not, strictly speaking, confederacies, they shared the nature of that kind of association. There was a common head, chieftain, or sovereign whose authority extended over the whole nation, and a number of subordinate vassals, or feudatories, who held large portions of land allotted to them and had numerous trains of INFERIOR vassals or retainers who occupied and cultivated that land on terms of fealty or obedience to the persons who held it. Each principal vassal was a kind of sovereign within his particular domain. The consequences were a continual opposition to the authority of the sovereign and frequent wars between the great barons or chief feudatories themselves. The power of the head of the nation was usually too weak either to keep the public peace or to protect the people from the oppression of their immediate lords. This period of European history is emphatically called by historians the times of feudal anarchy.

17.10.oldText: When the sovereign happened to be a man of vigorous and warlike temper and superior abilities, he would acquire a personal weight and influence that served, for the time, the purpose of a more regular authority. But in general the power of the barons triumphed over that of the prince. In many instances his rule was thrown off entirely, and the great fiefs were erected into independent principalities or States. In those cases where the monarch finally prevailed over his vassals, his success owed mainly to the tyranny of those vassals over their dependents. The barons, or nobles, equally the enemies of the sovereign and the oppressors of the common people, were dreaded and detested by both, until mutual danger and mutual interest produced a union between them fatal to the power of the aristocracy. Had the nobles, by clemency and justice, kept the loyalty and devotion of their retainers and followers, the contests between them and the prince would almost always have ended in their favor, and in the curtailment or overthrow of the royal authority.

17.11.oldText: This is no mere speculation or conjecture. Among the many illustrations of its truth that could be cited, Scotland furnishes a powerful example. The spirit of clanship, introduced early into that kingdom and uniting the nobles and their dependents by ties equivalent to kinship, made the aristocracy a constant overmatch for the power of the monarch—until the union with England subdued its fierce and ungovernable spirit and reduced it within those rules of subordination that a more rational and energetic system of civil polity had previously established in the latter kingdom.

17.12.oldText: The separate governments in a confederacy may aptly be compared to the feudal baronies, with this advantage in their favor: from the reasons already explained, they will generally have the confidence and goodwill of the people, and with such important support they will be able to oppose effectively all encroachments by the national government. We will be fortunate if they are not able to thwart its legitimate and necessary authority. The points of similarity lie in the rivalry of power applicable to both, and in the CONCENTRATION of large portions of the strength of the community into particular DEPOSITORIES—in one case at the disposal of individuals, in the other at the disposal of political bodies.

17.13.oldText: A brief review of the events that have attended confederate governments will further illustrate this important doctrine. Inattention to it has been the great source of our political mistakes and has misdirected our jealousy to the wrong side. This review will be the subject of some upcoming papers.

18.1.oldText: Among the confederacies of antiquity, the most significant was that of the Greek republics joined under the Amphictyonic council. From the best surviving accounts of this celebrated institution, it offers a very instructive parallel to the present Confederation of the American States.

18.2.oldText: Its members kept the character of independent and sovereign states, and they had equal votes in the federal council. This council had a general authority to propose and decide whatever it judged necessary for the common welfare of Greece. It could declare and wage war, settle all controversies between members as a final court, fine the aggressor, deploy the whole force of the confederacy against any disobedient party, and admit new members. The Amphictyons were guardians of religion and of the immense riches belonging to the temple of Delphos, where they had jurisdiction over disputes between the inhabitants and visitors who came to consult the oracle. To make the federal powers more effective, they swore a mutual oath to defend and protect the united cities, to punish those who broke this oath, and to take vengeance on anyone who profaned the temple.

18.3.oldText: In theory, and on paper, this set of powers seems entirely sufficient for any general purpose. In several important respects they go beyond the powers listed in our articles of confederation. The Amphictyons controlled the superstition of their age, one of the chief tools of government at that time. They had a declared authority to use force against rebellious cities, and they were sworn to use that authority whenever necessary.

18.4.oldText: The experiment, however, was very different from the theory. The powers, like those of our present Congress, were administered by deputies appointed by the cities in their political capacities, and were exercised over those cities in the same capacities. The result was weakness, disorder, and finally the destruction of the confederacy. The more powerful members, instead of being kept in check, took turns tyrannizing over all the rest. According to Demosthenes, Athens was master of Greece for seventy-three years. The Lacedaemonians ruled it next for twenty-nine years. After the battle of Leuctra, the Thebans had their turn at domination.

18.5.oldText: It happened all too often, according to Plutarch, that the deputies of the strongest cities intimidated and corrupted those of the weaker, and judgment then went in favor of the most powerful party.

18.6.oldText: Even during defensive and dangerous wars with Persia and Macedon, the members never acted together. More or fewer of them were always either dupes or paid agents of the common enemy. The intervals between foreign wars were filled with domestic upheavals, convulsions, and slaughter.

18.7.oldText: After the war with Xerxes ended, the Lacedaemonians demanded that several cities be expelled from the confederacy for the disloyal part they had played. The Athenians, seeing that this measure would cost the Lacedaemonians fewer allies than themselves, and would make them masters of the public deliberations, vigorously opposed and defeated the attempt. This piece of history shows at once the inefficiency of the union, the ambition and jealousy of its most powerful members, and the dependent and degraded condition of the rest. The smaller members, though entitled in theory to revolve in equal pride and majesty around the common center, had become in fact mere satellites of the larger bodies.

18.8.oldText: Had the Greeks been as wise as they were brave, says the Abbe Milot, experience would have taught them the necessity of a closer union. They would have used the peace that followed their victory over the Persians to put such a reform in place. Instead of this obvious policy, Athens and Sparta, swollen by the victories and glory they had won, became first rivals and then enemies. They did each other infinitely more harm than they had suffered from Xerxes. Their mutual jealousies, fears, hatreds, and injuries ended in the famous Peloponnesian war, which ended in the ruin and slavery of the Athenians who had begun it.

18.9.oldText: A weak government, even when not at war, is constantly shaken by internal divisions, and these never fail to bring fresh disasters from abroad. When the Phocians plowed up some consecrated ground belonging to the temple of Apollo, the Amphictyonic council, true to the superstition of the age, fined the sacrilegious offenders. Backed by Athens and Sparta, the Phocians refused to obey the decree. The Thebans, with several other cities, undertook to uphold the Amphictyons' authority and avenge the offended god. Being the weaker party, they invited the help of Philip of Macedon, who had secretly fueled the conflict. Philip eagerly seized the chance to carry out the plans he had long laid against the liberties of Greece. Through his intrigues and bribes he won over the popular leaders of several cities. By their influence and votes he gained admission to the Amphictyonic council, and through his cunning and his armies he made himself master of the confederacy.

18.10.oldText: Such were the consequences of the false principle on which this remarkable institution was founded. Had Greece been bound by a stricter confederation and persevered in her union, says one shrewd observer of her fate, she would never have worn the chains of Macedon, and might have proved a barrier to the vast designs of Rome.

18.11.oldText: The Achaean league, as it is called, was another association of Greek republics, and it gives us valuable instruction.

18.12.oldText: The Union here was far closer, and its organization much wiser, than in the previous case. As a result, although it did not escape a similar disaster, it certainly did not equally deserve one.

18.13.oldText: The cities making up this league kept their own municipal jurisdiction, appointed their own officers, and enjoyed perfect equality. The senate, in which they were represented, had the sole and exclusive right to make peace and war, to send and receive ambassadors, to enter into treaties and alliances, and to appoint a chief magistrate, or praetor. He commanded their armies and, with the advice and consent of ten senators, not only ran the government when the senate was not in session but had a major share in its deliberations when it was. The original constitution provided two praetors who shared the administration, but in practice a single one was preferred.

18.14.oldText: It appears that all the cities had the same laws and customs, the same weights and measures, and the same money. How far this came from the federal council's authority is unclear. It is only said that the cities were in a way compelled to receive the same laws and usages. When Lacedaemon was brought into the league by Philopoemen, this was accompanied by the abolition of the institutions and laws of Lycurgus, and the adoption of those of the Achaeans. The Amphictyonic confederacy, of which she had been a member, had left her in full enjoyment of her own government and laws. This single fact proves a very real difference in the spirit of the two systems.

18.15.oldText: It is much to be regretted that only such imperfect records of this curious political fabric remain. If its inner structure and regular workings could be known, it would probably shed more light on the science of federal government than any of the similar experiments we are familiar with.

18.16.oldText: One important fact seems to be confirmed by every historian who notices Achaean affairs. Both after the league was renewed by Aratus, and before its dissolution by the arts of Macedon, there was infinitely more moderation and justice in the administration of its government, and far less violence and sedition among its people, than in any of the cities exercising all the prerogatives of sovereignty alone. The Abbe Mably, in his observations on Greece, says that popular government, which was so stormy elsewhere, caused no disorders within the Achaean republic, BECAUSE IT WAS THERE TEMPERED BY THE GENERAL AUTHORITY AND LAWS OF THE CONFEDERACY.

18.17.oldText: We must not, however, conclude too quickly that faction did not disturb individual cities to some degree, much less that proper subordination and harmony reigned in the system as a whole. The opposite is sufficiently shown by the upheavals and the fate of the republic.

18.18.oldText: While the Amphictyonic confederacy lasted, that of the Achaeans, which included only the lesser cities, made little figure on the Greek stage. When the former fell to Macedon, the latter was spared by the policy of Philip and Alexander. Under the successors of these princes, however, a different policy prevailed. The arts of division were practiced on the Achaeans. Each city was lured into a separate interest, and the union dissolved. Some cities fell under Macedonian garrisons; others under usurpers who sprang from their own confusion. Shame and oppression soon awakened their love of liberty. A few cities reunited. Their example was followed by others as opportunities arose to cut down their tyrants. The league soon embraced almost the entire Peloponnesus. Macedon saw its progress but was prevented by internal dissensions from stopping it. All Greece caught the enthusiasm and seemed ready to join in one confederacy. Then jealousy and envy in Sparta and Athens of the rising glory of the Achaeans threw a fatal damper on the project. The fear of Macedonian power led the league to seek alliance with the kings of Egypt and Syria, who, as successors of Alexander, were rivals of the king of Macedon. This policy was defeated by Cleomenes, king of Sparta, whose ambition led him to make an unprovoked attack on his Achaean neighbors. As an enemy of Macedon, Cleomenes had enough influence with the Egyptian and Syrian princes to break their commitments to the league.

18.19.oldText: The Achaeans were now reduced to the dilemma of submitting to Cleomenes or begging help from Macedon, their former oppressor. They chose the latter. The quarrels of the Greeks always gave that powerful neighbor a welcome chance to meddle in their affairs. A Macedonian army quickly arrived. Cleomenes was defeated. The Achaeans soon learned, as so often happens, that a victorious and powerful ally is just another name for a master. The most they could obtain by their most submissive compliance was permission to keep their own laws. Philip, now on the throne of Macedon, by his tyrannies soon provoked fresh combinations among the Greeks. The Achaeans, though weakened by internal dissensions and by the revolt of Messene, one of their members, raised the standard of opposition with the Aetolians and Athenians joining them. Finding that even with this support they were not strong enough, they once more resorted to the dangerous expedient of bringing in foreign arms. The Romans, when invited, eagerly accepted. Philip was conquered and Macedon subdued. A new crisis followed for the league. Dissensions broke out among its members. The Romans encouraged these. Callicrates and other popular leaders became hired tools to mislead their countrymen. To feed discord and disorder more effectively, the Romans, to the astonishment of those who trusted their sincerity, had already proclaimed universal liberty (1) throughout Greece. With the same treacherous design they now lured members away from the league by appealing to their pride about violations of their sovereignty. By such tactics this union, the last hope of Greece and of ancient liberty, was torn apart. So much weakness and confusion were introduced that Roman arms had little trouble completing the ruin which Roman cunning had begun. The Achaeans were cut to pieces, and Achaia loaded with the chains under which it groans to this hour.

18.20.oldText: I have not thought it superfluous to give the outlines of this important piece of history. It teaches more than one lesson. As a supplement to the outlines of the Achaean constitution, it strikingly shows how federal bodies tend toward anarchy among the members rather than tyranny at the head.

18.21.oldText: 1. This was just another, more flattering name for the independence of the members from the federal head.

19.1.oldText: The examples of ancient confederacies cited in my last paper have not used up the supply of experimental instruction on this subject. There are existing institutions, founded on a similar principle, that deserve particular attention. The first that comes to mind is the Germanic body.

19.2.oldText: In the early ages of Christianity, Germany was occupied by seven distinct nations, with no common chief. The Franks, one of these nations, conquered the Gauls and founded the kingdom that took its name from them. In the ninth century Charlemagne, its warlike monarch, carried his victorious arms in every direction, and Germany became part of his vast dominions. When his sons divided up the empire, this part was set up as a separate and independent realm. Charlemagne and his immediate descendants held real imperial power, along with its symbols and dignity. But the principal vassals, whose fiefs had become hereditary and who composed the national diets that Charlemagne had not abolished, gradually threw off the yoke and rose to sovereign jurisdiction and independence. The force of imperial sovereignty was not enough to restrain such powerful dependents, or to preserve the unity and tranquility of the empire. The most furious private wars, with every kind of calamity, were waged between the various princes and states. The imperial authority, unable to keep public order, declined by stages until it was almost extinct in the anarchy that filled the long interval between the death of the last Suabian emperor and the accession of the first Austrian one. In the eleventh century the emperors enjoyed full sovereignty; in the fifteenth they had little more than the symbols and decorations of power.

19.3.oldText: Out of this feudal system, which itself has many of the important features of a confederacy, has grown the federal system that makes up the Germanic empire. Its powers are vested in a diet representing the component members of the confederacy; in the emperor, who is the executive magistrate, with a veto on the diet's decrees; and in the imperial chamber and the aulic council, two judicial tribunals with supreme jurisdiction over disputes that concern the empire or arise among its members.

19.4.oldText: The diet has the general power of legislating for the empire, of making war and peace, contracting alliances, assessing quotas of troops and money, building fortresses, regulating coinage, admitting new members, and subjecting disobedient members to the ban of the empire, by which the offending party is stripped of his sovereign rights and his possessions are forfeited. Members of the confederacy are expressly forbidden to enter into compacts harmful to the empire, to impose tolls and duties on each other's trade without the consent of the emperor and diet, to alter the value of money, to do injustice to one another, or to give aid or refuge to disturbers of the public peace. The ban is pronounced against any who break these restrictions. Members of the diet, in their official capacity, are subject in all cases to be judged by the emperor and diet, and in their private capacities by the aulic council and imperial chamber.

19.5.oldText: The emperor's prerogatives are numerous. The most important are: his exclusive right to make proposals to the diet; to veto its resolutions; to name ambassadors; to confer dignities and titles; to fill vacant electorates; to found universities; to grant privileges that do not harm the states of the empire; to receive and apply the public revenues; and generally to watch over the public safety. In certain cases the electors form a council to advise him. As emperor he holds no territory within the empire and receives no revenue for his support. But his revenue and dominions in his other capacities make him one of the most powerful princes in Europe.

19.6.oldText: From such a parade of constitutional powers, in the representatives and head of this confederacy, the natural assumption would be that it must form an exception to the general character of its sister systems. Nothing could be further from the reality. The fundamental principle on which it rests — that the empire is a community of sovereigns, that the diet is a representation of sovereigns, and that the laws are addressed to sovereigns — makes the empire a body without nerve, unable to regulate its own members, insecure against external dangers, and stirred by ceaseless turmoil within.

19.7.oldText: The history of Germany is a history of wars between the emperor and the princes and states; of wars among the princes and states themselves; of the lawlessness of the strong and the oppression of the weak; of foreign intrusions and foreign intrigues; of demands for men and money that were ignored or only partly complied with; of attempts to enforce them that came to nothing or were attended by slaughter and devastation, swallowing up the innocent with the guilty; in short, of general weakness, confusion, and misery.

19.8.oldText: In the sixteenth century, the emperor, with one part of the empire on his side, was seen at war with the other princes and states. In one of these conflicts the emperor himself was put to flight and very nearly captured by the elector of Saxony. The late king of Prussia was more than once pitted against his imperial sovereign, and usually proved more than a match for him. Disputes and wars among the members themselves have been so common that the German annals are crowded with the bloody pages describing them. Before the peace of Westphalia, Germany was devastated by a thirty years' war, in which the emperor with one half of the empire stood on one side, and Sweden with the other half on the opposite. Peace was eventually negotiated, and dictated by foreign powers, and its articles, to which foreign powers were parties, became a fundamental part of the Germanic constitution.

19.9.oldText: If, in some emergency, the nation happens to be more united by the necessity of self-defense, its situation is still deplorable. Military preparations must be preceded by so many tedious discussions, springing from the jealousies, pride, separate views, and clashing claims of sovereign bodies, that before the diet can settle the arrangements the enemy is already in the field, and before the federal troops are ready to take the field, the enemy is going into winter quarters.

19.10.oldText: The small body of national troops, which has been judged necessary in time of peace, is poorly maintained, badly paid, infected with local prejudices, and supported by irregular and unequal contributions to the treasury.

19.11.oldText: The impossibility of keeping order and dispensing justice among these sovereign subjects led to the experiment of dividing the empire into nine or ten circles or districts, giving them an internal organization, and charging them with the military execution of the laws against delinquent and stubborn members. This experiment has only served to show more fully the radical defect of the constitution. Each circle is a miniature picture of the deformities of this political monster. They either fail to carry out their commissions, or they do so with all the devastation and slaughter of civil war. Sometimes whole circles are themselves the defaulters, and so they multiply the very mischief they were created to remedy.

19.12.oldText: We can form some idea of this scheme of military coercion from a sample given by Thuanus. In Donawerth, a free and imperial city in the circle of Suabia, the Abbe de St. Croix had certain immunities reserved to him. While exercising these on some public occasions, he was attacked by the people of the city. As a result, the city was placed under the ban of the empire, and the Duke of Bavaria, though director of another circle, obtained the appointment to enforce it. He soon appeared before the city with a corps of ten thousand troops. Finding it a fit occasion (as he had secretly intended from the beginning) to revive an old claim — on the pretext that his ancestors had allowed the place to be detached from his territory (1) — he took possession of it in his own name, disarmed and punished the inhabitants, and reannexed the city to his domains.

19.13.oldText: It may be asked, then, what has so long kept this disjointed machine from falling completely to pieces? The answer is obvious. The weakness of most of the members, who are unwilling to expose themselves to the mercy of foreign powers; the weakness of most of the principal members, compared with the formidable powers all around them; the vast weight and influence the emperor draws from his separate hereditary dominions; and the interest he feels in preserving a system to which his family pride is attached, and which makes him the first prince in Europe — these causes prop up a feeble and uncertain Union. Meanwhile the repellent quality natural to sovereignty, which time only strengthens, prevents any reform founded on a proper consolidation. Nor is it to be supposed, even if this obstacle could be overcome, that the neighboring powers would allow a revolution that would give the empire the force and preeminence to which it is entitled. Foreign nations have long considered themselves interested in the changes brought by events in this constitution, and on various occasions have shown their policy of perpetuating its anarchy and weakness.

19.14.oldText: If more direct examples were needed, Poland, as a government over local sovereigns, might fairly be mentioned. No more striking proof could be given of the calamities flowing from such institutions. Equally unfit for self-government and self-defense, it has long been at the mercy of its powerful neighbors, who have lately had the mercy to relieve it of one third of its people and territory.

19.15.oldText: The connection among the Swiss cantons hardly amounts to a confederacy, though it is sometimes cited as an instance of the stability of such institutions.

19.16.oldText: They have no common treasury, no common troops even in war, no common coinage, no common judiciary, nor any other common mark of sovereignty.

19.17.oldText: They are held together by the peculiarity of their topographical position; by their individual weakness and insignificance; by the fear of powerful neighbors, to one of which they were once subject; by the few sources of contention among a people of such simple and homogeneous manners; by their joint interest in their dependent possessions; by the mutual aid they need for suppressing insurrections and rebellions, an aid expressly stipulated and often required and given; and by the necessity of some regular and permanent provision for settling disputes among the cantons. The arrangement is that the parties at variance shall each choose four judges from the neutral cantons, who, in case of disagreement, choose an umpire. This tribunal, under an oath of impartiality, gives a final ruling that all the cantons are bound to enforce. The competence of this regulation may be measured by a clause in their treaty of 1683 with Victor Amadeus of Savoy, in which he obliges himself to mediate disputes between the cantons and to use force, if necessary, against the stubborn party.

19.18.oldText: So far as their peculiar situation allows comparison with that of the United States, it confirms the principle being established. Whatever effectiveness the union may have had in ordinary cases, it is clear that the moment a real point of difference came up that could test its strength, it failed. The controversies on religion, which on three occasions kindled violent and bloody contests, may in fact be said to have severed the league. Since then the Protestant and Catholic cantons have had separate diets, where all the most important matters are settled, leaving the general diet little to do besides looking after the common bailages.

19.19.oldText: That separation had another consequence worth noting. It produced opposite alliances with foreign powers: Berne, at the head of the Protestant association, allied with the United Provinces, and Luzerne, at the head of the Catholic association, with France.

19.20.oldText: 1. Pfeffel, "Nouvel Abreg. Chronol. de l'Hist., etc., d'Allemagne," says the pretext was to indemnify himself for the cost of the expedition.

20.1.oldText: The United Netherlands is a confederacy of republics, or rather of aristocracies, of a very remarkable texture, yet it confirms all the lessons drawn from those we have already reviewed.

20.2.oldText: The union is composed of seven coequal and sovereign states, and each state or province is itself a composition of equal and independent cities. In all important matters, not only the provinces but the cities must be unanimous.

20.3.oldText: The sovereignty of the Union is represented by the States-General, usually consisting of about fifty deputies appointed by the provinces. They hold their seats — some for life, some for six, three, and one years. From two provinces they continue in their appointments at the pleasure of those provinces.

20.4.oldText: The States-General has authority to enter into treaties and alliances; to make war and peace; to raise armies and equip fleets; to set quotas and demand contributions. In all these cases, however, unanimity and the approval of the constituents are required. They have authority to appoint and receive ambassadors; to execute treaties and alliances already made; to provide for the collection of duties on imports and exports; to regulate the mint, with provision for the rights of the provinces; and to govern as sovereigns the dependent territories. The provinces are restrained, except by general consent, from entering into foreign treaties; from establishing imposts harmful to others or charging their neighbors with higher duties than their own subjects. A council of state, a chamber of accounts, and five colleges of admiralty assist and strengthen the federal administration.

20.5.oldText: The executive magistrate of the union is the stadtholder, who is now an hereditary prince. His main weight and influence in the republic come from this independent title; from his great patrimonial estates; from his family connections with some of the chief potentates of Europe; and, perhaps more than all, from his being stadtholder in the several provinces as well as for the union. In that provincial role he appoints town magistrates under certain regulations, executes provincial decrees, presides when he pleases in the provincial tribunals, and has throughout the power of pardon.

20.6.oldText: As stadtholder of the union he has, however, considerable prerogatives.

20.7.oldText: In his political role he has authority to settle disputes between the provinces when other methods fail; to take part in the deliberations of the States-General and in their particular conferences; to give audiences to foreign ambassadors; and to keep agents at foreign courts for his own affairs.

20.8.oldText: In his military role he commands the federal troops, provides for garrisons, and in general regulates military affairs. He fills all appointments from colonels to ensigns, and the governments and posts of fortified towns.

20.9.oldText: In his marine role he is admiral-general and oversees and directs everything related to naval forces and other naval affairs. He presides in the admiralties in person or by proxy, appoints lieutenant-admirals and other officers, and establishes courts-martial whose sentences are not carried out until he approves them.

20.10.oldText: His revenue, apart from his private income, amounts to three hundred thousand florins. The standing army he commands consists of about forty thousand men.

20.11.oldText: Such is the nature of the celebrated Belgic confederacy, as drawn on parchment. What characteristics has practice stamped on it? Weakness in the government; discord among the provinces; foreign influence and indignities; a precarious existence in peace, and special calamities from war.

20.12.oldText: It was long ago observed by Grotius that nothing but his countrymen's hatred of the house of Austria kept them from being ruined by the vices of their constitution.

20.13.oldText: The union of Utrecht, says another respectable writer, places an authority in the States-General that seems sufficient to ensure harmony, but the jealousy in each province makes the practice very different from the theory.

20.14.oldText: The same instrument, says another, obliges each province to levy certain contributions; but this article never could, and probably never will, be carried out, because the inland provinces, which have little commerce, cannot pay an equal quota.

20.15.oldText: In matters of contribution, it is the practice to set aside the articles of the constitution. The danger of delay forces the consenting provinces to furnish their quotas without waiting for the others, and then to obtain reimbursement from the others, by deputations, which are frequent, or otherwise as best they can. The great wealth and influence of the province of Holland enable her to accomplish both these purposes.

20.16.oldText: More than once it has happened that deficiencies had to be ultimately collected at the point of the bayonet. This is practicable, though dreadful, in a confederacy where one of the members exceeds in force all the rest, and where several of them are too small to think of resistance. But it is utterly impractical in one composed of members several of which are equal to each other in strength and resources, and each capable of a vigorous and persevering defense.

20.17.oldText: Foreign ministers, says Sir William Temple, who was himself a foreign minister, evade matters taken ad referendum by tampering with the provinces and cities. In 1726, the treaty of Hanover was delayed by these means a whole year. Instances of a similar nature are numerous and well known.

20.18.oldText: In critical emergencies, the States-General is often forced to overstep its constitutional bounds. In 1688 they concluded a treaty on their own at the risk of their heads. The treaty of Westphalia in 1648, by which their independence was formally and finally recognized, was concluded without the consent of Zealand. Even as recently as the last treaty of peace with Great Britain, the constitutional principle of unanimity was set aside. A weak constitution must necessarily end either in dissolution, for lack of proper powers, or in usurpation of the powers needed for public safety. Whether the usurpation, once begun, will stop at the safe point or go on to the dangerous extreme, must depend on the circumstances of the moment. Tyranny has perhaps grown more often out of the assumptions of power, called for by pressing emergencies under a defective constitution, than out of the full exercise of the largest constitutional authorities.

20.19.oldText: Despite the calamities produced by the stadtholdership, it has been supposed that without his influence in the individual provinces, the causes of anarchy plain in the confederacy would long ago have dissolved it. "Under such a government," says the Abbe Mably, "the Union could never have lasted, if the provinces had not within themselves a spring capable of quickening their slowness and forcing them to think alike. This spring is the stadtholder." Sir William Temple remarks that "in the intervals of the stadtholdership, Holland, by her riches and authority, which drew the others into a kind of dependence, supplied the place."

20.20.oldText: These are not the only circumstances that have controlled the tendency to anarchy and dissolution. The surrounding powers impose an absolute necessity of union to a certain degree, while at the same time they nourish, by their intrigues, the constitutional vices that keep the republic always somewhat at their mercy.

20.21.oldText: True patriots have long lamented the fatal tendency of these vices. They have made no fewer than four formal experiments through EXTRAORDINARY ASSEMBLIES, convened for the special purpose, to apply a remedy. As many times their commendable zeal has found it impossible to UNITE THE PUBLIC COUNCILS in reforming the known, the acknowledged, the fatal evils of the existing constitution. Let us pause, my fellow-citizens, for a moment over this melancholy and warning lesson of history. With the tear that drops for the calamities brought upon mankind by their conflicting opinions and selfish passions, let our gratitude mix a prayer of thanks to Heaven for the providential harmony that has marked the consultations for our political happiness.

20.22.oldText: A plan was also conceived to establish a general tax administered by the federal authority. This too had its opponents and failed.

20.23.oldText: This unhappy people now seem to be suffering, from popular convulsions, from quarrels among the states, and from actual invasion by foreign arms, the crisis of their destiny. All nations have their eyes fixed on the dreadful spectacle. The first wish prompted by humanity is that this severe trial may issue in such a revolution of their government as will establish their union and make it the parent of tranquility, freedom, and happiness. The next is that the asylum under which we trust the enjoyment of these blessings will soon be secured in this country, may receive and console them for the catastrophe of their own.

20.24.oldText: I make no apology for having dwelt so long on these federal precedents. Experience is the oracle of truth, and where its responses are unequivocal they ought to be conclusive and sacred. The important truth it unequivocally pronounces in this case is that a sovereignty over sovereigns, a government over governments, a legislation for communities as opposed to individuals, is in theory a contradiction in terms, and in practice subverts the order and ends of civil polity by substituting VIOLENCE in place of LAW, or the destructive COERCION of the SWORD in place of the mild and salutary COERCION of the MAGISTRACY.

21.0.oldText: Having taken a summary review in the last three numbers of the principal circumstances and events that have shaped the character and fate of other confederate governments, I will now proceed to enumerate the most important defects that have so far disappointed our hopes from the system established among ourselves. To form a sound and satisfactory judgment of the proper remedy, we absolutely must be well acquainted with the extent and severity of the disease.

21.1.oldText: The next most obvious defect of the existing Confederation is the total lack of a SANCTION for its laws. The United States as now composed has no power to compel obedience or to punish disobedience to its resolutions, whether by financial penalties, by suspending or stripping privileges, or by any other constitutional means. There is no express delegation of authority to it to use force against delinquent members. If such a right were imputed to the federal head as flowing from the nature of the social compact between the States, it must be by inference and construction, in the face of that part of the second article that declares "that each State shall retain every power, jurisdiction, and right, not EXPRESSLY delegated to the United States in Congress assembled." There is, no doubt, a striking absurdity in supposing that no such right exists, but we are reduced to a dilemma. We must either accept that supposition, preposterous as it may seem, or contradict and explain away a provision that has lately been a repeated theme of praise from those who oppose the new Constitution, and the absence of which from that plan has been the subject of much plausible criticism and severe censure. If we are unwilling to weaken the force of this celebrated provision, we must conclude that the United States offers the extraordinary spectacle of a government with not even the shadow of constitutional power to enforce its own laws. From the examples cited, it will appear that the American Confederacy in this respect stands set apart from every other institution of its kind, and presents a new and unparalleled phenomenon in the political world.

21.2.oldText: The lack of a mutual guaranty of the State governments is another major flaw in the federal plan. There is nothing of this kind declared in the articles that compose it. To imply a tacit guaranty from considerations of utility would be an even more flagrant departure from the clause just mentioned than to imply a tacit power of coercion from the same considerations. The lack of a guaranty, though it might in its consequences endanger the Union, does not so immediately attack its existence as the lack of a constitutional sanction for its laws.

21.3.oldText: Without a guaranty, we must give up the help to be drawn from the Union in repelling those domestic dangers that may sometimes threaten the existence of the State constitutions. Usurpation may rear its head in each State and trample on the people's liberties, while the national government could legally do nothing more than watch its encroachments with indignation and regret. A successful faction may set up a tyranny on the ruins of order and law, while no help could constitutionally be given by the Union to the friends and supporters of the government. The stormy situation from which Massachusetts has only just emerged proves that dangers of this kind are not merely speculative. Who can say what the outcome of her recent convulsions might have been if the malcontents had been led by a Caesar or a Cromwell? Who can predict what effect a despotism established in Massachusetts would have on the liberties of New Hampshire or Rhode Island, of Connecticut or New York?

21.4.oldText: Excessive pride in State importance has led some minds to object to a guaranty in the federal government as an officious meddling in the domestic affairs of the members. A scruple of this kind would deprive us of one of the chief advantages to be expected from union, and can only come from a misunderstanding of the provision itself. It would be no obstacle to reforms of a State constitution by a majority of the people in a legal and peaceable way. That right would remain undiminished. The guaranty could only operate against changes effected by violence. Toward preventing calamities of this kind, no number of checks is too many. The peace of society and the stability of government depend absolutely on the effectiveness of the precautions taken in this respect. Where the whole power of the government is in the hands of the people, there is the less excuse for using violent remedies for partial or occasional disorders of the State. The natural cure for misadministration in a popular or representative constitution is a change of men. A guaranty by national authority would be aimed as much against the usurpations of rulers as against the unrest and outrages of faction and sedition in the community.

21.5.oldText: The principle of regulating the contributions of the States to the common treasury by QUOTAS is another fundamental error in the Confederation. Its incompatibility with an adequate supply of national needs has already been pointed out, and has been amply shown by the trial that has been made of it. I speak of it now solely with a view to equality among the States. Anyone who has been used to considering the circumstances that produce and constitute national wealth must be satisfied that there is no common standard or barometer by which its degree can be measured. Neither the value of lands nor the number of people, both of which have been proposed in turn as the rule of State contributions, has any claim to being a fair representative. If we compare the wealth of the United Netherlands with that of Russia or Germany, or even of France, and at the same time compare the total value of lands and the aggregate population of that small district with the total value of lands and the aggregate population of the immense regions of any of those three countries, we will see at once that there is no comparison between the proportion of either of these two factors and the relative wealth of those nations. If the same parallel were drawn between several American States, it would yield a similar result. Compare Virginia with North Carolina, Pennsylvania with Connecticut, or Maryland with New Jersey, and we will be convinced that the relative ability of those States in raising revenue bears little or no analogy to their comparative stock of lands or to their comparative population. The point may be illustrated equally well by a similar process between the counties of the same State. No one familiar with the State of New York will doubt that the active wealth of King's County bears a much greater proportion to that of Montgomery than would appear if we took either the total value of lands or the total number of people as a criterion!

21.6.oldText: The wealth of nations depends on an infinite variety of causes. Situation, soil, climate, the nature of the products, the nature of the government, the genius of the citizens, the degree of information they possess, the state of commerce, of arts, of industry — these circumstances and many more, too complex, minute, or accidental to specify, cause differences in the relative opulence and riches of different countries that are hardly conceivable. The clear consequence is that there can be no common measure of national wealth, and therefore no general or fixed rule by which a state's ability to pay taxes can be determined. The attempt, then, to regulate the contributions of the members of a confederacy by any such rule must inevitably produce glaring inequality and extreme oppression.

21.7.oldText: This inequality alone would be enough in America to bring about the eventual destruction of the Union, if any way of enforcing compliance with its requisitions could be devised. The suffering States would not long agree to remain associated on a principle that distributes the public burdens with so unequal a hand, and that was calculated to impoverish and oppress the citizens of some States, while those of others would scarcely be aware of the small share of the weight they were required to bear. This, however, is an evil inseparable from the principle of quotas and requisitions.

21.8.oldText: There is no way to avoid this inconvenience except by authorizing the national government to raise its own revenues in its own way. Imposts, excises, and in general all duties on articles of consumption may be compared to a fluid that will, in time, find its level with the means of paying them. The amount each citizen contributes will to some degree be at his own option, and can be regulated by attention to his resources. The rich may be extravagant; the poor can be frugal. Private oppression can always be avoided by a judicious selection of objects fit for such impositions. If inequalities arise in some States from duties on particular objects, they will in all likelihood be balanced by proportional inequalities in other States from the duties on other objects. In the course of time and events, an equilibrium, as far as it is attainable in so complex a subject, will be established everywhere. Or, if inequalities should still exist, they would not be so great in degree, so uniform in operation, or so odious in appearance as those that would inevitably spring from quotas, on any scale that could possibly be devised.

21.9.oldText: It is a marked advantage of taxes on articles of consumption that they contain in their own nature a security against excess. They prescribe their own limit, which cannot be exceeded without defeating the goal proposed, namely an increase of revenue. Applied to this object, the saying is as true as it is witty: "in political arithmetic, two and two do not always make four." If duties are too high, they reduce consumption; collection is evaded; and the yield to the treasury is not as great as when they are kept within proper and moderate bounds. This forms a complete barrier against any material oppression of the citizens by taxes of this class, and is itself a natural limit on the power of imposing them.

21.10.oldText: Impositions of this kind usually fall under the heading of indirect taxes, and must for a long time form the chief part of the revenue raised in this country. Direct taxes, which mainly relate to land and buildings, may admit of a rule of apportionment. Either the value of land or the number of people may serve as a standard. The state of agriculture and the populousness of a country have been considered as nearly connected with each other. As a rule for the purpose intended, numbers, with a view to simplicity and certainty, are entitled to preference. In every country it is a Herculean task to obtain a valuation of the land; in a country imperfectly settled and progressive in improvement, the difficulties are increased almost to impracticability. The expense of an accurate valuation is, in all situations, a formidable objection. In a branch of taxation where no limits to the discretion of the government are to be found in the nature of things, fixing a definite rule, not incompatible with the end, may be attended with fewer inconveniences than leaving that discretion entirely at large.

22.0.oldText: In addition to the defects already enumerated in the existing federal system, there are others of no less importance, which together make it altogether unfit for the administration of the affairs of the Union.

22.1.oldText: The lack of a power to regulate commerce is admitted by all parties to be one of them. The usefulness of such a power has been anticipated under the first head of our inquiries, and for that reason, as well as from the universal conviction held on the subject, little needs to be added here. It is indeed obvious, on the most superficial view, that there is no object, whether for trade or finance, that more strongly demands a federal supervision. The lack of it has already blocked the formation of beneficial treaties with foreign powers, and has given rise to dissatisfaction between the States. No nation acquainted with the nature of our political association would be unwise enough to enter into stipulations with the United States by which they granted privileges of any importance, while they were aware that the engagements on the part of the Union might at any moment be violated by its members, and while they found from experience that they could enjoy every advantage they wanted in our markets without granting us any return except such as their momentary convenience might suggest. It is no surprise, therefore, that Mr. Jenkinson, in introducing into the House of Commons a bill for regulating the temporary intercourse between the two countries, prefaced its introduction by declaring that similar provisions in earlier bills had been found to answer every purpose for the commerce of Great Britain, and that it would be prudent to persist in the plan until it should appear whether the American government was likely to acquire greater consistency.(1)

22.2.oldText: Several States have tried, by separate prohibitions, restrictions, and exclusions, to influence the conduct of that kingdom in this matter. But the lack of concert, arising from the lack of a general authority and from clashing and dissimilar views in the State, has so far frustrated every experiment of the kind, and will keep doing so as long as the same obstacles to a uniformity of measures continue to exist.

22.3.oldText: The interfering and unneighborly regulations of some States, contrary to the true spirit of the Union, have on different occasions given just cause for offense and complaint to others. It is to be feared that examples of this nature, if not restrained by national control, would multiply and extend until they became no less serious sources of animosity and discord than they are injurious obstacles to commerce between the different parts of the Confederacy. "The commerce of the German empire(2) is in continual difficulty from the multiplicity of the duties which the several princes and states exact upon the merchandise passing through their territories, by which the fine streams and navigable rivers with which Germany is so happily watered are rendered almost useless." Though the genius of the people of this country might never let this description strictly apply to us, we may reasonably expect, from the gradual conflicts of State regulations, that the citizens of each would eventually come to be considered and treated by the others as little better than foreigners and aliens.

22.4.oldText: The power of raising armies, by the most obvious construction of the articles of Confederation, is merely a power of making requisitions on the States for quotas of men. This practice, in the course of the late war, was found full of obstructions to a vigorous and economical system of defense. It gave rise to a competition between the States that created a kind of auction for men. To furnish the quotas required of them, they outbid each other until bounties grew to an enormous and unsupportable size. The hope of a still further increase encouraged those willing to serve to delay their enlistment, and made them unwilling to engage for any considerable period. Hence the slow and scanty levies of men in the most critical emergencies of our affairs; short enlistments at unparalleled expense; continual fluctuations in the troops, ruinous to their discipline and frequently subjecting public safety to the perilous crisis of a disbanded army. Hence also those oppressive expedients for raising men that were resorted to on several occasions, which nothing but the enthusiasm of liberty could have made the people endure.

22.5.oldText: This method of raising troops is no less unfriendly to economy and vigor than it is to an equal distribution of the burden. The States near the seat of war, driven by motives of self-preservation, made efforts to furnish their quotas that even exceeded their abilities, while those at a distance from danger were for the most part as remiss as the others were diligent in their efforts. The immediate pressure of this inequality was not, in this case, as in the case of money contributions, eased by the hope of a final settlement. The States that did not pay their proportions of money could at least be charged with their deficiencies; but no account could be made of the deficiencies in the supplies of men. We will not, however, see much reason to regret the lack of this hope, when we consider how little prospect there is that the most delinquent States will ever be able to make compensation for their financial failures. The system of quotas and requisitions, whether applied to men or money, is in every view a system of weakness in the Union, and of inequality and injustice among the members.

22.6.oldText: The right of equal suffrage among the States is another objectionable part of the Confederation. Every idea of proportion and every rule of fair representation joins to condemn a principle that gives to Rhode Island an equal weight in the scale of power with Massachusetts, or Connecticut, or New York, and to Delaware an equal voice in the national deliberations with Pennsylvania, or Virginia, or North Carolina. Its operation contradicts the fundamental maxim of republican government, which requires that the sense of the majority should prevail. Sophistry may reply that sovereigns are equal, and that a majority of the votes of the States will be a majority of confederated America. But this kind of logical sleight of hand will never counteract the plain suggestions of justice and common-sense. It may happen that this majority of States is a small minority of the people of America;(3) and two-thirds of the people of America could not long be persuaded, on the strength of artificial distinctions and syllogistic subtleties, to submit their interests to the management and disposal of one-third. The larger States would after a while revolt against the idea of receiving the law from the smaller. To accept such a deprivation of their due importance in the political scale would be not only insensitive to the love of power, but even to sacrifice the desire of equality. It is neither rational to expect the first nor just to require the second. The smaller States, considering how peculiarly their safety and welfare depend on union, ought readily to give up a pretension that, if not relinquished, would prove fatal to its duration.

22.7.oldText: It may be objected that not seven but nine States, or two-thirds of the whole number, must consent to the most important resolutions, and so it might be inferred that nine States would always include a majority of the Union. But this does not address the impropriety of an equal vote between States of the most unequal size and population. Nor is the inference accurate in fact, for we can name nine States that contain less than a majority of the people;(4) and it is constitutionally possible that these nine may give the vote. Besides, there are matters of considerable importance decided by a bare majority. There are others on which doubts have been raised, which, if interpreted in favor of the sufficiency of a vote of seven States, would extend its operation to interests of the first magnitude. In addition to this, it is to be observed that there is a probability of an increase in the number of States, with no provision for a proportional increase in the ratio of votes.

22.8.oldText: But this is not all. What at first sight may seem a remedy is in reality a poison. To give a minority a veto over the majority — which is always the case where more than a majority is required for a decision — tends to subject the sense of the greater number to that of the lesser. Congress, from the absence of a few States, has frequently been in the situation of a Polish diet, where a single VOTE has been enough to halt all their movements. A sixtieth part of the Union, which is about the proportion of Delaware and Rhode Island, has several times been able to put a complete stop to its operations. This is one of those refinements which in practice has the opposite effect to what is expected from it in theory.
