The fears of the weaker, or the ambition of the stronger states, or confederacies, will set the same example in the New as Charles VII did in the Old World. The example will be followed here from the same motives that produced universal imitation there. Instead of deriving from our situation the precious advantage that Great Britain has derived from hers, the face of America will be but a copy of that of the continent of Europe. It will present liberty everywhere crushed between standing armies and perpetual taxes. The fortunes of disunited America will be even more disastrous than those of Europe. The sources of evil in the latter are confined to her own limits. No superior powers from another quarter of the globe intrigue among her rival nations, inflame their mutual animosities, and render them the instruments of foreign ambition. In America the miseries springing from her internal jealousies, contentions, and wars would form only a part of her lot. A plentiful addition of evils would have their source in that relation in which Europe stands to this quarter of the earth, and which no other quarter bears to Europe.

41.14.oldText: This picture of the consequences of disunion cannot be too highly colored, or too often exhibited. Every man who loves peace, every man who loves his country, every man who loves liberty, ought to have it ever before his eyes, that he may cherish in his heart a due attachment to the Union of America, and be able to set a due value on the means of preserving it.

41.15.oldText: Next to the effective establishment of the Union, the best possible precaution against danger from standing armies is a limitation of the term for which revenue may be appropriated to their support. The Constitution has prudently added this precaution. I will not repeat the observations I have already made on this subject. But it may not be improper to notice an argument against this part of the Constitution drawn from the policy and practice of Great Britain. It is said that the continuance of an army in that kingdom requires an annual vote of the legislature, while the American Constitution has lengthened this critical period to two years. This is the form in which the comparison is usually stated to the public. But is it a just form? Is it a fair comparison? Does the British Constitution restrain parliamentary discretion to one year? Does the American impose on Congress appropriations for two years? On the contrary, it cannot be unknown to the authors of this fallacy themselves that the British Constitution fixes no limit whatever to the discretion of the legislature, and that the American ties down the legislature to two years as the longest admissible term.

41.16.oldText: Had the argument from the British example been truly stated, it would have been: the term for which supplies may be appropriated to the army establishment, though unlimited by the British Constitution, has nevertheless in practice been limited by parliamentary discretion to a single year. Now, if in Great Britain — where the House of Commons is elected for seven years; where so great a proportion of the members are elected by so small a proportion of the people; where the electors are so corrupted by the representatives, and the representatives so corrupted by the Crown — the representative body can possess a power to make appropriations to the army for an indefinite term without desiring, or daring, to extend the term beyond a single year, ought not suspicion herself to blush in pretending that the representatives of the United States, elected freely by the whole body of the people every second year, cannot be safely entrusted with the discretion over such appropriations, expressly limited to the short period of TWO YEARS?

41.17.oldText: A bad cause seldom fails to betray itself. Of this truth, the management of the opposition to the federal government is an unvaried example. But among all the blunders committed, none is more striking than the attempt to enlist on that side the prudent jealousy entertained by the people of standing armies. The attempt has fully awakened public attention to that important subject and has led to investigations that must terminate in a thorough and universal conviction — not only that the Constitution has provided the most effective guards against danger from that quarter, but that nothing short of a Constitution fully adequate to the national defense and the preservation of the Union can save America from as many standing armies as it may be split into states or confederacies, and from such a progressive augmentation of these establishments in each as will render them as burdensome to the property and ominous to the liberties of the people as any establishment that may become necessary under a united and efficient government must be tolerable to the former and safe to the latter.

41.18.oldText: The palpable necessity of the power to provide and maintain a navy has protected that part of the Constitution against a spirit of censure that has spared few other parts. It must indeed be numbered among the greatest blessings of America that as her Union will be the only source of her maritime strength, so this will be a principal source of her security against danger from abroad. In this respect our situation bears another likeness to the insular advantage of Great Britain. The batteries most capable of repelling foreign enterprises against our safety are happily such as can never be turned by a perfidious government against our liberties.

41.19.oldText: The inhabitants of the Atlantic frontier are all deeply interested in this provision for naval protection. If they have hitherto been allowed to sleep quietly in their beds; if their property has remained safe against the predatory spirit of licentious adventurers; if their maritime towns have not yet been compelled to ransom themselves from the terrors of conflagration by yielding to the exactions of daring and sudden invaders — these instances of good fortune are not to be ascribed to the capacity of the existing government for the protection of those from whom it claims allegiance, but to causes that are fugitive and fallacious. Except perhaps Virginia and Maryland, which are peculiarly vulnerable on their eastern frontiers, no part of the Union ought to feel more anxiety on this subject than New York. Her seacoast is extensive. A very important district of the state is an island. The state itself is penetrated by a large navigable river for more than fifty leagues. The great emporium of its commerce, the great reservoir of its wealth, lies every moment at the mercy of events, and may almost be regarded as a hostage for ignominious compliances with the dictates of a foreign enemy, or even with the rapacious demands of pirates and barbarians. Should war result from the precarious situation of European affairs, and all the unruly passions attending it be let loose on the ocean, our escape from insults and depredations — not only on that element but every part of the other bordering on it — will be truly miraculous. In the present condition of America, the states more immediately exposed to these calamities have nothing to hope from the phantom of a general government that now exists. And if their single resources were equal to the task of fortifying themselves against the danger, the object to be protected would be almost consumed by the means of protecting it.

41.20.oldText: The power of regulating and calling forth the militia has already been sufficiently vindicated and explained.

41.21.oldText: The power of levying and borrowing money, being the sinew of that which is to be exerted in the national defense, is properly thrown into the same class with it. This power has also been examined already with much attention, and has, I trust, been clearly shown to be necessary, both in the extent and form given to it by the Constitution. I will address one additional reflection only to those who contend that the power should have been restrained to external taxation — by which they mean taxes on articles imported from other countries. It cannot be doubted that this will always be a valuable source of revenue; that for a considerable time it must be a principal source; that at this moment it is an essential one. But we may form very mistaken ideas if we do not remember in our calculations that the extent of revenue drawn from foreign commerce must vary with the variations both in the extent and the kind of imports, and that these variations do not correspond with the progress of population, which must be the general measure of public wants. As long as agriculture continues the sole field of labor, the importation of manufactures must increase as consumers multiply. As soon as domestic manufactures are begun by the hands not called for by agriculture, imported manufactures will decrease as the number of people increases. In a more remote stage, imports may consist in considerable part of raw materials to be wrought into articles for exportation, and will therefore require encouragement of bounties rather than to be loaded with discouraging duties. A system of government meant for duration ought to contemplate these revolutions and be able to accommodate itself to them.

41.22.oldText: Some who have not denied the necessity of the power of taxation have grounded a fierce attack against the Constitution on the language defining it. It has been urged and echoed that the power "to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises, to pay the debts, and provide for the common defense and general welfare of the United States" amounts to an unlimited commission to exercise every power that may be alleged necessary for the common defense or general welfare. No stronger proof could be given of the distress under which these writers labor for objections than their stooping to such a misconstruction.

41.23.oldText: Had no other enumeration or definition of the powers of Congress been found in the Constitution than the general expressions just cited, the authors of the objection might have had some color for it — though it would have been difficult to find a reason for so awkward a form of describing an authority to legislate in all possible cases. A power to destroy the freedom of the press, the trial by jury, or even to regulate the course of descents or the forms of conveyances must be very singularly expressed by the terms "to raise money for the general welfare."

41.24.oldText: But what color can the objection have when a specification of the objects alluded to by these general terms immediately follows, and is not even separated by a longer pause than a semicolon? If the different parts of the same instrument ought to be so expounded as to give meaning to every part that will bear it, shall one part of the same sentence be excluded altogether from a share in the meaning, and shall the more doubtful and indefinite terms be retained in their full extent while the clear and precise expressions are denied any signification whatever? For what purpose could the enumeration of particular powers be inserted, if these and all others were meant to be included in the preceding general power? Nothing is more natural or common than first to use a general phrase, then explain and qualify it by reciting particulars. But the idea of an enumeration of particulars that neither explain nor qualify the general meaning, and can have no other effect than to confound and mislead, is an absurdity, which we are reduced to the dilemma of charging either on the authors of the objection or on the authors of the Constitution. We must take the liberty of supposing it had not its origin with the latter.

41.25.oldText: The objection here is the more extraordinary, as it appears that the language used by the convention is a copy from the articles of Confederation. The objects of the Union among the states, as described in article third, are "their common defense, security of their liberties, and mutual and general welfare." The terms of article eighth are still more identical: "All charges of war and all other expenses that shall be incurred for the common defense or general welfare, and allowed by the United States in Congress, shall be defrayed out of a common treasury," etc. A similar language again occurs in article ninth. Construe either of these articles by the rules that would justify the construction put on the new Constitution, and they vest in the existing Congress a power to legislate in all cases whatsoever. But what would have been thought of that assembly, if, attaching themselves to these general expressions and disregarding the specifications that ascertain and limit their import, they had exercised an unlimited power of providing for the common defense and general welfare? I appeal to the objectors themselves whether they would in that case have employed the same reasoning in justification of Congress as they now make use of against the convention. How difficult it is for error to escape its own condemnation!

42.0.oldText: The second class of powers lodged in the general government consists of those that regulate intercourse with foreign nations: to make treaties; to send and receive ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls; to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations; and to regulate foreign commerce, including a power to prohibit, after the year 1808, the importation of slaves, and to lay an intermediate duty of ten dollars per head as a discouragement to such importations.

42.1.oldText: This class of powers forms an obvious and essential branch of federal administration. If we are to be one nation in any respect, it clearly ought to be in respect to other nations.

42.2.oldText: The powers to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors speak their own propriety. Both are comprised in the articles of Confederation, with this difference only: the former is freed by the convention's plan of an exception under which treaties might be substantially frustrated by state regulations; and a power of appointing and receiving "other public ministers and consuls" is expressly added to the former provision concerning ambassadors. The term "ambassador," if taken strictly as required by the second of the articles of Confederation, comprehends only the highest grade of public ministers and excludes the grades the United States will most likely prefer when foreign embassies are necessary. And under no latitude of construction will the term include consuls. Yet it has been found expedient, and has been the practice of Congress, to employ inferior grades of public ministers and to send and receive consuls.

42.3.oldText: It is true that where treaties of commerce stipulate the mutual appointment of consuls whose functions are connected with commerce, the admission of foreign consuls may fall within the power of making commercial treaties. And where no such treaties exist, the mission of American consuls into foreign countries may PERHAPS be covered under the authority given by the ninth article of the Confederation to appoint all such civil officers as may be necessary for managing the general affairs of the United States. But the admission of consuls into the United States, where no previous treaty has stipulated it, seems to have been nowhere provided for. Supplying this omission is one of the lesser instances in which the convention have improved on the model before them. But the most minute provisions become important when they prevent the necessity or the pretext for gradual and unobserved usurpations of power. A list of the cases in which Congress has been betrayed, or forced by the defects of the Confederation, into violations of their chartered authorities would not a little surprise those who have paid no attention to the subject. It would be no inconsiderable argument in favor of the new Constitution, which seems to have provided no less studiously for the lesser than for the more obvious and striking defects of the old.

42.4.oldText: The power to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations, belongs with equal propriety to the general government, and is a still greater improvement on the articles of Confederation. These articles contain no provision for offenses against the law of nations, and consequently leave it in the power of any indiscreet member to embroil the Confederacy with foreign nations. The provision of the federal articles on piracies and felonies extends no further than establishing courts for the trial of these offenses. The definition of piracies might perhaps, without inconvenience, be left to the law of nations, though a legislative definition of them is found in most municipal codes. A definition of felonies on the high seas is evidently necessary. Felony is a term of loose signification, even in the common law of England, and of various import in the statute law of that kingdom. But neither the common nor statute law of that, or of any other nation, ought to be a standard for the proceedings of this, unless previously made its own by legislative adoption. The meaning of the term as defined in the codes of the several states would be as impracticable as the former would be a dishonorable and illegitimate guide. It is not precisely the same in any two of the states, and varies in each with every revision of its criminal laws. For the sake of certainty and uniformity, therefore, the power of defining felonies in this case was in every respect necessary and proper.

42.5.oldText: The regulation of foreign commerce, having fallen within several views taken of this subject, has been too fully discussed to need additional proof here of its being properly submitted to the federal administration.

42.6.oldText: It would doubtless have been preferable that the power of prohibiting the importation of slaves had not been postponed until the year 1808, or rather that it had been allowed to take immediate effect. But it is not difficult to account either for this restriction on the general government or for the manner in which the whole clause is expressed. It ought to be considered as a great point gained in favor of humanity that a period of twenty years may terminate forever, within these states, a traffic which has so long and so loudly upbraided the barbarism of modern policy; that within that period, it will receive a considerable discouragement from the federal government, and may be totally abolished by a concurrence of the few states which continue the unnatural traffic, in the prohibitory example given by so great a majority of the Union. Happy would it be for the unfortunate Africans if an equal prospect lay before them of being redeemed from the oppressions of their European brethren!

42.7.oldText: Attempts have been made to pervert this clause into an objection against the Constitution — representing it on one side as a criminal toleration of an illicit practice, and on another as calculated to prevent voluntary and beneficial emigrations from Europe to America. I mention these misconstructions not to give them an answer, for they deserve none, but as specimens of the manner and spirit in which some have thought fit to conduct their opposition to the proposed government.

42.8.oldText: The powers included in the THIRD class are those providing for harmony and proper intercourse among the states.

42.9.oldText: Under this head might be included the particular restraints imposed on the authority of the states, and certain powers of the judicial department. But the former are reserved for a distinct class, and the latter will be examined particularly when we arrive at the structure and organization of the government. I shall confine myself to a cursory review of the remaining powers in this third description: to regulate commerce among the several states and the Indian tribes; to coin money and regulate its value, and that of foreign coin; to provide for the punishment of counterfeiting the current coin and securities of the United States; to fix the standard of weights and measures; to establish a uniform rule of naturalization and uniform laws of bankruptcy; to prescribe how the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of each state shall be proved, and the effect they shall have in other states; and to establish post offices and post roads.

42.10.oldText: The defect of power in the existing Confederacy to regulate commerce between its members is among those clearly pointed out by experience. To the proofs and remarks former papers have brought into view, it may be added that without this supplemental provision, the great and essential power of regulating foreign commerce would have been incomplete and ineffective. A very material object of this power was relieving the states which import and export through other states from the improper contributions levied on them by the latter. Were these at liberty to regulate trade between state and state, ways would be found to load the articles of import and export, during their passage through their jurisdiction, with duties that would fall on the makers of the latter and the consumers of the former. We may be assured by past experience that such a practice would be introduced by future contrivances. From that and from common knowledge of human affairs, it would nourish unceasing animosities and not improbably terminate in serious interruptions of public tranquility. To those who do not view the question through the medium of passion or interest, the desire of the commercial states to collect, in any form, an indirect revenue from their uncommercial neighbors must appear no less impolitic than unfair, since it would stimulate the injured party, by resentment as well as interest, to resort to less convenient channels for their foreign trade. But the mild voice of reason, pleading the cause of an enlarged and permanent interest, is too often drowned, before public bodies as well as individuals, by the clamors of an impatient avidity for immediate and immoderate gain.

42.11.oldText: The necessity of a superintending authority over the reciprocal trade of confederated states has been illustrated by other examples as well as our own. In Switzerland, where the Union is so very slight, each canton is obliged to allow merchandise a passage through its jurisdiction into other cantons without an augmentation of tolls. In Germany it is a law of the empire that the princes and states shall not lay tolls or customs on bridges, rivers, or passages without the consent of the emperor and the diet — though it appears from a quotation in an antecedent paper that the practice in this, as in many other instances in that confederacy, has not followed the law, and has produced there the mischiefs foreseen here. Among the restraints imposed by the Union of the Netherlands on its members, one is that they shall not establish imposts disadvantageous to their neighbors without general permission.

42.12.oldText: The regulation of commerce with the Indian tribes is very properly unfettered from two limitations in the articles of Confederation that render the provision obscure and contradictory. The power is there restrained to Indians not members of any of the states, and is not to violate or infringe the legislative right of any state within its own limits. What kind of Indians are to be deemed members of a state is not yet settled, and has been a question of frequent perplexity and contention in the federal councils. And how the trade with Indians, though not members of a state, yet residing within its legislative jurisdiction, can be regulated by an external authority without intruding on the internal rights of legislation, is absolutely incomprehensible. This is not the only case in which the articles of Confederation have inconsiderately endeavored to accomplish impossibilities — to reconcile a partial sovereignty in the Union with complete sovereignty in the states; to subvert a mathematical axiom by taking away a part and letting the whole remain.

42.13.oldText: All that needs to be remarked on the power to coin money, regulate its value, and that of foreign coin, is that by providing for this last case, the Constitution has supplied a material omission in the articles of Confederation. The authority of the existing Congress is restrained to the regulation of coin struck by their own authority, or that of the respective states. It must be seen at once that the proposed uniformity in the value of the current coin might be destroyed by subjecting that of foreign coin to the different regulations of the different states.

42.14.oldText: The punishment of counterfeiting the public securities, as well as the current coin, is submitted of course to that authority which is to secure the value of both.

42.15.oldText: The regulation of weights and measures is transferred from the articles of Confederation, and is founded on like considerations with the preceding power of regulating coin.

42.16.oldText: The dissimilarity in the rules of naturalization has long been remarked as a fault in our system, laying a foundation for intricate and delicate questions. In the fourth article of the Confederation it is declared "that the FREE INHABITANTS of each of these States, paupers, vagabonds, and fugitives from justice, excepted, shall be entitled to all privileges and immunities of FREE CITIZENS in the several States; and THE PEOPLE of each State shall, in every other, enjoy all the privileges of trade and commerce," etc. There is a confusion of language here that is remarkable. Why the terms FREE INHABITANTS are used in one part of the article, FREE CITIZENS in another, and PEOPLE in another; or what was meant by superadding to "all privileges and immunities of free citizens," "all the privileges of trade and commerce," cannot easily be determined. It seems to be a construction scarcely avoidable that those who come under the denomination of FREE INHABITANTS of a state, although not citizens of such state, are entitled in every other state to all the privileges of FREE CITIZENS of the latter — that is, to greater privileges than they may be entitled to in their own state. So it may be in the power of a particular state, or rather every state is laid under a necessity, not only to confer the rights of citizenship in other states upon any whom it may admit to such rights within itself, but upon any whom it may allow to become inhabitants within its jurisdiction. But were an exposition of the term "inhabitants" admitted that confined the stipulated privileges to citizens alone, the difficulty is diminished only, not removed. The very improper power would still be retained by each state of naturalizing aliens in every other state. In one state, residence for a short term confirms all the rights of citizenship. In another, qualifications of greater importance are required. An alien, therefore, legally incapacitated for certain rights in the latter, may, by previous residence only in the former, elude his incapacity, and thus the law of one state be preposterously rendered paramount to the law of another, within the jurisdiction of the other. We owe it to mere chance that very serious embarrassments on this subject have hitherto been escaped. By the laws of several states, certain descriptions of aliens, who had rendered themselves obnoxious, were laid under interdicts inconsistent not only with the rights of citizenship but with the privilege of residence. What would have been the consequence if such persons, by residence or otherwise, had acquired the character of citizens under the laws of another state, and then asserted their rights as such, both to residence and citizenship, within the state proscribing them? Whatever the legal consequences might have been, other consequences would probably have resulted, of too serious a nature not to be provided against. The new Constitution has accordingly, with great propriety, made provision against them, and all others proceeding from the defect of the Confederation on this head, by authorizing the general government to establish a uniform rule of naturalization throughout the United States.

42.17.oldText: The power of establishing uniform laws of bankruptcy is so intimately connected with the regulation of commerce, and will prevent so many frauds where the parties or their property may lie or be removed into different states, that the expediency of it seems unlikely to be drawn into question.

42.18.oldText: The power of prescribing by general laws the manner in which the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of each state shall be proved, and the effect they shall have in other states, is an evident and valuable improvement on the clause relating to this subject in the articles of Confederation. The meaning of the latter is extremely indeterminate and can be of little importance under any interpretation it will bear. The power here established may be rendered a very convenient instrument of justice, and be particularly beneficial on the borders of contiguous states, where the effects liable to justice may be suddenly and secretly translated, in any stage of the process, within a foreign jurisdiction.

42.19.oldText: The power of establishing post roads must, in every view, be a harmless power, and may, perhaps, by judicious management, become productive of great public conveniency. Nothing that tends to facilitate intercourse between the states can be deemed unworthy of the public care.

43.0.oldText: The fourth class comprises the following miscellaneous powers:

43.2.oldText: The utility of this power will scarcely be questioned. The copyright of authors has been solemnly adjudged in Great Britain to be a right of common law. The right to useful inventions seems with equal reason to belong to the inventors. The public good fully coincides in both cases with the claims of individuals. The states cannot separately make effective provisions for either, and most of them have anticipated the decision of this point by laws passed at the instance of Congress.

43.4.oldText: The indispensable necessity of complete authority at the seat of government carries its own evidence. It is a power exercised by every legislature of the Union, I might say of the world, by virtue of its general supremacy. Without it, not only might the public authority be insulted and its proceedings interrupted with impunity, but a dependence of the members of the general government on the state containing the seat of government, for protection in the exercise of their duty, might bring on the national councils an imputation of awe or influence — equally dishonorable to the government and dissatisfactory to the other members of the Confederacy. This consideration has the more weight as the gradual accumulation of public improvements at the stationary residence of the government would be too great a public pledge to be left in the hands of a single state, and would create so many obstacles to a removal of the government as still further to abridge its necessary independence. The extent of this federal district is sufficiently circumscribed to satisfy every jealousy of an opposite nature. As it is to be appropriated to this use with the consent of the state ceding it; as the state will no doubt provide in the compact for the rights and the consent of the citizens inhabiting it; as the inhabitants will find sufficient inducements of interest to become willing parties to the cession; as they will have had their voice in the election of the government which is to exercise authority over them; as a municipal legislature for local purposes, derived from their own suffrages, will of course be allowed them; and as the authority of the legislature of the state, and of the inhabitants of the ceded part of it, to concur in the cession will be derived from the whole people of the state in their adoption of the Constitution, every imaginable objection seems to be obviated.

43.5.oldText: The necessity of a like authority over forts, magazines, etc., established by the general government, is no less evident. The public money expended on such places, and the public property deposited in them, requires that they should be exempt from the authority of the particular state. Nor would it be proper for the places on which the security of the entire Union may depend to be in any degree dependent on a particular member of it. All objections and scruples are here also obviated by requiring the concurrence of the states concerned in every such establishment.

43.7.oldText: As treason may be committed against the United States, the authority of the United States ought to be enabled to punish it. But as new-fangled and artificial treasons have been the great engines by which violent factions, the natural offspring of free government, have usually wreaked their alternate malignity on each other, the convention has, with great judgment, opposed a barrier to this peculiar danger. They have inserted a constitutional definition of the crime, fixed the proof necessary for conviction of it, and restrained Congress, even in punishing it, from extending the consequences of guilt beyond the person of its author.

43.9.oldText: In the articles of Confederation, no provision is found on this important subject. Canada was to be admitted of right on her joining in the measures of the United States, and the other COLONIES (by which were evidently meant the other British colonies) at the discretion of nine states. The eventual establishment of NEW STATES seems to have been overlooked by the compilers of that instrument. We have seen the inconvenience of this omission, and the assumption of power into which Congress have been led by it. With great propriety, therefore, has the new system supplied the defect. The general precaution that no new states shall be formed without the concurrence of the federal authority, and that of the states concerned, is consonant to the principles which ought to govern such transactions. The particular precaution against the erection of new states by the partition of a state without its consent quiets the jealousy of the larger states, as that of the smaller is quieted by a like precaution against a junction of states without their consent.

43.10.oldText: 5. "To dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States," with a proviso, that "nothing in the Constitution shall be so construed as to prejudice any claims of the United States, or of any particular State."

43.11.oldText: This is a power of very great importance, and required by considerations similar to those that show the propriety of the former. The proviso annexed is proper in itself, and was probably rendered absolutely necessary by jealousies and questions concerning the Western territory sufficiently known to the public.

43.13.oldText: In a confederacy founded on republican principles, and composed of republican members, the superintending government ought clearly to possess authority to defend the system against aristocratic or monarchical innovations. The more intimate the nature of such a union, the greater interest the members have in each other's political institutions, and the greater right to insist that the forms of government under which the compact was entered into should be SUBSTANTIALLY maintained. But a right implies a remedy, and where else could the remedy be deposited than where it is deposited by the Constitution? Governments of dissimilar principles and forms have been found less adapted to a federal coalition of any sort than those of a kindred nature. "As the confederate republic of Germany," says Montesquieu, "consists of free cities and petty states, subject to different princes, experience shows us that it is more imperfect than that of Holland and Switzerland." "Greece was undone," he adds, "as soon as the king of Macedon obtained a seat among the Amphictyons." In the latter case, no doubt, the disproportionate force, as well as the monarchical form, of the new confederate had its share of influence on events. It may possibly be asked what need there could be for such a precaution, and whether it may not become a pretext for alterations in the state governments without the concurrence of the states themselves. These questions admit of ready answers. If the interposition of the general government should not be needed, the provision will be a harmless superfluity in the Constitution. But who can say what experiments may be produced by the caprice of particular states, by the ambition of enterprising leaders, or by the intrigues and influence of foreign powers? To the second question it may be answered that if the general government should interpose by virtue of this constitutional authority, it will be of course bound to pursue the authority. But the authority extends no further than to a GUARANTY of a republican form of government, which supposes a pre-existing government of the form to be guaranteed. As long, therefore, as the existing republican forms are continued by the states, they are guaranteed by the federal Constitution. Whenever the states may choose to substitute other republican forms, they have a right to do so, and to claim the federal guaranty for the latter. The only restriction imposed on them is that they shall not exchange republican for antirepublican Constitutions — a restriction which, it is presumed, will hardly be considered a grievance.

43.14.oldText: A protection against invasion is due from every society to the parts composing it. The latitude of the expression here used seems to secure each state not only against foreign hostility, but against ambitious or vindictive enterprises of its more powerful neighbors. The history both of ancient and modern confederacies proves that the weaker members of the union ought not to be insensible to the policy of this article.

43.15.oldText: Protection against domestic violence is added with equal propriety. It has been remarked that even among the Swiss cantons, which properly speaking are not under one government, provision is made for this object. The history of that league informs us that mutual aid is frequently claimed and afforded, as well by the most democratic as by the other cantons. A recent and well-known event among ourselves has warned us to be prepared for emergencies of a like nature.

43.16.oldText: At first view, it might seem not to square with republican theory to suppose either that a majority have not the right, or that a minority will have the force, to subvert a government — and consequently that federal interposition can never be required, but when it would be improper. But theoretic reasoning, in this as in most cases, must be qualified by the lessons of practice. Why may not illicit combinations for purposes of violence be formed by a majority of a state — especially a small state — as well as by a majority of a county, or a district of the same state? And if the authority of the state ought, in the latter case, to protect the local magistracy, ought not the federal authority, in the former, to support the state authority? Besides, certain parts of the state constitutions are so interwoven with the federal Constitution that a violent blow cannot be given to one without communicating the wound to the other. Insurrections in a state will rarely induce federal interposition, unless the number concerned in them bear some proportion to the friends of government. It will be much better that violence in such cases be repressed by the superintending power than that the majority be left to maintain their cause by a bloody and obstinate contest. The existence of a right to interpose will generally prevent the necessity of exerting it.

43.17.oldText: Is it true that force and right are necessarily on the same side in republican governments? May not the minor party possess such a superiority of pecuniary resources, of military talents and experience, or of secret aid from foreign powers, as will render it superior also in an appeal to the sword? May not a more compact and advantageous position turn the scale against a superior number so situated as to be less capable of a prompt and collected exertion of its strength? Nothing can be more chimerical than to imagine that in a trial of actual force, victory may be calculated by the rules that prevail in a census of the inhabitants, or which determine the event of an election! May it not happen, finally, that the minority of CITIZENS may become a majority of PERSONS by the accession of alien residents, of a casual concourse of adventurers, or of those whom the constitution of the state has not admitted to the rights of suffrage? I take no notice of an unhappy species of population abounding in some of the states, who, during the calm of regular government, are sunk below the level of men, but who, in the tempestuous scenes of civil violence, may emerge into the human character, and give a superiority of strength to any party with which they may associate themselves.

43.18.oldText: In cases where it may be doubtful on which side justice lies, what better umpires could be desired by two violent factions, flying to arms and tearing a state to pieces, than the representatives of confederate states, not heated by the local flame? To the impartiality of judges, they would unite the affection of friends. Happy would it be if such a remedy for its infirmities could be enjoyed by all free governments — if a project equally effective could be established for the universal peace of mankind!

43.19.oldText: Should it be asked what is to be the redress for an insurrection pervading all the states, and comprising a superiority of the entire force, though not a constitutional right? The answer must be that such a case, as it would be without the compass of human remedies, so it is fortunately not within the compass of human probability. It is a sufficient recommendation of the federal Constitution that it diminishes the risk of a calamity for which no possible constitution can provide a cure.

43.20.oldText: Among the advantages of a confederate republic enumerated by Montesquieu, an important one is, "that should a popular insurrection happen in one of the States, the others are able to quell it. Should abuses creep into one part, they are reformed by those that remain sound."

43.22.oldText: This can only be considered a declaratory proposition, and may have been inserted, among other reasons, for the satisfaction of the foreign creditors of the United States, who cannot be strangers to the pretended doctrine that a change in the political form of civil society has the magical effect of dissolving its moral obligations.

43.23.oldText: Among the lesser criticisms exercised on the Constitution, it has been remarked that the validity of engagements ought to have been asserted in favor of the United States as well as against them. In the spirit that usually characterizes little critics, the omission has been transformed and magnified into a plot against the national rights. The authors of this discovery may be told what few others need to be informed of: that as engagements are in their nature reciprocal, an assertion of their validity on one side necessarily involves a validity on the other. And that as the article is merely declaratory, the establishment of the principle in one case is sufficient for every case. They may be further told that every constitution must limit its precautions to dangers that are not altogether imaginary, and that no real danger can exist that the government would dare, with or even without this constitutional declaration before it, to remit the debts justly due to the public on the pretext here condemned.

43.25.oldText: That useful alterations would be suggested by experience could not but be foreseen. It was requisite, therefore, that a mode for introducing them should be provided. The mode preferred by the convention seems stamped with every mark of propriety. It guards equally against that extreme facility which would render the Constitution too mutable, and that extreme difficulty which might perpetuate its discovered faults. It moreover equally enables the general and the state governments to originate the amendment of errors as they may be pointed out by the experience on one side or the other. The exception in favor of the equality of suffrage in the Senate was probably meant as a palladium to the residual sovereignty of the states, implied and secured by that principle of representation in one branch of the legislature. It was probably insisted on by the states particularly attached to that equality. The other exception must have been admitted on the same considerations that produced the privilege defended by it.

43.27.oldText: This article speaks for itself. The express authority of the people alone could give due validity to the Constitution. To have required unanimous ratification of the thirteen states would have subjected the essential interests of the whole to the caprice or corruption of a single member. It would have marked a want of foresight in the convention which our own experience would have rendered inexcusable.

43.28.oldText: Two questions of a very delicate nature present themselves on this occasion: 1. On what principle can the Confederation, which stands in the solemn form of a compact among the states, be superseded without the unanimous consent of the parties to it? 2. What relation is to subsist between the nine or more states ratifying the Constitution, and the remaining few who do not become parties to it?

43.29.oldText: The first question is answered at once by recurring to the absolute necessity of the case; to the great principle of self-preservation; to the transcendent law of nature and of nature's God, which declares that the safety and happiness of society are the objects at which all political institutions aim, and to which all such institutions must be sacrificed. PERHAPS, also, an answer may be found without searching beyond the principles of the compact itself. It has been heretofore noted among the defects of the Confederation that in many of the states it had received no higher sanction than a mere legislative ratification. The principle of reciprocality seems to require that its obligation on the other states should be reduced to the same standard. A compact between independent sovereigns, founded on ordinary acts of legislative authority, can pretend to no higher validity than a league or treaty between the parties. It is an established doctrine on the subject of treaties that all the articles are mutually conditions of each other; that a breach of any one article is a breach of the whole treaty; and that a breach committed by either of the parties absolves the others, and authorizes them, if they please, to pronounce the compact violated and void. Should it unhappily be necessary to appeal to these delicate truths for a justification for dispensing with the consent of particular states to a dissolution of the federal pact, will not the complaining parties find it a difficult task to answer the MULTIPLIED and IMPORTANT infractions with which they may be confronted? The time has been when it was incumbent on us all to veil the ideas which this paragraph exhibits. The scene is now changed, and with it the part which the same motives dictate.

43.30.oldText: The second question is not less delicate, and the flattering prospect of its being merely hypothetical forbids overcurious discussion of it. It is one of those cases that must be left to provide for itself. In general it may be observed that although no political relation can subsist between the assenting and dissenting states, yet the moral relations will remain uncancelled. The claims of justice, both on one side and on the other, will be in force, and must be fulfilled; the rights of humanity must in all cases be duly and mutually respected; while considerations of a common interest, and above all, the remembrance of the endearing scenes which are past, and the anticipation of a speedy triumph over the obstacles to reunion, will, it is hoped, not urge in vain MODERATION on one side, and PRUDENCE on the other.

44.0.oldText: A FIFTH category of provisions supporting federal authority consists of the following restrictions placed on the authority of the individual States:

44.2.oldText: The ban on treaties, alliances, and confederations is already part of the existing Articles of Union. For reasons that need no explanation, it has been carried over into the new Constitution. The ban on letters of marque is also part of the old system, but it is somewhat broader in the new. Under the old rules, States could grant letters of marque after a declaration of war. Under the new rules, these licenses must be obtained from the United States government both before and during war. This change is fully justified by the value of having a uniform policy on all matters touching foreign powers, and by the need for direct national accountability in any matter for which the nation itself is held responsible.

44.3.oldText: The right to coin money, taken away from the States here, was left in their hands by the Confederation as a power shared with Congress, except that Congress alone could regulate the alloy and value of coins. Here too, the new provision improves on the old. As long as alloy and value depended on the central authority, a state right to coin money could only multiply expensive mints and produce coins of varied shapes and weights. The latter problem defeated one of the original reasons for giving the power to the federal head. And while a state right to coin might have spared the inconvenience of shipping gold and silver to a central mint for recoining, that purpose can be served just as well by local mints established under the central authority.

44.4.oldText: The extension of the prohibition to bills of credit will please every citizen in proportion to his love of justice and his understanding of what really creates public prosperity. Since the peace, America has suffered enormous losses from the destructive effects of paper money. It has poisoned the trust between citizens, the trust in public institutions, the industry and morals of the people, and the reputation of republican government. This amounts to a vast debt against the States that adopted this reckless policy. That debt will go unpaid for a long time, or rather it accumulates as a kind of guilt that can only be atoned for by voluntarily sacrificing on the altar of justice the very power that produced it. Beyond these moral considerations, note this: the same reasons that show why States should not regulate coinage prove with equal force that they should not be free to substitute paper currency for coin. If every State could set the value of its own coin, there might be as many different currencies as States, and trade between them would be obstructed. Retroactive changes in value could be made, injuring citizens of other States and stirring hostility among the States themselves. Foreign subjects could suffer in the same way, and the Union would be discredited and entangled by the bad judgment of a single member. None of these evils is any less likely when States issue paper money than when they coin gold or silver. The power to make anything but gold and silver legal tender for debts is taken from the States on the same principle as the power to issue paper currency.

44.5.oldText: Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws that impair contractual obligations violate the fundamental principles of the social contract and every principle of sound legislation. The first two are expressly forbidden by the declarations attached to some State constitutions, and all three are forbidden by the spirit and intent of these basic charters. Yet our own experience has taught us that additional safeguards against these dangers should not be left out. The convention has therefore rightly added this constitutional barrier in defense of personal security and private rights. I am much mistaken if, in doing so, they have not faithfully reflected the genuine views as well as the clear interests of their constituents. The sober people of America are tired of the fluctuating policies that have driven public business. They have watched with regret and indignation as sudden changes and legislative interference in matters affecting personal rights become opportunities for ambitious and influential speculators, and traps for the more industrious and less informed members of the community. They have also seen that one act of legislative interference is just the first link in a long chain of repetitions, with each new interference produced naturally by the effects of the last. They rightly conclude that some thorough reform is needed. Reform that will end speculation on public measures, encourage general prudence and industry, and restore an orderly course to society's business. The ban on titles of nobility is copied from the Articles of Confederation and needs no comment.

44.7.oldText: The restriction on State power over imports and exports rests on all the arguments that prove the need to give regulation of trade to the federal councils. There is no point in discussing it further here, except to note that the way the restriction is qualified seems well designed both to give the States reasonable discretion in handling their imports and exports, and to give the United States a reasonable check against any abuse of that discretion. The remaining details of this clause fall under reasoning that is either obvious or has already been fully developed, so they may be passed over without comment.

44.8.oldText: The SIXTH and final category consists of the various powers and provisions that give effect to all the rest.

44.10.oldText: Few parts of the Constitution have been attacked with more anger than this one, yet on a fair examination, no part can appear more completely unassailable. Without the SUBSTANCE of this power, the entire Constitution would be a dead letter. So those who object to this article as part of the Constitution can only mean that the FORM of the provision is improper. But have they considered whether a better form could have been used instead?

44.11.oldText: There are four other approaches the Constitution might have taken on this subject. They might have copied the second article of the existing Confederation, which would have forbidden the exercise of any power not EXPRESSLY delegated. They might have tried to make a positive list of the powers covered by the general terms "necessary and proper." They might have tried a negative list, specifying which powers were excluded from the general definition. Or they might have said nothing at all, leaving these necessary and proper powers to construction and inference.

44.12.oldText: If the convention had taken the first route by adopting the second article of Confederation, the new Congress would clearly be exposed, just as their predecessors were, to a forced choice. They could read "EXPRESSLY" so strictly that the government would be stripped of any real authority, or so loosely that the restriction would lose all force. It would be easy to show, if needed, that no important power delegated by the Articles of Confederation has been or could be exercised by Congress without resorting at some point to the doctrine of CONSTRUCTION or IMPLICATION. Since the powers delegated under the new system are more extensive, the government administering it would be even more strained by this same dilemma. It would have to choose between betraying the public interest by doing nothing, or violating the Constitution by exercising powers that are clearly necessary and proper but not EXPRESSLY granted.

44.13.oldText: If the convention had tried to make a positive list of the powers necessary and proper for carrying their other powers into effect, the attempt would have required a complete code of laws covering every subject the Constitution touches. That code would have to fit not only present circumstances but every possible change the future might bring. In every new application of a general power, the PARTICULAR POWERS that serve as the means of achieving the OBJECT of the general power must always vary with that object, and may often need to vary even when the object stays the same.

44.14.oldText: If they had tried to list the particular powers or means NOT necessary or proper for carrying out the general powers, the task would have been just as hopeless. It would also be open to this further objection: every gap in the list would amount to a positive grant of authority. To avoid this, if they had tried a partial list of exceptions and described the rest with the general terms NOT NECESSARY OR PROPER, the result would be that the list would include only a few of the excluded powers. Those few would be ones least likely to be claimed or tolerated, since the list would naturally pick the powers least necessary or proper. And the unnecessary and improper powers left in the rest would be less firmly excluded than if no partial list had been made.

44.15.oldText: If the Constitution had said nothing on this point, there can be no doubt that all the particular powers needed to carry out the general powers would still belong to the government by unavoidable implication. No principle is more clearly established in law or reason than this: wherever the end is required, the means are authorized. Wherever a general power to do something is granted, every particular power needed to do it is included. So if the convention had taken this last approach, every objection now raised against their plan would still have all its plausibility. And the real inconvenience would be that they would not have removed a pretext that could be seized on at critical moments to challenge the essential powers of the Union.

44.16.oldText: If the question is what happens when Congress misreads this part of the Constitution and exercises powers not warranted by its true meaning, my answer is the same as if they misread or stretched any other power vested in them. The same as if the general power had been broken down into specifics, and any one of those specifics were violated. The same, in short, as if the State legislatures violated their respective constitutional authorities. In the first instance, the success of the usurpation will depend on the executive and judicial departments, whose job is to interpret and give effect to legislative acts. As a last resort, the remedy must come from the people, who can annul the usurpers' acts by electing more faithful representatives. The truth is that this ultimate remedy can be relied on more confidently against unconstitutional acts of the federal legislature than against those of the State legislatures. The reason is plain: every such federal act will invade the rights of the States, so the States will always be ready to spot the encroachment, sound the alarm to the people, and use their local influence to bring about a change of federal representatives. There is no such intermediate body between State legislatures and the people watching over the States, so violations of State constitutions are more likely to go unnoticed and uncorrected.

44.18.oldText: The reckless zeal of the Constitution's opponents has led them to attack this clause as well, even though without it the Constitution would be obviously and fundamentally defective. To see this clearly, we need only imagine for a moment that the supremacy of the State constitutions had been left intact through a saving clause in their favor.

44.19.oldText: First, since these constitutions invest the State legislatures with absolute sovereignty in all cases not excepted by the existing Articles of Confederation, all the authorities in the proposed Constitution that go beyond those listed in the Confederation would be nullified. The new Congress would be reduced to the same powerless condition as their predecessors.

44.20.oldText: Second, since some State constitutions do not even expressly and fully recognize the existing powers of the Confederacy, an express saving of the supremacy of those State constitutions would, in those States, throw into question every power contained in the proposed Constitution.

44.21.oldText: Third, since State constitutions differ greatly from one another, it could happen that a treaty or national law of great and equal importance to all the States would conflict with some State constitutions but not others. It would therefore be valid in some States while having no effect in others.

44.22.oldText: In short, the world would have seen, for the first time, a system of government built on an inversion of the basic principles of all government. It would have seen the authority of the whole society everywhere subordinate to the authority of its parts. It would have seen a monster, in which the head was directed by the limbs.

44.24.oldText: Some have asked why it was thought necessary to bind State officials by oath to support the federal Constitution, while no equivalent oath was imposed on federal officers in support of the State constitutions.

44.25.oldText: Several reasons could be given for the distinction. I will offer just one, which is obvious and conclusive. Members of the federal government will play no part in carrying the State constitutions into effect. The members and officers of the State governments, by contrast, will play an essential part in giving effect to the federal Constitution. The election of the President and Senate will depend in every case on the State legislatures. The election of the House of Representatives will depend on the same authority in the first instance, and will likely always be conducted by the officers and according to the laws of the States.

44.26.oldText: 4. Among the provisions giving effect to the federal powers, we might add those that belong to the executive and judicial departments. But since these are reserved for examination elsewhere, I pass over them here.

44.27.oldText: We have now reviewed in detail every article that makes up the total power delegated to the federal government by the proposed Constitution, and we are brought to this undeniable conclusion: no part of that power is unnecessary or improper for accomplishing the necessary objects of the Union. The question, then, of whether this much power should be granted resolves into another question. Whether or not a government adequate to the needs of the Union should be established. In other words, whether the Union itself should be preserved.

45.0.oldText: HAVING shown that none of the powers transferred to the federal government is unnecessary or improper, the next question to consider is whether the whole bundle of them will be dangerous to the share of authority left in the individual States.

45.1.oldText: The opponents of the convention's plan, instead of first considering how much power was absolutely necessary for the federal government's purposes, have exhausted themselves on a secondary inquiry into the possible consequences of the proposed degree of power for the State governments. But if the Union, as has been shown, is essential to the security of the American people against foreign danger; if it is essential to their security against rivalries and wars between the States; if it is essential to guard them against the violent and oppressive factions that poison the blessings of liberty, and against the military establishments that gradually corrupt liberty itself; if, in short, the Union is essential to the happiness of the people of America, is it not absurd to argue against a government, without which the goals of the Union cannot be reached, that such a government may diminish the importance of the State governments? Was the American Revolution fought, was the American Confederacy formed, was the precious blood of thousands shed, and the hard-earned wealth of millions spent, not so the people of America could enjoy peace, liberty, and safety, but so that individual State governments and particular local establishments could enjoy a certain measure of power and wear certain dignities and attributes of sovereignty? We have heard the impious doctrine of the Old World, that the people were made for kings, not kings for the people. Is the same doctrine to be revived in the New World in another form, holding that the solid happiness of the people must be sacrificed to the ambitions of political institutions of a different shape? It is too early for politicians to assume we have forgotten that the public good, the real welfare of the great body of the people, is the supreme object to be pursued, and that no form of government has any value except as it is suited to achieving this object. Were the convention's plan harmful to public happiness, my voice would say: Reject the plan. Were the Union itself inconsistent with public happiness, my voice would say: Abolish the Union. In the same way, as far as the sovereignty of the States cannot be reconciled to the happiness of the people, every good citizen must say: Let the former be sacrificed to the latter. How far that sacrifice is necessary has been shown. How far what remains unsacrificed will be endangered is the question before us.

45.2.oldText: Several important considerations have been touched on in the course of these papers, undermining the assumption that the federal government's operation will gradually prove fatal to the State governments. The more I turn the subject over, the more fully convinced I am that the balance is much more likely to be disturbed by the weight of the latter than the former.

45.3.oldText: We have seen, in every example of ancient and modern confederacies, the strongest tendency on the part of the member states to strip the central government of its authorities, paired with a feeble capacity in the central government to defend itself against these encroachments. In most of these examples, the system has been so different from the one under consideration that we should be cautious about drawing any inference about ours from the fate of theirs. Still, since the States will retain a very large share of active sovereignty under the proposed Constitution, we should not entirely ignore the lesson. In the Achaean league, the federal head probably had a degree and kind of power that gave it considerable resemblance to the government framed by the convention. The Lycian Confederacy, as far as its principles and form have come down to us, must have borne an even closer analogy to it. Yet history does not tell us that either of them ever degenerated, or tended to degenerate, into a single consolidated government. On the contrary, we know that the ruin of one of them came from the inability of the federal authority to prevent the dissensions, and finally the disunion, of the subordinate authorities. These cases deserve our attention all the more because the external pressures binding their parts together were much greater and more numerous than in our case. So weaker internal bonds would have been enough to hold the members to the head and to one another.

45.4.oldText: We have seen the same tendency at work in the feudal system. Despite the lack of proper sympathy in nearly every case between local sovereigns and the people, and despite occasional sympathy between the general sovereign and the people, the local sovereigns usually prevailed in the rivalry of encroachments. If external dangers had not enforced internal harmony and order, and especially if the local sovereigns had held the affections of the people, the great kingdoms of Europe would today consist of as many independent princes as there were once feudal barons.

45.5.oldText: The State governments will have the advantage over the federal government, whether we compare them by the immediate dependence of one on the other, by the weight of personal influence each side will hold, by the powers vested in each, by the people's likely preference and support, or by the disposition and ability of each to resist and frustrate the measures of the other.

45.6.oldText: The State governments may be regarded as constituent and essential parts of the federal government, while the federal government is in no way essential to the operation or organization of the State governments. Without the State legislatures' participation, the President of the United States cannot be elected at all. They must always have a great share in his appointment, and may often determine it themselves. The Senate will be elected absolutely and exclusively by the State legislatures. Even the House of Representatives, though drawn directly from the people, will be chosen heavily under the influence of the same kind of men whose influence over the people gets them elected to the State legislatures. So each of the principal branches of the federal government will owe its existence more or less to the favor of the State governments, and must therefore feel a dependence that is far more likely to produce too obsequious an attitude toward them than too overbearing one. On the other side, the parts of the State governments will in no case owe their appointment to the direct action of the federal government, and very little, if at all, to the local influence of its members.

45.7.oldText: The number of people employed under the Constitution of the United States will be much smaller than the number employed under the individual States. So there will be less personal influence on the federal side than on the State side. The members of the legislative, executive, and judicial departments of thirteen or more States, plus the justices of the peace, militia officers, ministerial officers of justice, and all the county, city, and town officers, serving more than three million people, mingled with them and personally acquainted with every class and circle, must vastly outnumber and out-influence everyone employed in the federal administration. Compare the members of the three great departments of the thirteen States, leaving out the justices of the peace from the judiciary, with the members of the corresponding departments of the single Union government. Compare the militia officers serving three million people with the military and naval officers of any establishment within the bounds of probability or even possibility. From this view alone, the advantage of the States is clearly decisive. If the federal government has revenue collectors, the State governments will have theirs too. And since the federal collectors will be mainly on the seacoast and not very numerous, while the State collectors will be spread across the country and very numerous, the advantage on this point also lies on the same side. It is true that the Confederacy may exercise the power of collecting internal as well as external taxes throughout the States. But this power will probably not be used except for supplemental revenue. The States will likely first be given the option to supply their quotas through their own collections. Any eventual collection under the immediate authority of the Union will generally be made by officers and according to rules appointed by the States themselves. Indeed, it is highly probable that in other areas, particularly the organization of judicial power, State officers will be invested with the corresponding authority of the Union. Even if separate federal collectors of internal revenue were appointed, their total influence would not begin to compare with the multitude of State officers on the other side. Within every district assigned to a federal collector, there would be at least thirty or forty, or even more, officers of various kinds, many of them people of standing and weight, whose influence would lie on the side of the State.

45.8.oldText: The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government are few and defined. Those that remain with the State governments are numerous and indefinite. The federal powers will be exercised mainly on external matters, such as war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce, with which the power of taxation will mostly be connected. The powers reserved to the States will reach all the matters that, in ordinary affairs, concern the lives, liberties, and properties of the people, and the internal order, improvement, and prosperity of the State.

45.9.oldText: The federal government's operations will be most extensive and important in times of war and danger. The State governments will be most active in times of peace and security. Since the former periods will probably be a small fraction of the latter, the State governments will enjoy yet another advantage over the federal government here. In fact, the better the federal powers are made for national defense, the less frequent will be the scenes of danger that might raise the federal government's standing above the State governments.

45.10.oldText: If the new Constitution is examined accurately and fairly, it will be found that the change it proposes consists much less in adding NEW POWERS to the Union than in strengthening its ORIGINAL POWERS. The regulation of commerce, it is true, is a new power, but few oppose it and no one fears it. The powers relating to war and peace, armies and fleets, treaties and finance, along with the other major powers, are all already vested in the existing Congress by the Articles of Confederation. The proposed change does not enlarge these powers; it only substitutes a more effective way of administering them. The change related to taxation may be regarded as the most important. Yet the present Congress already has full authority to REQUIRE indefinite supplies of money from the States for the common defense and general welfare, just as the future Congress will have to require them of individual citizens. And the citizens will be no more bound to pay than the States themselves have been. If the States had complied promptly with the Articles of Confederation, or if their compliance could have been enforced by means as peaceable as those used successfully against individuals, our past experience gives little support to the view that the State governments would have lost their constitutional powers and gradually undergone full consolidation. To claim such an outcome would be to say that the existence of the State governments is incompatible with any system whatsoever that achieves the essential purposes of the Union.

46.0.oldText: RESUMING the subject of the last paper, I now turn to the question of whether the federal or the State governments will have the advantage in the people's preference and support. Despite the different ways they are appointed, we must regard both as substantially dependent on the great body of the citizens of the United States. I take this as given here regarding the federal government, reserving the proofs for another place. The federal and State governments are in fact different agents and trustees of the people, set up with different powers and designed for different purposes. The opponents of the Constitution seem to have lost sight of the people altogether in their reasoning on this subject. They have viewed these different establishments not only as mutual rivals and enemies, but as if no common authority above them controlled their attempts to seize each other's powers. These gentlemen need to be reminded of their error. They must be told that the ultimate authority, wherever derivative authority may sit, resides in the people alone. Whether either or which of these governments will be able to expand its sphere of jurisdiction at the other's expense will not depend merely on the comparative ambition or skill of those governments. Truth, no less than decency, requires that we suppose the outcome in every case to depend on the views and approval of their common constituents.

46.1.oldText: Many considerations, beyond those raised earlier, seem to put it beyond doubt that the people's first and most natural attachment will be to the governments of their respective States. Into State administration, a greater number of individuals will hope to rise. From State patronage, a greater number of offices and salaries will flow. By State oversight, the more domestic and personal interests of the people will be regulated and provided for. With State affairs, the people will be more familiar and minutely acquainted. And with State officials, a greater proportion of the people will share ties of personal acquaintance, friendship, and family or party loyalty. So the popular bias may well be expected to lean most strongly to that side.

46.2.oldText: Experience tells the same story. The federal administration, even though far less developed than what may be hoped under a better system, had during the war, and especially while the independent paper money was still trusted, an activity and importance as great as it could have under any future circumstances. It was also engaged in a course of measures aimed at protecting everything that was dear to the people and acquiring everything that was desirable. Yet it was consistently found that, after the brief enthusiasm for the early Congresses had passed, the people's attention and attachment turned back to their own State governments. The federal council was never the idol of popular favor, and opposition to proposed enlargements of its powers and importance was the standard position taken by men who hoped to build their political careers on the prepossessions of their fellow-citizens.

46.3.oldText: If, therefore, as has been remarked elsewhere, the people in future come to favor the federal over the State governments, the change can only result from such clear and irresistible proof of better administration that it overcomes all their prior leanings. In that case, the people surely should not be barred from giving most of their confidence where they find it most deserved. But even then, the State governments would have little to fear, because the federal power can, by its nature, be advantageously administered only within a certain sphere.

46.4.oldText: The remaining points on which I propose to compare the federal and State governments are the disposition and the ability that each may possess to resist and frustrate the measures of the other.

46.5.oldText: It has already been proved that members of the federal government will be more dependent on members of the State governments than the State officials will be on the federal. It has also appeared that the prepossessions of the people, on whom both depend, will lean more toward the State governments than the federal. So far as each government's disposition toward the other is shaped by these causes, the State governments must clearly have the advantage. But in another distinct and very important way, the advantage will lie on the same side. The prepossessions that members will themselves carry into the federal government will generally favor the States, while it will rarely happen that members of the State governments carry into their public councils a bias in favor of the general government. A local spirit will inevitably prevail much more in the members of Congress than a national spirit will prevail in the State legislatures.
