Everyone knows that a great proportion of the errors made by State legislatures comes from the members' tendency to sacrifice the broad and lasting interests of the State to the particular and separate views of the counties or districts where they live. And if they cannot widen their thinking enough to embrace the collective welfare of their own State, how can we imagine they will make the aggregate prosperity of the Union, and the dignity and respectability of its government, the objects of their affection and deliberation? For the same reason that members of the State legislatures will not adequately attach themselves to national objects, members of the federal legislature will likely attach themselves too much to local ones. The States will be to federal members what counties and towns are to State members. Measures will too often be decided by their probable effect not on national prosperity and happiness, but on the prejudices, interests, and pursuits of the governments and people of individual States. What is the spirit that has generally characterized the proceedings of Congress? A reading of their journals, and the candid admissions of those who have served in that assembly, will tell us that the members have too often acted as partisans of their respective States rather than as impartial guardians of a common interest. Where on one occasion improper sacrifices have been made of local concerns to enlarge the federal government, the great interests of the nation have suffered on a hundred occasions from undue attention to the local prejudices, interests, and views of the particular States. I do not mean by these reflections to suggest that the new federal government will not embrace a broader plan of policy than the existing government has pursued, much less that its views will be as confined as those of the State legislatures. I mean only that it will share enough of the spirit of both to be reluctant to invade the rights of the individual States or the prerogatives of their governments. The motives of the State governments to expand their prerogatives at the expense of the federal will not be matched by any reciprocal predisposition in the federal members.

46.6.oldText: Even if we were to grant that the federal government may feel an equal disposition with the State governments to push its power beyond proper limits, the States would still have the advantage in the means of defeating such encroachments. If an act of a particular State, though hostile to the national government, is generally popular in that State and does not too grossly violate the oaths of State officers, it is carried out immediately, by means on the spot, and depending on the State alone. The opposition of the federal government, or the intervention of federal officers, would only inflame the zeal of all parties on the State's side. The evil could not be prevented or repaired, if at all, without the use of means that must always be resorted to with reluctance and difficulty. On the other hand, if a federal measure is unpopular in particular States, which would seldom fail to be the case if the measure were unwarrantable and may sometimes happen even when the measure is warranted, the means of opposition are powerful and ready at hand. The unease of the people, their reluctance and perhaps refusal to cooperate with federal officers, the disapproval of the State executive, and the embarrassments created by legislative maneuvers that would often be added on such occasions, would create difficulties in any State that should not be underestimated. In a large State, they would form very serious obstacles. And where several adjoining States happened to share the same view, they would present obstructions the federal government would scarcely be willing to confront.

46.7.oldText: But ambitious encroachments by the federal government on the authority of the State governments would not provoke the opposition of just a single State, or of only a few. They would be signals of general alarm. Every State government would take up the common cause. Correspondence would be opened. Plans of resistance would be coordinated. One spirit would animate and direct the whole. The same combinations, in short, would result from fear of federal tyranny as were produced by the dread of a foreign yoke. And unless the proposed innovations were voluntarily abandoned, the same appeal to a trial of force would be made in this case as was made in the other. But what kind of madness could ever push the federal government to such an extreme? In the contest with Great Britain, one part of the empire was used against another. The more numerous part invaded the rights of the less numerous part. The attempt was unjust and unwise, but it was not in theory absolutely impossible. But what would be the contest in the case we are imagining? Who would be the parties? A few representatives of the people would be opposed to the people themselves, or rather one set of representatives would be contending against thirteen sets of representatives, with the whole body of their common constituents on the side of the latter.

46.8.oldText: The only refuge left for those who predict the downfall of the State governments is the fanciful supposition that the federal government may first build up a military force for the projects of ambition. The reasonings in these papers must have been employed to little purpose if it is now necessary to disprove the reality of this danger. To suppose that the people and the States would, for a long enough period, elect an unbroken succession of men ready to betray both. That the traitors would, throughout that period, uniformly and systematically pursue some fixed plan to expand the military establishment. That the State governments and people would silently and patiently watch the gathering storm and continue to supply its materials until it was ready to burst on their own heads. All this must seem to anyone more like the incoherent dreams of a delirious jealousy, or the misjudged exaggerations of fake zeal, than the sober concerns of genuine patriotism. Extravagant as the supposition is, let us make it anyway. Let a regular army, fully matching the country's resources, be formed and entirely devoted to the federal government. Even then, it would not be too much to say that the State governments, with the people on their side, would be able to repel the danger. According to the best estimates, the highest size a standing army can reach in any country is about one hundredth of the population, or one twenty-fifth of those able to bear arms. In the United States, that proportion would yield an army of no more than twenty-five or thirty thousand men. Against them would stand a militia of nearly half a million citizens armed and ready, officered by men chosen from among themselves, fighting for their common liberties, and united and led by governments that hold their affections and confidence. It may well be doubted whether a militia in this position could ever be defeated by such a small proportion of regular troops. Those most familiar with the recent successful resistance of this country against the British will be the most inclined to deny the possibility. Beyond the advantage of being armed, which Americans hold over the people of almost every other nation, the existence of subordinate governments to which the people are attached, and which appoint the militia officers, forms a barrier against the schemes of ambition more impassable than any a simple government of any form can offer. Despite the military establishments in the various kingdoms of Europe, which are pushed as far as public resources will bear, the governments are afraid to trust their people with arms. And it is uncertain whether even with arms alone the people would not be able to throw off their yokes. But if the people had the further advantage of local governments chosen by themselves, that could gather the national will and direct the national force, and of officers appointed from the militia by these governments, attached both to them and to the militia, it can be said with the greatest confidence that the throne of every tyranny in Europe would soon be overturned in spite of the legions surrounding it. Let us not insult the free and gallant citizens of America with the suspicion that they would be less able to defend rights they actually possess than the degraded subjects of arbitrary power would be to wrest theirs from their oppressors. Let us rather no longer insult them with the supposition that they could ever reduce themselves to the necessity of making the experiment, by blindly and tamely submitting to the long train of insidious measures that must precede and produce it.

46.9.oldText: The argument under this heading can be put in a very compact form, and it appears entirely conclusive. Either the way the federal government is to be constructed will make it sufficiently dependent on the people, or it will not. On the first supposition, that dependence will keep it from forming schemes offensive to its constituents. On the other supposition, it will not have the people's confidence, and its schemes of usurpation will be easily defeated by the State governments, who will be backed by the people.

46.10.oldText: Summing up the considerations stated in this paper and the last, they amount to the most convincing evidence that the powers proposed for the federal government are as little dangerous to those reserved to the individual States as they are absolutely necessary to accomplish the purposes of the Union. And all the alarms sounded about a planned and consequent annihilation of the State governments must, on the most charitable reading, be ascribed to the chimerical fears of those who raise them.

47.0.oldText: HAVING reviewed the general form of the proposed government and the overall mass of power assigned to it, I now turn to examining the particular structure of this government and the distribution of that power among its component parts.

47.1.oldText: One of the principal objections pressed by the more respectable opponents of the Constitution is its supposed violation of the political maxim that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments should be separate and distinct. They claim that in the structure of the federal government, no regard appears to have been paid to this essential precaution in favor of liberty. They say the various departments of power are distributed and blended in a way that destroys all symmetry and beauty of form, and exposes some essential parts of the structure to being crushed by the disproportionate weight of others.

47.2.oldText: No political truth is certainly of greater inherent value, or stamped with the authority of more enlightened champions of liberty, than the one on which this objection is based. The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judicial, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elected, may rightly be called the very definition of tyranny. So if the federal Constitution were really chargeable with such an accumulation of power, or with a mixture of powers tending dangerously toward such an accumulation, no further argument would be needed to inspire universal condemnation of the system. I am persuaded, however, that it can be made clear to everyone that this charge cannot be supported, and that the maxim it relies on has been completely misunderstood and misapplied. To form correct ideas on this important subject, we should investigate the sense in which the preservation of liberty requires that the three great departments of power be separate and distinct.

47.3.oldText: The oracle always consulted and cited on this subject is the celebrated Montesquieu. If he is not the author of this invaluable maxim in the science of politics, he at least has the merit of presenting and recommending it most effectively to mankind's attention. Let us first try to determine his meaning on this point.

47.4.oldText: The British Constitution was to Montesquieu what Homer has been to writers on the principles of epic poetry. As the latter have regarded the work of the immortal bard as the perfect model from which the principles and rules of the epic art are to be drawn, and by which all similar works are to be judged, so this great political critic seems to have viewed the Constitution of England as the standard, or in his own words, as the mirror of political liberty, and to have presented as elementary truths the various characteristic principles of that particular system. So that we may not mistake his meaning here, let us go back to the source from which the maxim was drawn.

47.5.oldText: Even at a glance, the British Constitution shows that the legislative, executive, and judicial departments are by no means totally separate and distinct from one another. The executive magistrate forms an integral part of the legislative authority. He alone has the prerogative of making treaties with foreign sovereigns, which, once made, have under certain limits the force of legislative acts. All members of the judicial department are appointed by him, can be removed by him on the address of the two Houses of Parliament, and form, when he chooses to consult them, one of his constitutional councils. One branch of the legislative department also serves as a great constitutional council to the executive chief. On the other hand, it is the sole holder of judicial power in cases of impeachment, and is invested with the supreme appellate jurisdiction in all other cases. The judges, in turn, are connected with the legislative department to the extent that they often attend and participate in its deliberations, though they are not allowed a legislative vote.

47.6.oldText: The reasons Montesquieu gives for his maxim are a further demonstration of his meaning. "When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body," he says, "there can be no liberty, because apprehensions may arise lest THE SAME monarch or senate should ENACT tyrannical laws to EXECUTE them in a tyrannical manner." Again: "Were the power of judging joined with the legislative, the life and liberty of the subject would be exposed to arbitrary control, for THE JUDGE would then be THE LEGISLATOR. Were it joined to the executive power, THE JUDGE might behave with all the violence of AN OPPRESSOR." Some of these reasons are explained more fully in other passages, but even briefly stated as they are here, they sufficiently establish the meaning we have given to this celebrated maxim of this celebrated author.

47.7.oldText: If we look into the constitutions of the various States, we find that despite the emphatic and in some cases unqualified terms in which this axiom has been laid down, there is not a single instance in which the various departments of power have been kept absolutely separate and distinct. New Hampshire, whose constitution was the most recently formed, seems to have been fully aware of the impossibility and inadvisability of avoiding any mixture whatsoever of these departments, and has qualified the doctrine by declaring "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary powers ought to be kept as separate from, and independent of, each other AS THE NATURE OF A FREE GOVERNMENT WILL ADMIT; OR AS IS CONSISTENT WITH THAT CHAIN OF CONNECTION THAT BINDS THE WHOLE FABRIC OF THE CONSTITUTION IN ONE INDISSOLUBLE BOND OF UNITY AND AMITY." Her constitution accordingly mixes these departments in several ways. The Senate, which is a branch of the legislative department, is also a judicial tribunal for the trial of impeachments. The President, who is the head of the executive department, is also the presiding member of the Senate, and besides an equal vote in all cases, has a casting vote in case of a tie. The executive head is himself eventually elective every year by the legislative department, and his council is every year chosen by and from the members of the same department. Several officers of state are also appointed by the legislature. And the members of the judicial department are appointed by the executive department.

47.8.oldText: The constitution of Massachusetts has shown sufficient if less pointed caution in expressing this fundamental article of liberty. It declares "that the legislative department shall never exercise the executive and judicial powers, or either of them; the executive shall never exercise the legislative and judicial powers, or either of them; the judicial shall never exercise the legislative and executive powers, or either of them." This declaration corresponds precisely with Montesquieu's doctrine as it has been explained, and is not violated in a single point by the convention's plan. It goes no further than to forbid any one of the entire departments from exercising the powers of another department. In the very Constitution to which it is prefixed, a partial mixture of powers has been allowed. The executive magistrate has a qualified veto on the legislative body, and the Senate, which is part of the legislature, is a court of impeachment for members of both the executive and judicial departments. The members of the judicial department, in turn, are appointable by the executive department and removable by the same authority on the address of the two legislative branches. Lastly, a number of officers of government are annually appointed by the legislative department. Since appointment to offices, particularly executive offices, is in its nature an executive function, the framers of the Constitution have, on this last point at least, violated the rule they themselves established.

47.9.oldText: I pass over the constitutions of Rhode Island and Connecticut, because they were formed before the Revolution, even before the principle under examination had become an object of political attention.

47.10.oldText: The constitution of New York contains no declaration on this subject, but appears clearly to have been framed with an eye to the danger of improperly blending the different departments. It nevertheless gives the executive magistrate a partial control over the legislative department; and, more than that, gives a similar control to the judicial department; and even blends the executive and judicial departments in the exercise of this control. In its council of appointment, members of the legislature are joined with the executive authority in the appointment of officers, both executive and judicial. And its court for the trial of impeachments and correction of errors is to consist of one branch of the legislature and the principal members of the judicial department.

47.11.oldText: The constitution of New Jersey has blended the different powers of government more than any of the preceding ones. The governor, who is the executive magistrate, is appointed by the legislature; is chancellor and ordinary, or surrogate of the State; is a member of the Supreme Court of Appeals; and is president, with a casting vote, of one of the legislative branches. The same legislative branch acts again as executive council to the governor and, with him, constitutes the Court of Appeals. The members of the judicial department are appointed by the legislative department and removable by one branch of it on the impeachment of the other.

47.12.oldText: Under the constitution of Pennsylvania, the president, who is the head of the executive department, is annually elected by a vote in which the legislative department predominates. Together with an executive council, he appoints the members of the judicial department, and forms a court of impeachment for the trial of all officers, judicial as well as executive. The judges of the Supreme Court and justices of the peace also seem to be removable by the legislature, and the executive power of pardoning in certain cases is referred to the same department. The members of the executive council are made EX-OFFICIO justices of the peace throughout the State.

47.13.oldText: In Delaware, the chief executive magistrate is annually elected by the legislative department. The speakers of the two legislative branches are vice-presidents in the executive department. The executive chief, with six others appointed three by each of the legislative branches, constitutes the Supreme Court of Appeals. He is joined with the legislative department in appointing the other judges. Throughout the States, the members of the legislature may at the same time be justices of the peace. In this State, the members of one branch of the legislature are EX-OFFICIO justices of the peace, as are the members of the executive council. The principal officers of the executive department are appointed by the legislative, and one branch of the latter forms a court of impeachments. All officers may be removed on address of the legislature.

47.14.oldText: Maryland has adopted the maxim in the most unqualified terms, declaring that the legislative, executive, and judicial powers of government ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other. Her constitution, nonetheless, makes the executive magistrate appointable by the legislative department, and the members of the judiciary appointable by the executive department.

47.15.oldText: The language of Virginia is even more pointed on this subject. Her constitution declares "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments shall be separate and distinct; so that neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other; nor shall any person exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time, except that the justices of county courts shall be eligible to either House of Assembly." Yet we find not only this express exception regarding members of the inferior courts, but also that the chief magistrate, with his executive council, is appointable by the legislature; that two members of the council are removed every three years at the legislature's pleasure; and that all the principal offices, both executive and judicial, are filled by that same department. The executive prerogative of pardon is also, in one case, vested in the legislative department.

47.16.oldText: The constitution of North Carolina, which declares "that the legislative, executive, and supreme judicial powers of government ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other," at the same time refers to the legislative department the appointment not only of the executive chief, but of all the principal officers within both that department and the judiciary.

47.17.oldText: In South Carolina, the constitution makes the executive magistracy eligible by the legislative department. It also gives the legislature the appointment of the members of the judicial department, including even justices of the peace and sheriffs, and the appointment of officers in the executive department, down to captains in the army and navy of the State.

47.18.oldText: In the constitution of Georgia, where it is declared "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments shall be separate and distinct, so that neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other," we find that the executive department is to be filled by appointments of the legislature, and that the executive prerogative of pardon is to be finally exercised by the same authority. Even justices of the peace are to be appointed by the legislature.

47.19.oldText: In citing these cases, in which the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments have not been kept totally separate and distinct, I do not wish to be regarded as an advocate for the particular organizations of the various State governments. I am fully aware that, among the many excellent principles they exemplify, they bear strong marks of the haste, and even stronger marks of the inexperience, under which they were framed. It is too obvious that in some cases the fundamental principle under consideration has been violated by too great a mixture, and even an actual consolidation, of the different powers, and that in no instance has adequate provision been made for maintaining in practice the separation drawn on paper. What I have wanted to show is that the charge brought against the proposed Constitution, of violating the sacred maxim of free government, is warranted neither by the real meaning attached to that maxim by its author, nor by the sense in which it has so far been understood in America. This interesting subject will be taken up again in the next paper.

48.0.oldText: The previous paper showed that the political maxim we examined does not require the legislative, executive, and judicial departments to be entirely disconnected from each other. Now I will show something further. Unless these departments are connected and blended enough to give each a constitutional check on the others, the separation that the maxim requires—essential to free government—can never in practice be properly maintained.

48.1.oldText: Everyone agrees that the powers belonging to one department should not be directly and fully exercised by either of the others. It is equally clear that none of them should hold, directly or indirectly, an overriding influence over the others in carrying out their respective powers. No one will deny that power tends to encroach, and that it must be effectively restrained from going beyond its assigned limits. After distinguishing in theory the several classes of power—legislative, executive, or judicial—the next and hardest task is to provide some practical security for each against invasion by the others. What this security should be is the great problem to be solved.

48.2.oldText: Will it be enough to mark out precisely the boundaries of these departments in the constitution and to trust those parchment barriers to hold back the encroaching spirit of power? This was the security relied on by the framers of most American constitutions. But experience tells us that this provision has been greatly overrated. Some stronger defense is absolutely necessary to protect the weaker members of government from the more powerful ones. The legislative department is everywhere extending the scope of its activity and pulling all power into its impetuous vortex.

48.3.oldText: The founders of our republics deserve so much credit for the wisdom they showed that pointing out their errors is an unpleasant task. But truth requires us to note this. They never seemed to take their eyes off one danger to liberty—the overgrown, all-grasping prerogative of a hereditary monarch supported by a hereditary branch of the legislature. They seem never to have remembered the danger from legislative usurpations, which, by gathering all power in the same hands, must lead to the same tyranny that executive usurpations threaten.

48.4.oldText: In a government where extensive prerogatives are placed in the hands of a hereditary monarch, the executive department is rightly seen as the source of danger. It is watched with all the jealousy that a zeal for liberty should inspire. In a democracy, where a multitude of people personally exercise legislative functions, they are continually exposed to ambitious intrigues from their executive officers. Their incapacity for regular deliberation and concerted action makes this worse, and tyranny may well arise on some favorable occasion from that quarter. But in a representative republic the executive office is carefully limited in both the extent and duration of its power. The legislative power is exercised by an assembly that, inspired by a supposed influence over the people, has fearless confidence in its own strength. It is numerous enough to feel all the passions that drive a multitude, yet not so numerous as to be incapable of pursuing those passions through reasonable means. It is against the enterprising ambition of this department that the people should direct all their jealousy and exhaust all their precautions.

48.5.oldText: The legislative department gains a superiority in our governments from other circumstances too. Its constitutional powers are at once more extensive and less open to precise limits. So it can more easily mask, under complicated and indirect measures, the encroachments it makes on the coordinate departments. In legislative bodies it is often a genuinely difficult question whether a particular measure will or will not extend beyond the legislative sphere. By contrast, executive power is restrained within a narrower compass and is simpler in nature, while the judiciary is marked by landmarks still less uncertain. Any attempt at usurpation by either of these departments would immediately reveal itself and fail. Nor is that all. The legislative department alone has access to the people's pockets. In some constitutions it has full discretion, and in all a prevailing influence, over the salaries of those who fill the other departments. This creates a dependence that gives still greater opportunity for legislative encroachments.

48.6.oldText: I have appealed to our own experience to confirm what I am saying. If proofs were needed, they could be multiplied endlessly. I could find a witness in every citizen who has taken part in or paid attention to the course of public affairs. I could gather records in abundance from the archives of every State in the Union. But for more concise and equally satisfactory evidence, I will point to the example of two States, attested by two unimpeachable authorities.

48.7.oldText: The first example is Virginia, a State which, as we have seen, has expressly declared in its constitution that the three great departments should not be intermixed. The authority in support of this is Mr. Jefferson, who, besides his other advantages for observing the operation of the government, was himself its chief magistrate. To convey fully the ideas his experience impressed on him, I must quote a substantial passage from his very interesting Notes on the State of Virginia, p. 195. "All the powers of government, legislative, executive, and judiciary, result to the legislative body. Concentrating these in the same hands is precisely the definition of despotic government. It will be no relief that these powers are exercised by many hands rather than one. One hundred and seventy-three despots would surely be as oppressive as one. Let those who doubt it look at the republic of Venice. Nor will it help us that they are chosen by ourselves. An ELECTIVE DESPOTISM was not the government we fought for. We fought for a government founded on free principles, in which the powers of government would be so divided and balanced among several bodies of magistracy that none could exceed their legal limits without being effectively checked and restrained by the others. For this reason, the convention that passed the ordinance of government laid its foundation on this basis: that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments should be separate and distinct, so that no person could exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time. BUT NO BARRIER WAS PROVIDED BETWEEN THESE SEVERAL POWERS. The judiciary and the executive members were left dependent on the legislature for their salaries in office, and some of them for their continuance in it. If, therefore, the legislature assumes executive and judiciary powers, no opposition is likely to be made; nor, if made, can it be effective. In that case they may cast their proceedings into the form of acts of Assembly, which will render them binding on the other branches. They have accordingly, IN MANY instances, DECIDED RIGHTS that should have been left to JUDICIARY CONTROVERSY, and THE DIRECTION OF THE EXECUTIVE, DURING THE WHOLE TIME OF THEIR SESSION, IS BECOMING HABITUAL AND FAMILIAR."

48.8.oldText: The other State I will use as an example is Pennsylvania, and the other authority is the Council of Censors, which met in 1783 and 1784. Part of this body's duty, as set out in the constitution, was "to inquire whether the constitution had been preserved inviolate in every part; and whether the legislative and executive branches of government had performed their duty as guardians of the people, or assumed to themselves, or exercised, other or greater powers than they are entitled to by the constitution." In carrying out this trust, the council had to compare both the legislative and executive proceedings with the constitutional powers of these departments. From the facts they listed—most of which both sides in the council acknowledged—it appears that the constitution had been flagrantly violated by the legislature in many important instances.

48.9.oldText: A great number of laws had been passed that violated, without any apparent necessity, the rule requiring all bills of a public nature to be printed in advance for the people's consideration. This was one of the main precautions the constitution relied on against improper legislative acts.

48.10.oldText: The constitutional right to trial by jury had been violated, and powers had been assumed that the constitution had not delegated.

48.12.oldText: The salaries of judges, which the constitution expressly required to be fixed, had been varied from time to time. Cases belonging to the judiciary were frequently drawn into legislative cognizance and determination.

48.13.oldText: Anyone who wishes to see the specific items under each of these heads can consult the journals of the council, which are in print. Some of them, it will be found, may be attributable to peculiar circumstances connected with the war. But the greater part may be considered the spontaneous offshoots of an ill-constituted government.

48.14.oldText: It also appears that the executive department had not been innocent of frequent constitutional breaches. Three observations are in order here. FIRST, many of the instances were either directly produced by the necessities of the war or recommended by Congress or the commander-in-chief. SECOND, in most other instances, the executive conformed to either the declared or the known sentiments of the legislative department. THIRD, Pennsylvania's executive department is distinguished from those of the other States by the number of members composing it. In this respect, it has as much affinity to a legislative assembly as to an executive council. Being exempt from the restraint of individual responsibility for the body's acts, and drawing confidence from mutual example and joint influence, unauthorized measures would naturally be more freely hazarded than where the executive is administered by a single hand or by a few hands.

48.15.oldText: The conclusion I am justified in drawing from these observations is this. A mere parchment demarcation of the constitutional limits of the several departments is not a sufficient guard against the encroachments that lead to a tyrannical concentration of all the powers of government in the same hands.

49.0.oldText: The author of the "Notes on the State of Virginia," quoted in the last paper, has appended to that valuable work the draft of a constitution. It had been prepared to be laid before a convention expected to be called in 1783 by the legislature, to establish a constitution for that commonwealth. The plan, like everything from the same pen, shows a turn of thinking that is original, comprehensive, and accurate. It deserves all the more attention because it equally displays a fervent attachment to republican government and an enlightened view of the dangerous tendencies against which it must be guarded. One of the precautions he proposes—on which he ultimately seems to rely as the safeguard of the weaker departments against invasions by the stronger—is perhaps entirely his own. Since it relates directly to our present inquiry, it should not be overlooked.

49.1.oldText: His proposal is, "that whenever any two of the three branches of government shall concur in opinion, each by the voices of two thirds of their whole number, that a convention is necessary for altering the constitution, or CORRECTING BREACHES OF IT, a convention shall be called for the purpose."

49.2.oldText: The people are the only legitimate fountain of power, and from them the constitutional charter—under which the several branches of government hold their power—is derived. So it seems strictly consistent with republican theory to return to that same original authority, not only whenever it may be necessary to enlarge, reduce, or remodel the powers of government, but also whenever any one of the departments encroaches on the chartered authorities of the others. The several departments are perfectly coordinate by the terms of their common commission. Clearly, none of them can claim an exclusive or superior right to settle the boundaries between their respective powers. So how are the encroachments of the stronger to be prevented, or the wrongs of the weaker to be redressed, without an appeal to the people themselves? As grantors of the commissions, only they can declare its true meaning and enforce its observance.

49.3.oldText: There is certainly great force in this reasoning. It must be allowed to prove that a constitutional road to the decision of the people should be marked out and kept open for certain great and extraordinary occasions. But there appear to be insurmountable objections against the proposed appeal to the people as a general provision for keeping the several departments within their constitutional limits.

49.4.oldText: First, the provision does not reach the case of a combination of two of the departments against the third. The legislative authority has many means of operating on the motives of the other departments. If it could win over either of the others—or even one third of its members—the remaining department could gain no advantage from this remedial provision. I do not dwell on this objection, because it might be thought to bear on the form of the principle rather than on the principle itself.

49.5.oldText: Second, there is an objection inherent in the principle. Every appeal to the people would imply some defect in the government. Frequent appeals would largely deprive the government of that veneration which time bestows on everything, and without which perhaps even the wisest and freest governments would not possess the necessary stability. If it is true that all governments rest on opinion, it is equally true that the strength of opinion in each individual, and its practical influence on his conduct, depend largely on how many he supposes share the same opinion. Human reason, like man himself, is timid and cautious when left alone. It gains firmness and confidence in proportion to the number with which it is associated. When the examples that fortify opinion are ANCIENT as well as NUMEROUS, they are known to have a double effect. In a nation of philosophers, this consideration could be ignored. Reverence for the laws would be sufficiently instilled by the voice of enlightened reason. But a nation of philosophers is as unlikely as the philosophical race of kings Plato wished for. In every other nation, the most rational government will not find it a superfluous advantage to have the prejudices of the community on its side.

49.6.oldText: An even more serious objection to frequent referrals of constitutional questions to the decision of the whole society is the danger of disturbing public tranquility by stirring up public passions too strongly. The revisions of our established forms of government have been successful, and that success does great honor to the virtue and intelligence of the American people. Even so, it must be admitted that the experiments are of too delicate a nature to be unnecessarily multiplied. We must remember that all the existing constitutions were formed in the midst of a danger which suppressed the passions most hostile to order and concord. They were formed amid an enthusiastic confidence of the people in their patriotic leaders, which silenced the ordinary diversity of opinion on great national questions. They were formed amid a universal ardor for new and opposite forms, produced by a universal resentment and indignation against the old government. And no spirit of party connected with the changes to be made, or the abuses to be reformed, could mix its leaven into the operation. The future situations in which we are usually likely to find ourselves do not offer any equivalent safeguard against the danger we anticipate.

49.7.oldText: But the greatest objection of all is this. The decisions that would probably result from such appeals would not serve the purpose of maintaining the constitutional balance of government. We have seen that the tendency of republican governments is toward an aggrandizement of the legislature at the expense of the other departments. So the appeals to the people would usually be made by the executive and judicial departments. But whether made by one side or the other, would each side enjoy equal advantages on trial? Consider their different situations. The members of the executive and judicial departments are few in number, and can be personally known to only a small part of the people. The judges, by the mode of their appointment as well as by its nature and permanence, are too far removed from the people to share much in their preferences. The executives are generally objects of jealousy, and their administration is always liable to be discolored and rendered unpopular. The members of the legislative department, by contrast, are numerous. They are distributed throughout and live among the people at large. Their connections of blood, friendship, and acquaintance embrace a large portion of the most influential part of society. The nature of their public trust implies a personal influence among the people, and that they are more directly the confidential guardians of the people's rights and liberties. With these advantages, it can hardly be supposed that the opposing party would have an equal chance of a favorable outcome.

49.8.oldText: But the legislative party would not only be able to plead their cause most successfully with the people. They would probably be constituted as the judges themselves. The same influence that had gained them election into the legislature would gain them a seat in the convention. If this should not be the case with all of them, it would probably be the case with many, and almost certainly with those leading figures on whom everything depends in such bodies. In short, the convention would be composed mainly of men who had been, were currently, or expected to be members of the department whose conduct was on trial. They would therefore be parties to the very question they were to decide.

49.9.oldText: Yet sometimes appeals might be made under circumstances less adverse to the executive and judicial departments. The usurpations of the legislature might be so flagrant and sudden as to admit no specious coloring. A strong party among the legislators themselves might side with the other branches. The executive power might be in the hands of a particular favorite of the people. In such a posture of things, the public decision might be less swayed by preferences for the legislative party. But still, it could never be expected to turn on the true merits of the question. It would inevitably be tied up with the spirit of pre-existing parties, or of parties springing out of the question itself. It would be tied up with persons of distinguished character and extensive influence in the community. It would be pronounced by the very men who had been agents in, or opponents of, the measures to which the decision related. The PASSIONS, therefore, not the REASON, of the public would sit in judgment. But it is the reason of the public, alone, that ought to control and regulate the government. The passions ought to be controlled and regulated by the government.

49.10.oldText: We found in the last paper that mere declarations in the written constitution are not sufficient to restrain the several departments within their legal rights. It appears in this paper that occasional appeals to the people would be neither a proper nor an effective provision for that purpose. How far the provisions of a different nature contained in the plan quoted above might be adequate, I do not examine. Some of them are unquestionably founded on sound political principles, and all are framed with remarkable ingenuity and precision.

50.0.oldText: Some may argue that instead of OCCASIONAL appeals to the people, which are open to the objections raised against them, PERIODICAL appeals are the proper and adequate means of PREVENTING AND CORRECTING INFRACTIONS OF THE CONSTITUTION.

50.1.oldText: Note that in examining these expedients, I am limiting myself to their fitness for ENFORCING the Constitution—keeping the several departments of power within their proper bounds—without specifically considering them as provisions for ALTERING the Constitution itself. In this first view, appeals to the people at fixed periods appear to be nearly as unsuitable as appeals on particular occasions as they emerge. If the periods are separated by short intervals, the measures to be reviewed and corrected will be of recent date and will be connected with all the circumstances that tend to vitiate and pervert the result of occasional revisions. If the periods are far apart, the same remark will apply to all recent measures. And while the remoteness of the others may favor a dispassionate review of them, this advantage is inseparable from inconveniences that seem to counterbalance it. First, a distant prospect of public censure would be a very feeble restraint on power against those excesses to which it might be driven by the force of present motives. Is it to be imagined that a legislative assembly of one or two hundred members, eagerly bent on some favorite object and breaking through constitutional restraints in pursuit of it, would be stopped in its course by considerations drawn from a censorial review of their conduct ten, fifteen, or twenty years in the future? Second, the abuses would often have completed their harmful effects before the remedial provision could be applied. And finally, where this might not be the case, they would be of long standing, would have taken deep root, and would not easily be eradicated.

50.2.oldText: The scheme of revising the constitution to correct recent breaches of it, along with other purposes, has actually been tried in one of the States. One of the objects of the Council of Censors that met in Pennsylvania in 1783 and 1784 was, as we have seen, to inquire "whether the constitution had been violated, and whether the legislative and executive departments had encroached upon each other." This important and novel political experiment deserves very particular attention from several angles. In some respects, perhaps—as a single experiment made under somewhat peculiar circumstances—it may not be considered absolutely conclusive. But as applied to the case under consideration, it involves some facts that I venture to note as a complete and satisfactory illustration of the reasoning I have employed.

50.3.oldText: First. It appears, from the names of the gentlemen who composed the council, that some at least of its most active members had also been active and leading figures in the parties that already existed in the State.

50.4.oldText: Second. It appears that the same active and leading members of the council had been active and influential members of the legislative and executive branches within the period to be reviewed. They had even been patrons or opponents of the very measures now to be tested against the constitution. Two of the members had been vice-presidents of the State, and several others had served on the executive council within the seven preceding years. One of them had been speaker, and a number of others were distinguished members of the legislative assembly within the same period.

50.5.oldText: Third. Every page of their proceedings testifies to the effect of all these circumstances on the temper of their deliberations. Throughout the council's existence, it was split into two fixed and violent parties. The fact is acknowledged and lamented by the members themselves. Had that not been the case, the face of their proceedings supplies an equally satisfactory proof. On every question, however unimportant in itself or unconnected with the others, the same names stand invariably opposed on the rival columns. Any unbiased observer may infer, without danger of mistake and without meaning to reflect on either party or any individuals of either, that PASSION, not REASON, unfortunately must have presided over their decisions. When men exercise their reason coolly and freely on a variety of distinct questions, they inevitably fall into different opinions on some of them. When they are governed by a common passion, their opinions—if they can even be called opinions—will be the same.

50.6.oldText: Fourth. It is at least debatable whether the decisions of this body, in several instances, did not misconstrue the limits set for the legislative and executive departments instead of reducing and confining them to their constitutional places.

50.7.oldText: Fifth. I have never understood that the council's decisions on constitutional questions, whether rightly or wrongly formed, had any effect in changing the practice founded on legislative constructions. It even appears, if I am not mistaken, that in one instance the contemporary legislature denied the council's constructions and actually prevailed in the contest.

50.8.oldText: This censorial body therefore proves at the same time, by its investigations, the existence of the disease, and by its example, the ineffectiveness of the remedy.

50.9.oldText: This conclusion cannot be overturned by saying that the State in which the experiment was made was at that crisis, and had been for a long time before, violently heated and distracted by the rage of party. Is it to be presumed that at any future seven-year period the same State will be free from parties? Is it to be presumed that any other State, at the same or any other given period, will be exempt from them? Such an event ought to be neither presumed nor desired. The extinction of parties necessarily implies either a universal alarm for the public safety, or the absolute extinction of liberty.

50.10.oldText: Even if the precaution were taken of excluding from the assemblies elected by the people—those convened to review the previous administration of the government—all persons who had been involved with the government within that period, the difficulties would not be removed. The important task would probably fall on men who, having inferior capacities, would in other respects be little better qualified. Although they might not have been personally involved in the administration, and therefore not direct agents in the measures to be examined, they would probably have been entangled in the parties connected with those measures and have been elected under their auspices.

51.0.oldText: What expedient, then, shall we finally turn to in order to maintain in practice the necessary partition of power among the several departments laid down in the Constitution? The only answer is this. Since all these external provisions have proved inadequate, the defect must be supplied by so contriving the interior structure of the government that its several constituent parts, by their mutual relations, become the means of keeping each other in their proper places. Without presuming to attempt a full development of this important idea, I will hazard a few general observations. They may perhaps place the idea in a clearer light and help us form a more accurate judgment of the principles and structure of the government planned by the convention.

51.1.oldText: To lay a proper foundation for the separate and distinct exercise of the different powers of government—which to a certain extent everyone admits is essential to the preservation of liberty—it is clear that each department should have a will of its own. Therefore each should be so constituted that the members of each have as little role as possible in appointing the members of the others. If this principle were rigorously followed, it would require all the appointments for the supreme executive, legislative, and judicial offices to be drawn from the same fountain of authority—the people—through channels having no communication with one another. Perhaps such a plan for constructing the several departments would be less difficult in practice than it may appear in contemplation. Some difficulties, however, and some additional expense would attend its execution. Some deviations from the principle must therefore be admitted. In the constitution of the judicial department in particular, it might be inexpedient to insist rigorously on the principle. First, because peculiar qualifications are essential in the members, the primary consideration should be to select the mode of choice that best secures these qualifications. Second, because the permanent tenure by which the appointments are held in that department must soon destroy any sense of dependence on the authority that conferred them.

51.2.oldText: It is equally clear that the members of each department should be as little dependent as possible on those of the others for the salaries attached to their offices. If the executive magistrate or the judges were not independent of the legislature on this point, their independence in every other respect would be merely nominal.

51.3.oldText: But the great security against a gradual concentration of the several powers in the same department consists in giving those who administer each department the necessary constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments by the others. The provision for defense must, in this case as in all others, be made commensurate with the danger of attack. Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. The interest of the man must be connected with the constitutional rights of the place. It may be a reflection on human nature that such devices should be necessary to control the abuses of government. But what is government itself, but the greatest of all reflections on human nature? If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself. A dependence on the people is no doubt the primary control on the government. But experience has taught mankind the necessity of auxiliary precautions.

51.4.oldText: This policy of supplying, by opposite and rival interests, the defect of better motives, can be traced through the whole system of human affairs, private as well as public. We see it particularly displayed in all the subordinate distributions of power. The constant aim is to divide and arrange the several offices so that each may be a check on the other—so that the private interest of every individual may be a sentinel over the public rights. These inventions of prudence cannot be any less necessary in the distribution of the supreme powers of the State.

51.5.oldText: But it is not possible to give each department an equal power of self-defense. In republican government, the legislative authority necessarily predominates. The remedy for this inconvenience is to divide the legislature into different branches, and to make them—by different modes of election and different principles of action—as little connected with each other as the nature of their common functions and their common dependence on the society will allow. It may even be necessary to guard against dangerous encroachments by still further precautions. As the weight of the legislative authority requires that it be thus divided, the weakness of the executive may require, on the other hand, that it be fortified. An absolute veto on the legislature appears at first sight to be the natural defense with which the executive magistrate should be armed. But perhaps it would be neither entirely safe nor alone sufficient. On ordinary occasions it might not be exerted with the necessary firmness, and on extraordinary occasions it might be treacherously abused. May not this defect of an absolute veto be supplied by some qualified connection between this weaker department and the weaker branch of the stronger department, by which the latter may be led to support the constitutional rights of the former, without being too much detached from the rights of its own department?

51.6.oldText: If the principles on which these observations are founded are sound—as I persuade myself they are—and if they are applied as a criterion to the several State constitutions and to the federal Constitution, it will be found that if the federal Constitution does not perfectly correspond with them, the State constitutions are infinitely less able to bear such a test.

51.7.oldText: There are, moreover, two considerations particularly applicable to the federal system of America that place that system in a very interesting point of view.

51.8.oldText: First. In a single republic, all the power surrendered by the people is submitted to the administration of a single government, and usurpations are guarded against by dividing the government into distinct and separate departments. In the compound republic of America, the power surrendered by the people is first divided between two distinct governments, and then the portion allotted to each is subdivided among distinct and separate departments. A double security therefore arises for the rights of the people. The different governments will control each other, at the same time that each will be controlled by itself.

51.9.oldText: Second. It is of great importance in a republic not only to guard the society against the oppression of its rulers, but to guard one part of the society against the injustice of the other part. Different interests necessarily exist in different classes of citizens. If a majority is united by a common interest, the rights of the minority will be insecure. There are only two methods of providing against this evil. One is to create a will in the community independent of the majority—that is, independent of the society itself. The other is to include in the society so many separate descriptions of citizens that an unjust combination of a majority of the whole becomes very improbable, if not impracticable. The first method prevails in all governments possessing a hereditary or self-appointed authority. This is at best a precarious security, because a power independent of the society may as readily embrace the unjust views of the major as the rightful interests of the minor party, and may possibly be turned against both. The second method will be exemplified in the federal republic of the United States. While all authority in it will be derived from and dependent on the society, the society itself will be broken into so many parts, interests, and classes of citizens that the rights of individuals, or of the minority, will be in little danger from interested combinations of the majority. In a free government the security for civil rights must be the same as that for religious rights. It consists in one case in the multiplicity of interests, and in the other in the multiplicity of sects. The degree of security in both cases will depend on the number of interests and sects, and this may be presumed to depend on the extent of territory and number of people included under the same government. This view of the subject must particularly recommend a proper federal system to all the sincere and considerate friends of republican government. It shows that in exact proportion as the territory of the Union may be formed into more limited Confederacies, or States, oppressive combinations of a majority will be facilitated. The best security under the republican forms, for the rights of every class of citizens, will be diminished. And consequently the stability and independence of some member of the government—the only other security—must be proportionately increased. Justice is the end of government. It is the end of civil society. It always has been and always will be pursued until it is obtained, or until liberty is lost in the pursuit. In a society in whose forms the stronger faction can readily unite and oppress the weaker, anarchy may as truly be said to reign as in a state of nature, where the weaker individual is not secured against the violence of the stronger. And just as, in that state of nature, even the stronger individuals are prompted by the uncertainty of their condition to submit to a government that may protect the weak as well as themselves, so in this society the more powerful factions or parties will gradually be induced, by a similar motive, to wish for a government that will protect all parties, the weaker as well as the more powerful. It can hardly be doubted that if the State of Rhode Island were separated from the Confederacy and left to itself, the insecurity of rights under a popular form of government within such narrow limits would be exposed by such repeated oppressions of factious majorities that some power altogether independent of the people would soon be called for by the voice of the very factions whose misrule had demonstrated the need of it. In the extended republic of the United States, and among the great variety of interests, parties, and sects which it embraces, a coalition of a majority of the whole society could seldom take place on any other principles than those of justice and the general good. There being thus less danger to a minor from the will of a major party, there must also be less pretext for providing security for the minor party by introducing into the government a will not dependent on the major party—or, in other words, a will independent of the society itself. It is no less certain than it is important—despite contrary opinions that have been entertained—that the larger the society, provided it lies within a practical sphere, the more capable it will be of self-government. And happily for the REPUBLICAN CAUSE, the practicable sphere may be extended very greatly by a judicious modification and mixture of the FEDERAL PRINCIPLE.

52.0.oldText: The first thing to examine about this part of the government concerns the qualifications of voters and elected officials. The qualifications of voters will be the same as those for voters in the most numerous branch of the State legislatures. The definition of the right to vote is rightly seen as a fundamental article of republican government. The convention therefore had to define and establish this right in the Constitution. Leaving it open for occasional regulation by Congress would have been improper, for the reason just given. Submitting it to the discretion of State legislatures would have been improper for the same reason. It would also have made too dependent on State governments that branch of the federal government which ought to depend on the people alone. Reducing the different qualifications in the different States to one uniform rule would probably have been as unsatisfactory to some States as it would have been difficult for the convention. The provision the convention made therefore appears to be the best option available. It must satisfy every State, because it conforms to the standard already established, or which may be established, by the State itself. It will be safe for the United States, because, being fixed by the State constitutions, it cannot be altered by the State governments. There is no fear that the people of the States will alter this part of their constitutions in a way that abridges the rights guaranteed to them by the federal Constitution.

52.1.oldText: The qualifications for elected representatives are less carefully defined by the State constitutions and are also more open to uniform treatment. The convention therefore properly considered and regulated them. A representative of the United States must be at least twenty-five years old. He must have been a citizen of the United States for seven years. At the time of his election, he must live in the State he is to represent. And during his service, he must hold no other office under the United States. Under these reasonable limits, the door to this part of the federal government is open to merit of every kind. Native or naturalized, young or old, rich or poor, of any religious faith — all may serve.

52.2.oldText: The term for which representatives will be elected is the second matter to consider about this branch. To decide whether this article is sound, two questions must be examined. First, will biennial elections be safe in this case? Second, are they necessary or useful?

52.3.oldText: First. Liberty requires that the government in general share a common interest with the people. It is especially essential that the branch under consideration depend immediately on the people and feel close sympathy with them. Frequent elections are unquestionably the only policy by which this dependence and sympathy can be effectively secured. But what specific frequency is absolutely necessary cannot be calculated precisely. It must depend on a variety of related circumstances. Let us consult experience, the guide that should always be followed when it can be found.

52.4.oldText: The system of representation, as a substitute for the citizens meeting in person, was at most very imperfectly known to ancient politics. Only in modern times can we expect to find instructive examples. And even here, to avoid research that is too vague and scattered, we should confine ourselves to the few examples best known and most analogous to our case. The first to consider is the House of Commons in Great Britain. The history of this branch of the English Constitution before Magna Carta is too obscure to teach us much. Even its very existence has been disputed by political historians. The earliest later records show that parliaments were to MEET only every year, not that they were to be ELECTED every year. And even these annual sessions were left so much to the king's discretion that, under various pretexts, royal ambition often contrived very long and dangerous gaps between them. To remedy this grievance, a statute in the reign of Charles II provided that the gaps should not extend beyond three years. When William III came to the throne and a revolution took place, the subject was taken up again more seriously. It was declared a fundamental right of the people that parliaments ought to be held FREQUENTLY. By another statute passed a few years later in the same reign, the term "frequently," which had referred to the three-year period set under Charles II, was given a precise meaning. It was expressly enacted that a new parliament must be called within three years after the previous one ended. The last change, from three to seven years, was introduced early in the present century, during alarm over the Hanoverian succession. From these facts it appears that the greatest frequency of elections deemed necessary in that kingdom for binding representatives to their constituents does not exceed every three years. And if we judge from the degree of liberty retained even under seven-year elections, with all the other flaws in the parliamentary constitution, we cannot doubt this. A reduction from seven to three years, with the other necessary reforms, would extend the people's influence over their representatives enough to satisfy us. Biennial elections under the federal system cannot possibly threaten the necessary dependence of the House of Representatives on their constituents.

52.5.oldText: Elections in Ireland, until recently, were regulated entirely by the discretion of the crown. They were seldom repeated except when a new monarch came to the throne, or some other contingent event occurred. The parliament that began with George II continued throughout his whole reign, a period of about thirty-five years. The only dependence the representatives had on the people consisted in the people's right to fill occasional vacancies by electing new members, and in the chance of some event producing a general new election. The Irish parliament's ability to defend the rights of its constituents, even where the will to do so existed, was severely limited by the crown's control over the subjects of their deliberation. Recently, if I am not mistaken, these restraints have been broken. Eight-year parliaments have also been established. What effect this partial reform may produce must be left to further experience. The example of Ireland, viewed this way, sheds little light on our subject. As far as we can draw any conclusion from it, it must be this. If the people of that country have been able to retain any liberty at all under such disadvantages, biennial elections would secure them every degree of liberty that depends on a proper connection between representatives and the people.

52.6.oldText: Let us bring our inquiry closer to home. The example of these States, when they were British colonies, deserves particular attention. It is so well known that little needs to be said. The principle of representation, in at least one branch of the legislature, was established in all of them. But the periods of election varied. They ranged from one to seven years. Do we have any reason to infer, from the spirit and conduct of the representatives of the people before the Revolution, that biennial elections would have been dangerous to the public liberties? The spirit displayed everywhere at the start of the struggle, which overcame the obstacles to independence, is the best proof that a sufficient measure of liberty had been enjoyed everywhere. It inspired both a sense of liberty's worth and a zeal for its proper extension. This is true as much of the colonies whose elections were least frequent as of those whose elections were most frequent. Virginia was the colony that stood first in resisting the parliamentary usurpations of Great Britain. It was also the first to embrace, by public act, the resolution of independence. Yet in Virginia, if I have not been misinformed, elections under the former government were every seven years. I cite this example not as proof of any peculiar merit, since the priority in those instances was probably accidental. Still less do I cite it as showing any advantage in SEVEN-YEAR elections. Compared with greater frequency they are unacceptable. I cite it merely as proof, and a very substantial proof, that the liberties of the people can be in no danger from BIENNIAL elections.

52.7.oldText: The conclusion drawn from these examples will be considerably strengthened by recalling three points. First, the federal legislature will possess only part of that supreme legislative authority which is fully vested in the British Parliament, and which, with a few exceptions, was exercised by the colonial assemblies and the Irish legislature. It is a well-founded maxim that, where no other circumstances affect the case, the greater the power, the shorter its duration ought to be. Conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely its duration may be extended. Second, it has been shown elsewhere that the federal legislature will be restrained not only by its dependence on the people, as other legislative bodies are, but it will also be watched and controlled by the several State legislatures, which other legislative bodies are not. Third, no comparison can be made between the means available to the more permanent branches of the federal government for seducing the House of Representatives from its duty to the people, if they should be inclined to do so, and the means of influence over the popular branch possessed by the other branches of government cited above. With less power to abuse, the federal representatives can be less tempted on one side, and will be doubly watched on the other.

53.0.oldText: I will be reminded here, perhaps, of the common saying, "where annual elections end, tyranny begins." If it is true, as has often been remarked, that proverbial sayings are generally founded in reason, it is no less true that, once established, they are often applied to cases their reason does not cover. I need not look beyond the case before us for proof. What is the reason on which this proverbial saying rests? No one will subject himself to ridicule by pretending that any natural connection exists between the sun or the seasons and the period within which human virtue can withstand the temptations of power. Happily for humankind, liberty is not, in this respect, confined to any single point in time. It lies between extremes that allow enough latitude for all the variations required by the various situations and circumstances of civil society. The election of magistrates might be daily, weekly, or monthly, as well as annual, if it were thought useful, as in some instances it actually has been. And if circumstances may require deviating from the rule on one side, why not on the other side too? Looking at the periods established among ourselves for electing the most numerous branches of the State legislatures, we find them by no means coinciding any more than they do for elections of other civil magistrates. In Connecticut and Rhode Island, the periods are every six months. In the other States, except South Carolina, they are annual. In South Carolina they are biennial — as proposed for the federal government. Here is a difference of four to one between the longest and shortest periods. Yet it would not be easy to show that Connecticut or Rhode Island is better governed, or enjoys a greater share of rational liberty, than South Carolina. Nor is either of these States distinguished in these respects, for these reasons, from the States whose elections differ from both.

53.1.oldText: In searching for the grounds of this doctrine, I can find only one, and it does not apply to our case. The important distinction so well understood in America — between a Constitution established by the people and unalterable by the government, and a law established by the government and alterable by the government — seems to have been little understood and even less observed in any other country. Wherever the supreme legislative power has resided, it has been supposed that full power to change the form of government also resides there. Even in Great Britain, where the principles of political and civil liberty have been most discussed, and where we hear most of the rights of the Constitution, the authority of Parliament is held to be supreme and uncontrollable, with regard to the Constitution as well as to ordinary objects of legislation. They have accordingly, in several cases, actually changed by legislative acts some of the most fundamental articles of government. They have, in particular, changed the period of election on several occasions. On the last such occasion, they not only introduced seven-year elections in place of three-year ones, but by the same act continued themselves in office four years beyond the term for which the people had elected them. Attention to these dangerous practices has produced very natural alarm among the devotees of free government, of which frequent elections is the cornerstone. It has led them to seek some security for liberty against the danger to which it is exposed. Where no Constitution paramount to the government either existed or could be obtained, no constitutional security similar to that established in the United States could be attempted. Some other security therefore had to be sought. What better security could the case admit than selecting some simple and familiar period of time as a standard for measuring the danger of innovations, fixing the national sentiment, and uniting patriotic exertions? The most simple and familiar period of time applicable to the subject was a year. Hence the doctrine has been instilled by laudable zeal, to erect some barrier against the gradual innovations of an unlimited government, that the advance toward tyranny was to be measured by the distance of departure from the fixed point of annual elections. But what need is there to apply this expedient to a government limited, as the federal government will be, by the authority of a paramount Constitution? Or who will pretend that the liberties of the people of America will not be more secure under biennial elections, fixed unalterably by such a Constitution, than those of any other nation would be where elections were annual, or even more frequent, but subject to alteration by the ordinary power of government?

53.2.oldText: The second question is whether biennial elections are necessary or useful. The answer to this question, in the affirmative, will appear from several very obvious considerations.

53.3.oldText: No one can be a competent legislator who does not add, to upright intentions and sound judgment, a certain knowledge of the subjects on which he is to legislate. Part of this knowledge can be acquired through information available to men in private as well as public stations. Another part can only be obtained, or at least thoroughly obtained, by actual experience in the position that requires its use. The period of service should therefore, in all such cases, bear some proportion to the extent of practical knowledge needed for proper performance of the service. The period of legislative service established in most of the States for the more numerous branch is, as we have seen, one year. The question can then be put in this simple form: does the period of two years bear no greater proportion to the knowledge needed for federal legislation than one year does to the knowledge needed for State legislation? Merely stating the question this way suggests the answer that ought to be given.

53.4.oldText: In a single State, the necessary knowledge concerns the existing laws, which are uniform throughout the State and with which all the citizens are more or less familiar. It also concerns the general affairs of the State, which lie within a small compass, are not very diverse, and occupy much of the attention and conversation of every class of people. The great theater of the United States presents a very different scene. The laws are far from uniform — they vary in every State. Meanwhile, the public affairs of the Union are spread over a very extensive region. They are extremely diversified by the local affairs connected with them, and can hardly be correctly learned anywhere except in the central councils to which the representatives of every part of the empire bring knowledge of them. Yet some knowledge of the affairs, and even the laws, of all the States ought to be possessed by the members from each State. How can foreign trade be properly regulated by uniform laws without some acquaintance with the commerce, the ports, the customs, and the regulations of the different States? How can trade between the different States be properly regulated without some knowledge of their relative situations in these and other respects? How can taxes be judiciously imposed and effectively collected if they are not adapted to the different laws and local circumstances relating to these objects in the different States?
