How can uniform regulations for the militia be properly provided without similar knowledge of the many internal circumstances by which the States differ from each other? These are the principal objects of federal legislation. They strongly suggest the extensive information that representatives ought to acquire. The other domestic objects will require a proportional degree of information regarding them.

53.5.oldText: It is true that all these difficulties will, by degrees, be greatly diminished. The most laborious task will be the proper inauguration of the government and the initial formation of a federal code. Improvements on the first drafts will every year become both easier and fewer. Past transactions of the government will be a ready and accurate source of information for new members. The affairs of the Union will become more and more objects of curiosity and conversation among citizens at large. And the increased exchange among those of different States will contribute much to spreading mutual knowledge of their affairs. This in turn will contribute to a general assimilation of their manners and laws. But with all these reductions, the business of federal legislation must continue to so far exceed, in both novelty and difficulty, the legislative business of a single State, that the longer period of service assigned to those who transact it is justified.

53.6.oldText: There is a branch of knowledge belonging to a federal representative that has not yet been mentioned: foreign affairs. In regulating our own commerce, he ought to be acquainted not only with the treaties between the United States and other nations, but also with the commercial policy and laws of other nations. He ought not to be wholly ignorant of the law of nations. As far as it is a proper object of municipal legislation, that subject is committed to the federal government. Although the House of Representatives does not directly participate in foreign negotiations and arrangements, the necessary connection between the several branches of public affairs means these particular branches will frequently deserve attention in the ordinary course of legislation. Sometimes they will demand particular legislative sanction and cooperation. Some portion of this knowledge can no doubt be acquired in a man's study. But some of it can only be derived from the public sources of information. And all of it will be acquired most effectively by practical attention to the subject during actual service in the legislature.

53.7.oldText: There are other considerations, perhaps less important, but not unworthy of notice. The distance many representatives will be obliged to travel, and the arrangements that distance makes necessary, would be a much more serious objection for fit men if service were limited to a single year, than if it were extended to two years. No argument can be drawn on this subject from the case of the delegates to the existing Congress. They are elected annually, true, but their re-election is considered by the legislative assemblies almost a matter of course. The election of representatives by the people would not be governed by the same principle.

53.8.oldText: A few of the members, as happens in all such assemblies, will possess superior talents. By frequent reelections they will become long-standing members. They will thoroughly master the public business and perhaps not be unwilling to take advantage of those advantages. The greater the proportion of new members, and the less the information of the bulk of the members, the more apt they will be to fall into the snares laid for them. This remark is no less applicable to the relationship between the House of Representatives and the Senate.

53.9.oldText: Even in single States that are large and hold only one legislative session a year, frequent elections carry an inconvenience along with their advantages. False elections cannot be investigated and annulled in time for the decision to have its proper effect. If a return can be obtained, no matter by what unlawful means, the irregular member, who takes his seat as a matter of course, is sure to hold it long enough to serve his purposes. This gives a very harmful encouragement to the use of unlawful means for obtaining irregular returns. If federal legislative elections were annual, this practice could become a very serious abuse, particularly in the more distant States. Each house is, as it must be, the judge of the elections, qualifications, and returns of its members. Whatever improvements experience may suggest for simplifying and speeding the process in disputed cases, so much of a year would unavoidably elapse before an illegitimate member could be removed from his seat that the prospect of such an event would be little check on unfair and illicit means of obtaining a seat.

53.10.oldText: All these considerations taken together justify us in affirming this. Biennial elections will be as useful to the affairs of the public as we have seen they will be safe to the liberty of the people.

54.0.oldText: The next matter I will examine concerning the House of Representatives is the apportionment of its members among the several States. This is to be determined by the same rule used for direct taxes.

54.1.oldText: It is not disputed that the number of people in each State should be the standard for regulating the proportion of representatives for each State. The establishment of the same rule for apportioning taxes will probably be little contested either, though the rule itself in this case is by no means founded on the same principle. In the former case, the rule refers to the personal rights of the people, with which it has a natural and universal connection. In the latter, it refers to the proportion of wealth, of which it is in no case a precise measure, and in ordinary cases a very poor one. But despite the imperfection of the rule when applied to the relative wealth and contributions of the States, it is clearly the least objectionable among the practicable rules. It had too recently received the general sanction of America not to find a ready preference with the convention.

54.2.oldText: All this will perhaps be admitted, it may be said. But does it follow, from admitting numbers as the measure of representation, or slaves combined with free citizens as a ratio of taxation, that slaves ought to be included in the numerical rule of representation? Slaves are considered as property, not as persons. They ought therefore to be included in estimates of taxation, which are based on property, and excluded from representation, which is regulated by a census of persons. This is the objection, as I understand it, stated in its full force. I shall be equally candid in stating the reasoning that may be offered on the opposite side.

54.3.oldText: "We subscribe to the doctrine," one of our Southern brethren might observe, "that representation relates more immediately to persons, and taxation more immediately to property. We agree in applying this distinction to the case of our slaves. But we must deny the claim that slaves are considered merely as property, and in no respect as persons. The true state of the case is that they share both qualities. Our laws consider them, in some respects, as persons, and in other respects as property. In being compelled to labor, not for himself but for a master; in being able to be sold by one master to another; and in being subject at all times to be restrained in his liberty and chastised in his body by the capricious will of another — the slave may appear to be degraded from the human rank and classed with those irrational animals which the law calls property. But on the other hand, in being protected in his life and limbs against the violence of all others, even the master of his labor and his liberty; and in being himself punishable for all violence committed against others — the slave is no less clearly regarded by the law as a member of society, not as a part of irrational creation; as a moral person, not as a mere article of property. The federal Constitution therefore decides with great propriety on the case of our slaves when it views them in the mixed character of persons and property. This is in fact their true character. It is the character bestowed on them by the laws under which they live. It will not be denied that these laws are the proper criterion. For it is only on the pretext that the laws have transformed the negroes into property that their place in the count of numbers is disputed. And it is admitted that if the laws were to restore the rights that have been taken away, the negroes could no longer be refused an equal share of representation with the other inhabitants.

54.4.oldText: "This question may be placed in another light. It is agreed on all sides that numbers are the best scale of wealth and taxation, just as they are the only proper scale of representation. Would the convention have been impartial or consistent if they had rejected the slaves from the list of inhabitants when shares of representation were calculated, but inserted them on the list when the tariff of contributions was adjusted? Could it reasonably be expected that the Southern States would join in a system that considered their slaves in some degree as men when burdens were to be imposed, but refused to consider them in the same light when advantages were to be conferred? Might not some surprise also be expressed that those who reproach the Southern States with the barbarous policy of considering as property a part of their human brethren should themselves contend that the government to which all the States are parties ought to consider this unfortunate race more completely in the unnatural light of property than the very laws of which they complain?

54.5.oldText: "It may be replied, perhaps, that slaves are not included in the count of representatives in any of the States that hold them. They neither vote themselves nor add to the votes of their masters. On what principle, then, ought they to be taken into the federal estimate of representation? In rejecting them altogether, the Constitution would, in this respect, have followed the very laws that have been appealed to as the proper guide.

54.6.oldText: "This objection is repelled by a single observation. It is a fundamental principle of the proposed Constitution that, just as the total number of representatives allotted to the several States is determined by a federal rule based on the total number of inhabitants, so the right of choosing this allotted number in each State is to be exercised by such part of the inhabitants as the State itself may designate. The qualifications on which the right of suffrage depends are perhaps not the same in any two States. In some States the difference is very material. In every State, a certain proportion of inhabitants are deprived of this right by the State constitution, who will nevertheless be included in the census by which the federal Constitution apportions the representatives. From this point of view, the Southern States might retort the complaint by insisting that the principle laid down by the convention required no regard be had to the policy of particular States toward their own inhabitants. Consequently, the slaves, as inhabitants, should have been admitted to the census according to their full number, just like other inhabitants who, by the policy of other States, are not admitted to all the rights of citizens. A rigorous adherence to this principle, however, is waived by those who would gain by it. All they ask is that equal moderation be shown on the other side. Let the case of the slaves be considered as it is in truth, a peculiar one. Let the compromise expedient of the Constitution be mutually adopted, which regards them as inhabitants but as debased by servitude below the equal level of free inhabitants — which regards the SLAVE as divested of two-fifths of the MAN.

54.7.oldText: "After all, may not another ground be taken on which this article of the Constitution will admit a still readier defense? We have so far proceeded on the idea that representation related to persons only, and not at all to property. But is it a just idea? Government is instituted no less for protection of property than of persons. The one as well as the other, therefore, may be considered as represented by those charged with the government. On this principle, in several of the States, and particularly in the State of New York, one branch of the government is intended more especially to be the guardian of property. It is accordingly elected by that part of society most interested in this object of government. In the federal Constitution, this policy does not prevail. The rights of property are committed to the same hands as the personal rights. Some attention ought, therefore, to be paid to property in the choice of those hands.

54.8.oldText: "For another reason, the votes allowed in the federal legislature to the people of each State ought to bear some proportion to the comparative wealth of the States. States have not, like individuals, an influence over each other arising from superior advantages of fortune. If the law allows a wealthy citizen but a single vote in choosing his representative, the respect and consequence he derives from his fortunate situation very frequently guide the votes of others to the candidates of his choice. Through this imperceptible channel the rights of property are conveyed into public representation. A State possesses no such influence over other States. It is not probable that the richest State in the Confederacy will ever influence the choice of a single representative in any other State. Nor will the representatives of the larger and richer States possess any other advantage in the federal legislature, over the representatives of other States, than what may result from their superior number alone. As far, therefore, as their superior wealth and weight may justly entitle them to any advantage, it ought to be secured to them by a superior share of representation. The new Constitution is, in this respect, materially different from the existing Confederation, as well as from that of the United Netherlands and other similar confederacies. In each of the latter, the effect of the federal resolutions depends on the subsequent and voluntary resolutions of the states composing the union. Hence the states, though possessing an equal vote in the public councils, have unequal influence corresponding with the unequal importance of these subsequent and voluntary resolutions. Under the proposed Constitution, the federal acts will take effect without the necessary intervention of the individual States. They will depend merely on the majority of votes in the federal legislature. Consequently each vote, whether from a larger or smaller State, or a State more or less wealthy or powerful, will have an equal weight and effect — in the same manner as votes individually given in a State legislature, by the representatives of unequal counties or other districts, have each a precise equality of value and effect. If there is any difference in the case, it proceeds from the difference in the personal character of the individual representative, rather than from any regard to the extent of the district from which he comes."

54.9.oldText: Such is the reasoning that an advocate for the Southern interests might use on this subject. Although it may seem a little strained at some points, on the whole I must confess that it fully reconciles me to the scale of representation which the convention has established.

54.10.oldText: In one respect, establishing a common measure for representation and taxation will have a very salutary effect. The accuracy of the census obtained by Congress will necessarily depend, to a considerable degree, on the willingness, if not the cooperation, of the States. It is therefore very important that the States feel as little bias as possible to either inflate or reduce the count of their numbers. Were their share of representation alone governed by this rule, they would have an interest in exaggerating their inhabitants. Were the rule to decide their share of taxation alone, the contrary temptation would prevail. By extending the rule to both objects, the States will have opposite interests, which will check and balance each other and produce the necessary impartiality.

55.0.oldText: The number of which the House of Representatives is to consist forms another very interesting point of view from which this branch of the federal legislature may be considered. Scarcely any article in the whole Constitution seems to be made more worthy of attention by the weight of character and the apparent force of argument with which it has been attacked. The charges brought against it are these. First, that so small a number of representatives will be an unsafe trustee of the public interests. Second, that they will not have proper knowledge of the local circumstances of their numerous constituents. Third, that they will be drawn from that class of citizens which will sympathize least with the feelings of the mass of the people, and be most likely to aim at a permanent elevation of the few at the expense of the many. Fourth, that defective as the number will be at first, it will become more and more disproportionate by the increase of the people and the obstacles that will prevent a corresponding increase in the number of representatives.

55.1.oldText: In general it may be remarked on this subject that no political problem is less open to a precise solution than that of the most convenient number for a representative legislature. Nor is there any point on which the policy of the several States is more at variance, whether we compare their legislative assemblies directly with each other or consider the proportions they bear to their constituents. Setting aside the difference between the smallest and largest States — Delaware, whose most numerous branch consists of twenty-one representatives, and Massachusetts, where it amounts to between three and four hundred — a very considerable difference is observable among States nearly equal in population. The number of representatives in Pennsylvania is not more than one-fifth of that in Massachusetts. New York, whose population is to that of South Carolina as six to five, has little more than one-third of the number of representatives. As great a disparity prevails between Georgia and Delaware or Rhode Island. In Pennsylvania, representatives bear no greater proportion to their constituents than one for every four or five thousand. In Rhode Island, they bear a proportion of at least one for every thousand. According to the constitution of Georgia, the proportion may run as high as one to every ten electors, and must unavoidably far exceed the proportion in any of the other States.

55.2.oldText: Another general remark to be made is that the ratio between representatives and the people ought not to be the same where the people are very numerous as where they are very few. Were the representatives in Virginia regulated by the standard in Rhode Island, they would now amount to between four and five hundred, and twenty or thirty years from now, to a thousand. On the other hand, the ratio of Pennsylvania, if applied to Delaware, would reduce that State's representative assembly to seven or eight members. Nothing can be more fallacious than to base our political calculations on arithmetical principles. Sixty or seventy men may more properly be trusted with a given degree of power than six or seven. But it does not follow that six or seven hundred would be a proportionally better depository. And if we extend the supposition to six or seven thousand, the whole reasoning ought to be reversed. The truth is that in all cases at least a certain number seems necessary to secure the benefits of free consultation and discussion, and to guard against too easy a combination for improper purposes. On the other hand, the number ought to be kept within a certain limit at most, to avoid the confusion and intemperance of a multitude. In all very numerous assemblies, of whatever character, passion never fails to wrest the scepter from reason. Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.

55.3.oldText: It is also necessary to recall here the observations applied to the case of biennial elections. For the same reason that the limited powers of the Congress, and the control of the State legislatures, justify less frequent elections than public safety might otherwise require, the members of Congress need be less numerous than if they possessed the whole power of legislation, and were under no restraints other than the ordinary ones of other legislative bodies.

55.4.oldText: With these general ideas in mind, let us weigh the objections raised against the proposed number of members of the House of Representatives. First, it is said that so small a number cannot safely be trusted with so much power.

55.5.oldText: The number of which this branch of the legislature will consist at the start of the government will be sixty-five. Within three years a census is to be taken, when the number may be increased to one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. Every successive ten-year period the census is to be renewed, and increases may continue to be made under the above limitation. It is no extravagant guess that the first census, at the rate of one for every thirty thousand, will raise the number of representatives to at least one hundred. Counting the negroes at three-fifths, it can scarcely be doubted that the population of the United States will by then, if it does not already, amount to three million. After twenty-five years, at the projected rate of increase, the number of representatives will reach two hundred, and after fifty years, four hundred. This is a number that I presume will end all fears arising from the smallness of the body. I take for granted here what I will, in answering the fourth objection, hereafter show — that the number of representatives will be increased from time to time in the manner provided by the Constitution. On the contrary supposition, I would admit the objection has very great weight indeed.

55.6.oldText: The true question to be decided then is this. Is the smallness of the number, as a temporary regulation, dangerous to public liberty? Will sixty-five members for a few years, and a hundred or two hundred for a few more, be a safe depository for a limited and well-guarded power of legislating for the United States? I must own that I could not give a negative answer to this question without first erasing every impression I have received about the present genius of the people of America, the spirit that animates the State legislatures, and the principles incorporated into the political character of every class of citizens. I cannot conceive that the people of America, in their present temper, or under any circumstances that can soon arise, will choose, and every second year repeat the choice of, sixty-five or a hundred men disposed to form and pursue a scheme of tyranny or treachery. I cannot conceive that the State legislatures, which must feel so many motives to watch the federal legislature, and which possess so many means of counteracting it, would fail to detect or defeat a conspiracy of the latter against the liberties of their common constituents. I am equally unable to conceive that there are now, or can be in any short time, in the United States, any sixty-five or hundred men capable of recommending themselves to the choice of the people at large, who would either desire or dare, within the short space of two years, to betray the solemn trust committed to them. What change of circumstances, time, and a fuller population of our country may produce requires a prophetic spirit to declare, which I do not pretend to have. But judging from the circumstances now before us, and from their probable state within a moderate period of time, I must declare that the liberties of America cannot be unsafe in the number of hands proposed by the federal Constitution.

55.7.oldText: From what quarter can the danger come? Are we afraid of foreign gold? If foreign gold could so easily corrupt our federal rulers and enable them to ensnare and betray their constituents, how has it happened that we are at this time a free and independent nation? The Congress that conducted us through the Revolution was a less numerous body than its successors will be. They were not chosen by, nor responsible to, their fellow-citizens at large. Though appointed yearly, and recallable at pleasure, they were generally continued for three years, and before the ratification of the federal articles, for a still longer term. They held their consultations always under the veil of secrecy. They had the sole transaction of our affairs with foreign nations. Throughout the war they had the fate of their country more in their hands than will ever, we hope, be the case with our future representatives. Given the greatness of the prize at stake and the eagerness of the party that lost it, it may well be supposed that the use of means other than force would not have been scrupled. Yet we know by happy experience that the public trust was not betrayed. Nor has the purity of our public councils in this respect ever suffered, even from the whispers of slander.

55.8.oldText: Is the danger feared from the other branches of the federal government? But where are the means to be found by the President, or the Senate, or both? Their official salaries, we may presume, will not, and without a previous corruption of the House of Representatives cannot, more than suffice for very different purposes. Their private fortunes, since they must all be American citizens, cannot possibly be sources of danger. The only means they can possess, then, will be in the dispensing of appointments. Is it here that suspicion rests her charge? Sometimes we are told that this fund of corruption is to be exhausted by the President in subduing the virtue of the Senate. Now, the fidelity of the other House is to be the victim. The improbability of such a mercenary and treacherous combination among the several members of government — standing on as different foundations as republican principles will well admit, and at the same time accountable to the society over which they are placed — ought alone to quiet this apprehension. But fortunately, the Constitution has provided a still further safeguard. Members of Congress are made ineligible for any civil offices that may be created, or whose salaries may be increased, during the term of their election. No offices, therefore, can be dealt out to existing members except such as may become vacant by ordinary casualties. To suppose that these would be sufficient to purchase the guardians of the people, selected by the people themselves, is to renounce every rule by which events ought to be calculated, and to substitute an indiscriminate and unbounded jealousy with which all reasoning must be vain. The sincere friends of liberty who give themselves up to the extravagances of this passion are not aware of the injury they do their own cause. As there is a degree of depravity in mankind that requires a certain degree of caution and distrust, so there are other qualities in human nature that justify a certain portion of esteem and confidence. Republican government presupposes the existence of these qualities to a higher degree than any other form. Were the pictures drawn by the political jealousy of some among us faithful likenesses of human character, the inference would be that there is not sufficient virtue among men for self-government, and that nothing less than the chains of despotism can restrain them from destroying and devouring one another.

56.0.oldText: The second charge against the House of Representatives is that it will be too small to possess due knowledge of the interests of its constituents.

56.1.oldText: Since this objection clearly proceeds from comparing the proposed number of representatives with the great extent of the United States, the number of inhabitants, and the diversity of their interests — without taking into account the circumstances that will distinguish the Congress from other legislative bodies — the best answer is a brief explanation of these peculiarities.

56.2.oldText: It is a sound and important principle that the representative ought to be acquainted with the interests and circumstances of his constituents. But this principle can extend no further than to those circumstances and interests to which the authority and care of the representative relate. Ignorance of various minute and particular objects that do not lie within the compass of legislation is consistent with every attribute necessary to a proper performance of the legislative trust. In determining the extent of information required for exercising a particular authority, recourse must be had to the objects within the scope of that authority.

56.3.oldText: What are to be the objects of federal legislation? Those most important, and which seem most to require local knowledge, are commerce, taxation, and the militia.

56.4.oldText: A proper regulation of commerce requires much information, as has been remarked elsewhere. But as far as this information relates to the laws and local situation of each individual State, a very few representatives would be quite sufficient vehicles to convey it to the federal councils.

56.5.oldText: Taxation will consist, in great measure, of duties involved in the regulation of commerce. So far the preceding remark applies to this object. As far as it may consist of internal collections, more diffuse knowledge of the State's circumstances may be necessary. But will not this also be possessed in sufficient degree by a very few intelligent men, broadly elected within the State? Divide the largest State into ten or twelve districts, and there will be no peculiar local interests in any that will not be within the knowledge of the district's representative. Besides this source of information, the laws of the State, framed by representatives from every part of it, will themselves be almost a sufficient guide. In every State, regulations on this subject have been made and must continue to be made, which will in many cases leave little more for the federal legislature to do than to review the different laws and reduce them into one general act. A skillful individual in his study, with all the local codes before him, might compile a law on some subjects of taxation for the whole Union, without any aid from oral information. It may be expected that whenever internal taxes may be necessary, and particularly in cases requiring uniformity throughout the States, the more simple objects will be preferred. To be fully sensible of the ease this will give to this branch of federal legislation by the assistance of the State codes, we need only suppose for a moment that this or any other State were divided into a number of parts, each having and exercising within itself a power of local legislation. Is it not evident that a degree of local information and preparatory labor would be found in the several volumes of their proceedings, which would very much shorten the labors of the general legislature, and render a much smaller number of members sufficient for it? The federal councils will derive great advantage from another circumstance. The representatives of each State will not only bring with them a considerable knowledge of its laws, and a local knowledge of their respective districts, but will probably in all cases have been members, and may even at the very time be members, of the State legislature, where all the local information and interests of the State are assembled. From there it may easily be conveyed by a very few hands into the legislature of the United States.

56.6.oldText: (The observations made on the subject of taxation apply with greater force to the case of the militia. For however different the rules of discipline may be in different States, they are the same throughout each particular State. They depend on circumstances that can differ but little in different parts of the same State.)

56.7.oldText: (With regard to the regulation of the militia, there are scarcely any circumstances about which local knowledge can be said to be necessary. The general face of the country, whether mountainous or level, most fit for operations of infantry or cavalry, is almost the only consideration of this nature that can occur. The art of war teaches general principles of organization, movement, and discipline, which apply universally.)

56.8.oldText: The attentive reader will see that the reasoning used here, to prove the sufficiency of a moderate number of representatives, in no respect contradicts what was urged on another occasion regarding the extensive information that representatives ought to possess and the time that might be necessary for acquiring it. This information, so far as it may relate to local objects, is rendered necessary and difficult, not by a difference of laws and local circumstances within a single State, but by those among different States. Taking each State by itself, its laws are the same and its interests are little diversified. A few men, therefore, will possess all the knowledge needed for proper representation. Were the interests and affairs of each individual State perfectly simple and uniform, knowledge of them in one part would imply knowledge of them in every other, and the whole State might be competently represented by a single member taken from any part of it. Comparing the different States together, we find a great dissimilarity in their laws, and in many other circumstances connected with the objects of federal legislation, with all of which the federal representatives ought to have some acquaintance. While a few representatives from each State, then, may bring with them due knowledge of their own State, every representative will have much information to acquire concerning all the other States. The changes of time, as remarked before, on the comparative situation of the different States, will have an assimilating effect. The effect of time on the internal affairs of the States, taken singly, will be just the contrary. At present, some of the States are little more than a society of farmers. Few of them have made much progress in those branches of industry that give variety and complexity to the affairs of a nation. These, however, will in all of them be the fruits of a more advanced population, and will require, on the part of each State, a fuller representation. The foresight of the convention has accordingly taken care that the progress of population may be accompanied with a proper increase in the representative branch of the government.

56.9.oldText: The experience of Great Britain, which presents to mankind so many political lessons of both warning and example, and which has been frequently consulted in these inquiries, corroborates the result of the reflections we have just made. The number of inhabitants in the two kingdoms of England and Scotland cannot be put at less than eight million. The representatives of these eight million in the House of Commons number five hundred and fifty-eight. Of this number, one-ninth are elected by three hundred and sixty-four persons, and one-half by five thousand seven hundred and twenty-three persons. It cannot be supposed that the half thus elected, and who do not even reside among the people at large, can add anything either to the security of the people against the government or to the knowledge of their circumstances and interests in the legislative councils. On the contrary, it is notorious that they are more frequently the representatives and instruments of the executive magistrate than the guardians and advocates of popular rights. They might therefore, with great propriety, be considered as something more than a mere deduction from the real representatives of the nation. We will, however, consider them in this light alone. We will not extend the deduction to a considerable number of others who do not reside among their constituents, are very faintly connected with them, and have very little particular knowledge of their affairs. With all these concessions, only two hundred and seventy-nine persons will be the depository of the safety, interest, and happiness of eight million. That is to say, there will be one representative only to maintain the rights and explain the situation of TWENTY-EIGHT THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED AND SEVENTY constituents, in an assembly exposed to the whole force of executive influence and extending its authority to every object of legislation within a nation whose affairs are in the highest degree diversified and complicated. Yet it is very certain not only that a valuable portion of freedom has been preserved under all these circumstances, but that the defects in the British code are chargeable, in a very small proportion, on the legislature's ignorance of the people's circumstances. Allowing this case the weight due to it, and comparing it with that of the House of Representatives as explained above, it seems to give the fullest assurance that a representative for every THIRTY THOUSAND INHABITANTS will render the latter both a safe and competent guardian of the interests committed to it.

57.0.oldText: The third charge against the House of Representatives is that it will be drawn from that class of citizens which will have least sympathy with the mass of the people, and be most likely to aim at an ambitious sacrifice of the many to the aggrandizement of the few.

57.1.oldText: Of all the objections framed against the federal Constitution, this is perhaps the most extraordinary. While the objection itself is leveled against a pretended oligarchy, its principle strikes at the very root of republican government.

57.2.oldText: The aim of every political constitution is, or ought to be, first to obtain for rulers men who possess the most wisdom to discern, and the most virtue to pursue, the common good of society. Next, it is to take the most effective precautions for keeping them virtuous while they continue to hold their public trust. The elective mode of obtaining rulers is the characteristic policy of republican government. The means relied on in this form of government for preventing their degeneracy are numerous and various. The most effective is such a limitation of the term of appointments as will maintain a proper responsibility to the people.

57.3.oldText: Let me now ask: what circumstance is there in the constitution of the House of Representatives that violates the principles of republican government, or favors the elevation of the few on the ruins of the many? Let me ask whether every circumstance is not, on the contrary, strictly conformable to these principles, and scrupulously impartial to the rights and pretensions of every class and description of citizens?

57.4.oldText: Who are to be the electors of the federal representatives? Not the rich more than the poor. Not the learned more than the ignorant. Not the haughty heirs of distinguished names more than the humble sons of obscurity and ill fortune. The electors are to be the great body of the people of the United States. They are to be the same people who exercise the right in every State of electing the corresponding branch of the State legislature.

57.5.oldText: Who are to be the objects of popular choice? Every citizen whose merit may recommend him to the esteem and confidence of his country. No qualification of wealth, of birth, of religious faith, or of civil profession is permitted to fetter the judgment or disappoint the inclination of the people.

57.6.oldText: If we consider the situation of the men on whom the free votes of their fellow-citizens may confer the representative trust, we shall find it involves every security that can be devised or desired for their fidelity to their constituents.

57.7.oldText: First, since they will have been distinguished by the preference of their fellow-citizens, we are to presume that in general they will also be somewhat distinguished by those qualities which entitle them to it, and which promise a sincere and scrupulous regard to the nature of their engagements.

57.8.oldText: Second, they will enter into public service under circumstances that cannot fail to produce at least a temporary affection for their constituents. There is in every breast a sensitivity to marks of honor, favor, esteem, and confidence, which, apart from all considerations of interest, is some pledge for grateful and benevolent returns. Ingratitude is a common topic of declamation against human nature, and it must be confessed that instances of it are too frequent and flagrant, in both public and private life. But the universal and extreme indignation it inspires is itself proof of the energy and prevalence of the contrary sentiment.

57.9.oldText: Third, those ties that bind the representative to his constituents are strengthened by motives of a more selfish nature. His pride and vanity attach him to a form of government that favors his pretensions and gives him a share in its honors and distinctions. Whatever hopes or projects might be entertained by a few aspiring characters, it must generally happen that a great proportion of the men deriving their advancement from their influence with the people would have more to hope from preserving the favor than from innovations in the government subversive of the authority of the people.

57.10.oldText: All these securities, however, would be very insufficient without the restraint of frequent elections. Hence, fourth, the House of Representatives is so constituted as to support in the members a habitual recollection of their dependence on the people. Before the sentiments impressed on their minds by the mode of their elevation can be erased by the exercise of power, they will be compelled to anticipate the moment when their power is to cease, when their exercise of it is to be reviewed, and when they must descend to the level from which they were raised — there to remain forever, unless a faithful discharge of their trust establishes their title to a renewal of it.

57.11.oldText: I will add, as a fifth circumstance in the situation of the House of Representatives restraining them from oppressive measures, that they can make no law that will not have its full operation on themselves and their friends, as well as on the great mass of society. This has always been deemed one of the strongest bonds by which human policy can connect the rulers and the people together. It creates between them that communion of interests and sympathy of sentiments of which few governments have furnished examples — but without which every government degenerates into tyranny. If it be asked, what is to restrain the House of Representatives from making legal discriminations in favor of themselves and a particular class of society? I answer: the genius of the whole system; the nature of just and constitutional laws; and above all, the vigilant and manly spirit that animates the people of America — a spirit that nourishes freedom, and in return is nourished by it.

57.12.oldText: If this spirit shall ever be so far debased as to tolerate a law not binding on the legislature, as well as on the people, the people will be prepared to tolerate anything but liberty.

57.13.oldText: Such will be the relation between the House of Representatives and their constituents. Duty, gratitude, interest, ambition itself — these are the chords by which they will be bound to fidelity and sympathy with the great mass of the people. It is possible that these may all be insufficient to control the caprice and wickedness of man. But are they not all that government will admit, and that human prudence can devise? Are they not the genuine and characteristic means by which republican government provides for the liberty and happiness of the people? Are they not the same means on which every State government in the Union relies for attaining these important ends? What, then, are we to understand by the objection this paper has combated? What are we to say to the men who profess the most flaming zeal for republican government, yet boldly impeach its fundamental principle? Who pretend to be champions for the right and capacity of the people to choose their own rulers, yet maintain that they will prefer those only who will immediately and infallibly betray the trust committed to them?

57.14.oldText: Were the objection to be read by one who had not seen the mode prescribed by the Constitution for the choice of representatives, he could suppose nothing less than that some unreasonable property qualification was attached to the right of suffrage; or that the right of eligibility was limited to persons of particular families or fortunes; or at least that the mode prescribed by the State constitutions was, in some respect, very grossly departed from. We have seen how far such a supposition would err on the first two points. Nor would it, in fact, be less mistaken on the last. The only difference discoverable between the two cases is that each representative of the United States will be elected by five or six thousand citizens, while in the individual States the election of a representative is left to about as many hundreds. Will it be pretended that this difference is sufficient to justify an attachment to the State governments and an abhorrence of the federal government? If this is the point on which the objection turns, it deserves to be examined.

57.15.oldText: Is it supported by REASON? This cannot be said without maintaining that five or six thousand citizens are less capable of choosing a fit representative, or more liable to be corrupted by an unfit one, than five or six hundred. Reason, on the contrary, assures us that, just as in so great a number a fit representative would be most likely to be found, so the choice would be less likely to be diverted from him by the intrigues of the ambitious or the bribes of the rich.

57.16.oldText: Is the CONSEQUENCE drawn from this doctrine acceptable? If we say that five or six hundred citizens are as many as can jointly exercise their right of suffrage, must we not deprive the people of the immediate choice of their public servants in every instance where the administration of government does not require as many representatives as will amount to one for that number of citizens?

57.17.oldText: Is the doctrine warranted by FACTS? It was shown in the last paper that the real representation in the British House of Commons very little exceeds the proportion of one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. Besides a variety of powerful causes that do not exist here, and which favor in that country the pretensions of rank and wealth, no person is eligible as a representative of a county unless he possesses real estate of the clear value of six hundred pounds sterling per year. Nor of a city or borough, unless he possesses a like estate of half that annual value. To this qualification on the part of the county representatives is added another on the part of the county electors, which restrains the right of suffrage to persons having a freehold estate of an annual value of more than twenty pounds sterling, according to the present value of money. Despite these unfavorable circumstances, and despite some very unequal laws in the British code, it cannot be said that the representatives of the nation have elevated the few on the ruins of the many.

57.18.oldText: But we need not resort to foreign experience on this subject. Our own is explicit and decisive. The districts in New Hampshire in which the senators are chosen immediately by the people are nearly as large as will be necessary for her representatives in Congress. Those of Massachusetts are larger than will be necessary for that purpose, and those of New York still more so. In New York, the members of Assembly for the cities and counties of New York and Albany are elected by very nearly as many voters as will be entitled to a representative in Congress, calculating on the number of sixty-five representatives only. It makes no difference that in these senatorial districts and counties a number of representatives are voted for by each elector at the same time. If the same electors at the same time are capable of choosing four or five representatives, they cannot be incapable of choosing one. Pennsylvania is an additional example. Some of her counties, which elect her State representatives, are almost as large as her districts will be by which her federal representatives will be elected. The city of Philadelphia is supposed to contain between fifty and sixty thousand souls. It will therefore form nearly two districts for the choice of federal representatives. Yet it forms only one county, in which every elector votes for each of its representatives in the State legislature. And what may appear still more directly to our purpose, the whole city actually elects a SINGLE MEMBER for the executive council. This is the case in all the other counties of the State.

57.19.oldText: Are not these facts the most satisfactory proofs of the fallacy employed against the branch of the federal government under consideration? Has it appeared on trial that the senators of New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and New York, or the executive council of Pennsylvania, or the members of the Assembly in the two last States, have betrayed any peculiar disposition to sacrifice the many to the few, or are in any respect less worthy of their places than the representatives and magistrates appointed in other States by very small divisions of the people?

57.20.oldText: But there are cases of stronger character than any I have yet quoted. One branch of the legislature of Connecticut is so constituted that each member of it is elected by the whole State. So is the governor of that State, of Massachusetts, and of this State, and the president of New Hampshire. I leave every man to decide whether the result of any one of these experiments can be said to support a suspicion that a diffuse mode of choosing representatives of the people tends to elevate traitors and undermine public liberty.

58.0.oldText: The remaining charge against the House of Representatives, which I am to examine, is grounded on a supposition that the number of members will not be increased from time to time as the progress of population may demand.

58.1.oldText: It has been admitted that this objection, if well supported, would have great weight. The following observations will show that, like most other objections against the Constitution, it can only proceed from a partial view of the subject, or from a jealousy that discolors and disfigures every object beheld.

58.2.oldText: 1. Those who urge the objection seem not to have recalled that the federal Constitution will not suffer by comparison with the State constitutions in the security provided for a gradual increase in the number of representatives. The number that is to prevail in the first instance is declared to be temporary. Its duration is limited to the short term of three years.

58.3.oldText: Within every successive ten-year period, a census of inhabitants is to be repeated. The unequivocal objects of these regulations are these. First, to readjust from time to time the apportionment of representatives to the number of inhabitants, with the single exception that each State shall have at least one representative. Second, to increase the number of representatives at the same intervals, under the sole limitation that the whole number shall not exceed one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. If we review the constitutions of the several States, we shall find that some of them contain no determinate regulations on this subject. Others correspond pretty much on this point with the federal Constitution. The most effective security in any of them resolves into a mere directory provision.

58.4.oldText: 2. As far as experience has gone on this subject, a gradual increase of representatives under the State constitutions has at least kept pace with that of the constituents. The former have been as ready to concur in such measures as the latter have been to call for them.

58.5.oldText: 3. There is a peculiarity in the federal Constitution that ensures watchful attention in a majority both of the people and of their representatives to a constitutional increase of the latter. The peculiarity lies in this. One branch of the legislature is a representation of citizens, the other of the States. In the former, consequently, the larger States will have most weight. In the latter, the advantage will favor the smaller States. From this circumstance it may with certainty be inferred that the larger States will be strenuous advocates for increasing the number and weight of that part of the legislature in which their influence predominates. And it so happens that only four of the largest will have a majority of the whole votes in the House of Representatives. Should the representatives or people of the smaller States therefore at any time oppose a reasonable addition of members, a coalition of a very few States will be sufficient to overrule the opposition. Such a coalition, despite the rivalry and local prejudices that might prevent it on ordinary occasions, would not fail to take place when not merely prompted by common interest, but justified by equity and the principles of the Constitution.

58.6.oldText: It may be alleged perhaps that the Senate would be prompted by like motives to an opposing coalition. Since their concurrence would be indispensable, the just and constitutional views of the other branch might be defeated. This is the difficulty that has probably created the most serious apprehensions in the jealous friends of a numerous representation. Fortunately it is among the difficulties that, existing only in appearance, vanish on close and accurate inspection. The following reflections will, if I am not mistaken, be admitted to be conclusive and satisfactory on this point.

58.7.oldText: Despite the equal authority that will exist between the two houses on all legislative subjects, except the originating of money bills, it cannot be doubted that the House — composed of the greater number of members, when supported by the more powerful States, and speaking the known and determined sense of a majority of the people — will have no small advantage in a question depending on the comparative firmness of the two houses.

58.8.oldText: This advantage must be increased by the consciousness, felt by the same side, of being supported in its demands by right, by reason, and by the Constitution; and the consciousness, on the opposite side, of contending against the force of all these solemn considerations.

58.9.oldText: It is further to be considered that, in the gradation between the smallest and largest States, there are several that, though most likely in general to range themselves among the former, are too little removed in extent and population from the latter to second an opposition to their just and legitimate pretensions. Hence it is by no means certain that a majority of votes, even in the Senate, would be unfriendly to proper increases in the number of representatives.

58.10.oldText: It will not be looking too far to add that the senators from all the new States may be won over to the just views of the House of Representatives by an expedient too obvious to be overlooked. Since these States will, for a great length of time, advance in population with peculiar rapidity, they will be interested in frequent reapportionments of the representatives to the number of inhabitants. The large States therefore, who will prevail in the House of Representatives, will have nothing to do but to make reapportionments and increases mutually conditions of each other. The senators from all the most growing States will be bound to contend for the latter, by the interest their States will feel in the former.

58.11.oldText: These considerations seem to afford ample security on this subject, and ought alone to satisfy all the doubts and fears indulged regarding it. Admitting, however, that they should all be insufficient to subdue the unjust policy of the smaller States, or their predominant influence in the councils of the Senate, a constitutional and infallible resource still remains with the larger States, by which they will be able at all times to accomplish their just purposes. The House of Representatives cannot only refuse, but they alone can propose, the supplies needed for the support of government. They, in a word, hold the purse — that powerful instrument by which we behold, in the history of the British Constitution, an infant and humble representation of the people gradually enlarging the sphere of its activity and importance, and finally reducing, as far as it seems to have wished, all the overgrown prerogatives of the other branches of government. This power over the purse may, in fact, be regarded as the most complete and effective weapon with which any constitution can arm the immediate representatives of the people, for obtaining redress of every grievance, and for carrying into effect every just and salutary measure.

58.12.oldText: But will not the House of Representatives be as much interested as the Senate in maintaining the government in its proper functions, and will they not therefore be unwilling to stake its existence or its reputation on the pliancy of the Senate? Or, if such a trial of firmness between the two branches were hazarded, would not one be as likely to yield first as the other? These questions will create no difficulty for those who reflect that, in all cases, the smaller the number, and the more permanent and conspicuous the station, of men in power, the stronger must be the interest they will individually feel in whatever concerns the government. Those who represent the dignity of their country in the eyes of other nations will be particularly sensitive to every prospect of public danger, or of dishonorable stagnation in public affairs. To those causes we are to ascribe the continual triumph of the British House of Commons over the other branches of government, whenever the engine of a money bill has been employed. An absolute inflexibility on the side of the latter, although it could not have failed to involve every department of the state in general confusion, has neither been apprehended nor experienced. The utmost degree of firmness that can be displayed by the federal Senate or President will not be more than equal to a resistance in which they will be supported by constitutional and patriotic principles.

58.13.oldText: In this review of the Constitution of the House of Representatives, I have passed over the circumstances of economy, which, in the present state of affairs, might have had some effect in lessening the temporary number of representatives. Disregard of these would probably have been as rich a theme of declamation against the Constitution as the smallness of the number proposed has been. I omit also any remarks on the difficulty that might be found, under present circumstances, in engaging in federal service a large number of such characters as the people will probably elect. One observation, however, I must be permitted to add on this subject as claiming, in my judgment, very serious attention. It is this: in all legislative assemblies, the greater the number composing them, the fewer will be the men who in fact direct their proceedings. First, the more numerous an assembly, of whatever characters composed, the greater is known to be the ascendancy of passion over reason. Second, the larger the number, the greater will be the proportion of members of limited information and weak capacity. It is precisely on characters of this description that the eloquence and address of the few are known to act with all their force. In the ancient republics, where the whole body of the people assembled in person, a single orator, or an artful statesman, was generally seen to rule with as complete a sway as if a scepter had been placed in his single hand. On the same principle, the more multitudinous a representative assembly may be made, the more it will partake of the infirmities incident to collective meetings of the people. Ignorance will be the dupe of cunning, and passion the slave of sophistry and declamation. The people can never err more than in supposing that, by multiplying their representatives beyond a certain limit, they strengthen the barrier against the government of a few. Experience will forever admonish them that, on the contrary, AFTER SECURING A SUFFICIENT NUMBER FOR THE PURPOSES OF SAFETY, OF LOCAL INFORMATION, AND OF DIFFUSIVE SYMPATHY WITH THE WHOLE SOCIETY, they will counteract their own views by every addition to their representatives. The countenance of the government may become more democratic, but the soul that animates it will be more oligarchic. The machine will be enlarged, but the fewer, and often the more secret, will be the springs by which its motions are directed.

58.14.oldText: As connected with the objection against the number of representatives, may properly be noticed here the objection raised against the number made competent for legislative business. It has been said that more than a majority ought to have been required for a quorum, and in particular cases, if not all, more than a majority of a quorum for a decision. That some advantages might have resulted from such a precaution cannot be denied. It might have been an additional shield to some particular interests, and another obstacle generally to hasty and partial measures. But these considerations are outweighed by the inconveniences in the opposite scale. In all cases where justice or the general good might require new laws to be passed, or active measures to be pursued, the fundamental principle of free government would be reversed. It would no longer be the majority that would rule. The power would be transferred to the minority. Were the defensive privilege limited to particular cases, an interested minority might take advantage of it to screen themselves from equitable sacrifices to the general welfare, or, in particular emergencies, to extort unreasonable indulgences. Lastly, it would facilitate and foster the baneful practice of secessions — a practice that has shown itself even in States where a majority only is required; a practice subversive of all the principles of order and regular government; a practice that leads more directly to public convulsions, and the ruin of popular governments, than any other yet displayed among us.

59.0.oldText: The natural order of the subject leads us to consider here the provision of the Constitution that authorizes the national legislature to regulate, in the last resort, the election of its own members. It is in these words: "The TIMES, PLACES, and MANNER of holding elections for senators and representatives shall be prescribed in each State by the legislature thereof; but the Congress may, at any time, by law, make or alter SUCH REGULATIONS, except as to the PLACES of choosing senators." This provision has not only been declaimed against by those who condemn the Constitution wholesale, but it has also been censured by those who have objected with less latitude and greater moderation. In one instance it has been thought objectionable by a gentleman who has declared himself the advocate of every other part of the system.

59.1.oldText: I am greatly mistaken, however, if there is any article in the whole plan more completely defensible than this. Its propriety rests on the evidence of this plain proposition: EVERY GOVERNMENT OUGHT TO CONTAIN IN ITSELF THE MEANS OF ITS OWN PRESERVATION. Every just reasoner will, at first sight, approve adherence to this rule in the work of the convention. He will disapprove every deviation from it that may not appear to have been dictated by the necessity of incorporating into the work some particular ingredient with which a rigid conformity to the rule was incompatible. Even in this case, though he may acquiesce in the necessity, he will not cease to regard and to regret a departure from so fundamental a principle, as a portion of imperfection in the system that may prove the seed of future weakness, and perhaps anarchy.

59.2.oldText: It will not be alleged that an election law could have been framed and inserted in the Constitution that would have been always applicable to every probable change in the situation of the country. It will therefore not be denied that a discretionary power over elections ought to exist somewhere. It will, I presume, be as readily conceded that there were only three ways in which this power could have been reasonably modified and disposed: it must either have been lodged wholly in the national legislature, or wholly in the State legislatures, or primarily in the latter and ultimately in the former. The last mode has, with reason, been preferred by the convention. They have submitted the regulation of elections for the federal government, in the first instance, to the local administrations, which, in ordinary cases, and when no improper views prevail, may be both more convenient and more satisfactory. But they have reserved to the national authority a right to interpose whenever extraordinary circumstances might render that interposition necessary to its safety.

59.3.oldText: Nothing can be more evident than that an exclusive power of regulating elections for the national government, in the hands of the State legislatures, would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy. They could at any moment annihilate it by neglecting to provide for the choice of persons to administer its affairs. It is to little purpose to say that a neglect or omission of this kind would not be likely to take place. The constitutional possibility of the thing, without an equivalent for the risk, is an unanswerable objection. Nor has any satisfactory reason yet been assigned for incurring that risk. The extravagant surmises of a distempered jealousy can never be dignified with that character. If we are in a humor to presume abuses of power, it is as fair to presume them on the part of the State governments as on the part of the general government. As it is more consonant with the rules of just theory to trust the Union with the care of its own existence than to transfer that care to any other hands, if abuses of power are to be hazarded on the one side or the other, it is more rational to hazard them where the power would naturally be placed than where it would unnaturally be placed.

59.4.oldText: Suppose an article had been introduced into the Constitution empowering the United States to regulate the elections for the particular States. Would any man have hesitated to condemn it, both as an unwarrantable transposition of power, and as a premeditated engine for the destruction of the State governments? The violation of principle, in this case, would have required no comment. To an unbiased observer, it will not be less apparent in the project of subjecting the existence of the national government, in a similar respect, to the pleasure of the State governments. An impartial view of the matter cannot fail to result in a conviction that each, as far as possible, ought to depend on itself for its own preservation.

59.5.oldText: As an objection to this position, it may be remarked that the constitution of the national Senate would involve, in its full extent, the danger that is suggested might flow from an exclusive power in the State legislatures to regulate the federal elections. It may be alleged that, by declining the appointment of senators, they might at any time give a fatal blow to the Union. From this it may be inferred that, since its existence would be thus rendered dependent upon them in so essential a point, there can be no objection to entrusting them with it in the particular case under consideration. The interest of each State, it may be added, to maintain its representation in the national councils, would be a complete security against an abuse of the trust.

59.6.oldText: This argument, though specious, will not, on examination, be found solid. It is certainly true that the State legislatures, by forbearing the appointment of senators, may destroy the national government. But it does not follow that, because they have a power to do this in one instance, they ought to have it in every other. There are cases in which the harmful tendency of such a power may be far more decisive, without any motive equally cogent with that which must have regulated the conduct of the convention regarding the formation of the Senate, to recommend their admission into the system. So far as that construction may expose the Union to the possibility of injury from the State legislatures, it is an evil. But it is an evil that could not have been avoided without excluding the States, in their political capacities, wholly from a place in the organization of the national government. If this had been done, it would doubtless have been interpreted as an entire dereliction of the federal principle. It would certainly have deprived the State governments of that absolute safeguard they will enjoy under this provision. But however wise it may have been to submit in this instance to an inconvenience, for the attainment of a necessary advantage or a greater good, no inference can be drawn from this to favor an accumulation of the evil where no necessity urges, nor any greater good invites.

59.7.oldText: It may be easily discerned also that the national government would run a much greater risk from a power in the State legislatures over the elections of its House of Representatives than from their power of appointing the members of its Senate. The senators are to be chosen for the period of six years. There is to be a rotation, by which the seats of a third of them are to be vacated and replenished every two years. No State is to be entitled to more than two senators, and a quorum of the body is to consist of sixteen members. The joint result of these circumstances would be that a temporary combination of a few States to interrupt the appointment of senators could neither annul the existence nor impair the activity of the body. It is not from a general and permanent combination of the States that we can have anything to fear. The first might proceed from sinister designs in the leading members of a few of the State legislatures. The last would suppose a fixed and rooted disaffection in the great body of the people, which will either never exist at all, or will, in all probability, proceed from an experience of the inaptitude of the general government for the advancement of their happiness — in which event no good citizen could desire its continuance.

59.8.oldText: But with regard to the federal House of Representatives, there is intended to be a general election of members once every two years. If the State legislatures were to be invested with an exclusive power of regulating these elections, every period of making them would be a delicate crisis in the national situation, which might issue in a dissolution of the Union, if the leaders of a few of the most important States had entered into a previous conspiracy to prevent an election.

59.9.oldText: I shall not deny that there is a degree of weight in the observation that the interests of each State, to be represented in the federal councils, will be a security against the abuse of a power over its elections in the hands of the State legislatures. But the security will not be considered complete by those who attend to the force of an obvious distinction between the interest of the people in the public welfare, and the interest of their local rulers in the power and consequence of their offices. The people of America may be warmly attached to the government of the Union, at times when the particular rulers of particular States, stimulated by the natural rivalry of power and by the hopes of personal aggrandizement, and supported by a strong faction in each of those States, may be in a very opposite temper. This diversity of sentiment between a majority of the people and the individuals who have the greatest credit in their councils is exemplified in some of the States at the present moment, on the present question. The scheme of separate confederacies, which will always multiply the chances of ambition, will be a never-failing bait to all such influential characters in the State administrations as are capable of preferring their own gain and advancement to the public welfare. With so effective a weapon in their hands as the exclusive power of regulating elections for the national government, a combination of a few such men, in a few of the most considerable States, where the temptation will always be the strongest, might accomplish the destruction of the Union, by seizing the opportunity of some casual dissatisfaction among the people (which they may themselves perhaps have excited), to discontinue the choice of members for the federal House of Representatives. It ought never to be forgotten that a firm union of this country, under an effective government, will probably be an increasing object of jealousy to more than one nation of Europe; and that enterprises to subvert it will sometimes originate in the intrigues of foreign powers, and will seldom fail to be patronized and abetted by some of them. Its preservation therefore ought, in no case that can be avoided, to be committed to the guardianship of any but those whose situation will uniformly beget an immediate interest in the faithful and vigilant performance of the trust.

60.0.oldText: We have seen that an uncontrollable power over the elections to the federal government could not, without hazard, be committed to the State legislatures. Let us now see what would be the danger on the other side — that is, from confiding the ultimate right of regulating its own elections to the Union itself. It is not pretended that this right would ever be used to exclude any State from its share in the representation. The interest of all would, in this respect at least, be the security of all. But it is alleged that it might be used in such a manner as to promote the election of some favorite class of men to the exclusion of others, by confining the places of election to particular districts, and rendering it impracticable for the citizens at large to take part in the choice. Of all chimerical suppositions, this seems the most chimerical. On the one hand, no rational calculation of probabilities would lead us to imagine that the disposition such conduct so violent and extraordinary would imply could ever find its way into the national councils. On the other hand, it may be concluded with certainty that, if so improper a spirit should ever gain admittance into them, it would display itself in a form altogether different and far more decisive.

60.1.oldText: The improbability of the attempt may be satisfactorily inferred from this single reflection: it could never be made without causing an immediate revolt of the great body of the people, headed and directed by the State governments. It is not difficult to conceive that this characteristic right of freedom may, in certain turbulent and factious seasons, be violated, with respect to a particular class of citizens, by a victorious and overbearing majority. But that so fundamental a privilege, in a country so situated and enlightened, should be invaded to the prejudice of the great mass of the people, by the deliberate policy of the government, without occasioning a popular revolution, is altogether inconceivable and incredible.

60.2.oldText: In addition to this general reflection, there are considerations of a more precise nature that forbid all apprehension on the subject. The dissimilarity in the ingredients that will compose the national government, and still more in the manner in which they will be brought into action in its various branches, must form a powerful obstacle to a concert of views in any partial scheme of elections. There is sufficient diversity in the state of property, in the genius, manners, and habits of the people of the different parts of the Union, to occasion a material diversity of disposition in their representatives toward the different ranks and conditions in society. And though an intimate exchange under the same government will promote a gradual assimilation in some of these respects, there are causes, as well physical as moral, that may, in greater or lesser degree, permanently nourish different propensities and inclinations in this respect. But the circumstance most likely to have the greatest influence in the matter will be the dissimilar modes of constituting the several component parts of the government. The House of Representatives being elected immediately by the people, the Senate by the State legislatures, the President by electors chosen for that purpose by the people — there would be little probability of a common interest cementing these different branches in a predilection for any particular class of electors.

60.3.oldText: As to the Senate, it is impossible that any regulation of "time and manner," which is all that is proposed to be submitted to the national government regarding that body, can affect the spirit that will direct the choice of its members. The collective sense of the State legislatures can never be influenced by extraneous circumstances of that sort — a consideration which alone ought to satisfy us that the discrimination apprehended would never be attempted. For what inducement could the Senate have to concur in a preference in which itself would not be included? Or to what purpose would it be established, with reference to one branch of the legislature, if it could not be extended to the other? The composition of the one would in this case counteract that of the other. We can never suppose that it would embrace the appointments to the Senate, unless we can at the same time suppose the voluntary cooperation of the State legislatures. If we make the latter supposition, it then becomes immaterial where the power in question is placed — whether in their hands or in those of the Union.

60.4.oldText: But what is to be the object of this capricious partiality in the national councils? Is it to be exercised in a discrimination between the different departments of industry, or between the different kinds of property, or between the different degrees of property? Will it lean in favor of the landed interest, or the moneyed interest, or the mercantile interest, or the manufacturing interest? Or, to speak in the fashionable language of the adversaries to the Constitution, will it court the elevation of "the wealthy and the well-born," to the exclusion and debasement of all the rest of society?

60.5.oldText: If this partiality is to be exerted in favor of those concerned in any particular description of industry or property, I presume it will readily be admitted that the competition for it will lie between landed men and merchants. I do not scruple to affirm that it is infinitely less likely that either of them should gain an ascendant in the national councils, than that the one or the other should predominate in all the local councils.
