It would not perhaps be rash to predict that, as a means of influence, it will be found to outweigh all the peculiar attributes of the Senate.

66.7.oldText: A THIRD objection to the Senate as a court of impeachments is drawn from the agency they are to have in the appointments to office. It is imagined that they would be too indulgent judges of the conduct of men, in whose official creation they had participated. The principle of this objection would condemn a practice which is to be seen in all the State governments, if not in all the governments with which we are acquainted — I mean that of rendering those who hold offices during pleasure, dependent on the pleasure of those who appoint them. With equal plausibility might it be alleged in this case, that the favoritism of the latter would always be an asylum for the misbehavior of the former. But that practice, in contradiction to this principle, proceeds upon the presumption that the responsibility of those who appoint, for the fitness and competency of the persons on whom they bestow their choice, and the interest they will have in the respectable and prosperous administration of affairs, will inspire a sufficient disposition to dismiss from a share in it all such who, by their conduct, shall have proved themselves unworthy of the confidence reposed in them. Though facts may not always correspond with this presumption, yet if it be, in the main, just, it must destroy the supposition that the Senate, who will merely sanction the choice of the Executive, should feel a bias, toward the objects of that choice, strong enough to blind them to the evidences of guilt so extraordinary, as to have induced the representatives of the nation to become its accusers.

66.8.oldText: If any further arguments were necessary to evince the improbability of such a bias, it might be found in the nature of the agency of the Senate in the business of appointments. It will be the office of the President to NOMINATE, and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to APPOINT. There will, of course, be no exertion of CHOICE on the part of the Senate. They may defeat one choice of the Executive, and oblige him to make another, but they cannot themselves CHOOSE — they can only ratify or reject the choice of the President. They might even entertain a preference for some other person, at the very moment they were assenting to the one proposed, because there might be no positive ground of opposition to him. They could not be sure, if they withheld their assent, that the subsequent nomination would fall upon their own favorite, or upon any other person in their estimation more meritorious than the one rejected. Thus it could hardly happen that the majority of the Senate would feel any other complacency toward the object of an appointment than such as the appearances of merit might inspire, and the proofs of the want of it destroy.

66.9.oldText: A FOURTH objection to the Senate in the capacity of a court of impeachments is derived from its union with the Executive in the power of making treaties. This, it has been said, would constitute the senators their own judges, in every case of a corrupt or perfidious execution of that trust. After having combined with the Executive in betraying the interests of the nation in a ruinous treaty, what prospect, it is asked, would there be of their being made to suffer the punishment they would deserve, when they were themselves to decide upon the accusation brought against them for the treachery of which they have been guilty?

66.10.oldText: This objection has been circulated with more earnestness and with greater show of reason than any other which has appeared against this part of the plan, and yet I am deceived if it does not rest upon an erroneous foundation.

66.11.oldText: The security essentially intended by the Constitution against corruption and treachery in the formation of treaties, is to be sought for in the numbers and characters of those who are to make them. The JOINT AGENCY of the Chief Magistrate of the Union, and of two-thirds of the members of a body selected by the collective wisdom of the legislatures of the several States, is designed to be the pledge for the fidelity of the national councils in this particular. The convention might with propriety have meditated the punishment of the Executive, for a deviation from the instructions of the Senate, or a want of integrity in the conduct of the negotiations committed to him. They might also have had in view the punishment of a few leading individuals in the Senate, who should have prostituted their influence in that body as the mercenary instruments of foreign corruption. But they could not, with more or with equal propriety, have contemplated the impeachment and punishment of two-thirds of the Senate, consenting to an improper treaty, than of a majority of that or of the other branch of the national legislature, consenting to a pernicious or unconstitutional law — a principle which, I believe, has never been admitted into any government. How, in fact, could a majority in the House of Representatives impeach themselves? Not better, it is evident, than two-thirds of the Senate might try themselves. And yet what reason is there that a majority of the House of Representatives, sacrificing the interests of the society by an unjust and tyrannical act of legislation, should escape with impunity, more than two-thirds of the Senate, sacrificing the same interests in an injurious treaty with a foreign power? The truth is that, in all such cases, it is essential to the freedom and to the necessary independence of the deliberations of the body, that the members of it should be exempt from punishment for acts done in a collective capacity. The security to the society must depend on the care which is taken to confide the trust to proper hands, to make it their interest to execute it with fidelity, and to make it as difficult as possible for them to combine in any interest opposite to that of the public good.

66.12.oldText: So far as might concern the misbehavior of the Executive in perverting the instructions or contravening the views of the Senate, we need not be apprehensive of the want of a disposition in that body to punish the abuse of their confidence or to vindicate their own authority. We may thus far count upon their pride, if not upon their virtue. So far even as might concern the corruption of leading members, by whose arts and influence the majority may have been inveigled into measures odious to the community, if the proofs of that corruption should be satisfactory, the usual propensity of human nature will warrant us in concluding that there would be commonly no defect of inclination in the body to divert the public resentment from themselves by a ready sacrifice of the authors of their mismanagement and disgrace.

66.13.oldText: 1. In that of New Jersey, also, the final judiciary authority is in a branch of the legislature. In New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and South Carolina, one branch of the legislature is the court for the trial of impeachments.

67.0.oldText: The constitution of the executive department of the proposed government claims our attention next.

67.1.oldText: There is hardly any part of the system that could have been attended with greater difficulty in the arrangement of it than this. Perhaps none has been inveighed against with less candor or criticized with less judgment.

67.2.oldText: Here the writers against the Constitution seem to have taken pains to signalize their talent for misrepresentation. Calculating on the aversion of the people to monarchy, they have endeavored to enlist all their jealousies and apprehensions in opposition to the intended President of the United States — not merely as the embryo, but as the full-grown progeny, of that detested parent. To establish the pretended affinity, they have not scrupled to draw resources even from the regions of fiction. The authorities of a magistrate — in few instances greater, in some instances less, than those of a governor of New York — have been magnified into more than royal prerogatives. He has been decorated with attributes superior in dignity and splendor to those of a king of Great Britain. He has been shown to us with the diadem sparkling on his brow and the imperial purple flowing in his train. He has been seated on a throne surrounded with minions and mistresses, giving audience to the envoys of foreign potentates, in all the supercilious pomp of majesty. The images of Asiatic despotism and voluptuousness have scarcely been wanting to crown the exaggerated scene. We have been taught to tremble at the terrific visages of murdering janizaries, and to blush at the unveiled mysteries of a future seraglio.

67.3.oldText: Attempts so extravagant as these to disfigure or, it might rather be said, to metamorphose the object, render it necessary to take an accurate view of its real nature and form. This is needed both to ascertain its true aspect and genuine appearance, and to unmask the disingenuity and expose the fallacy of the counterfeit resemblances which have been so insidiously, as well as industriously, propagated.

67.4.oldText: In executing this task, there is no man who would not find it an arduous effort either to behold with moderation, or to treat with seriousness, the devices, no less weak than wicked, which have been contrived to pervert the public opinion in relation to the subject. They so far exceed the usual though unjustifiable licenses of party artifice, that even in a disposition the most candid and tolerant, they must force the sentiments which favor an indulgent construction of the conduct of political adversaries to give place to a voluntary and unreserved indignation. It is impossible not to bestow the imputation of deliberate imposture and deception upon the gross pretense of a similitude between a king of Great Britain and a magistrate of the character marked out for that of the President of the United States. It is still more impossible to withhold that imputation from the rash and barefaced expedients which have been employed to give success to the attempted imposition.

67.5.oldText: In one instance, which I cite as a sample of the general spirit, the temerity has proceeded so far as to ascribe to the President of the United States a power which by the instrument reported is EXPRESSLY allotted to the Executives of the individual States. I mean the power of filling casual vacancies in the Senate.

67.6.oldText: This bold experiment upon the discernment of his countrymen has been hazarded by a writer who (whatever may be his real merit) has had no inconsiderable share in the applauses of his party, and who, upon this false and unfounded suggestion, has built a series of observations equally false and unfounded. Let him now be confronted with the evidence of the fact, and let him, if he is able, justify or extenuate the shameful outrage he has offered to the dictates of truth and to the rules of fair dealing.

67.7.oldText: The second clause of the second section of the second article empowers the President of the United States "to nominate, and by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other OFFICERS of United States whose appointments are NOT in the Constitution OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR, and WHICH SHALL BE ESTABLISHED BY LAW." Immediately after this clause follows another in these words: "The President shall have power to fill up all VACANCIES that may happen DURING THE RECESS OF THE SENATE, by granting commissions which shall EXPIRE AT THE END OF THEIR NEXT SESSION." It is from this last provision that the pretended power of the President to fill vacancies in the Senate has been deduced. A slight attention to the connection of the clauses, and to the obvious meaning of the terms, will satisfy us that the deduction is not even colorable.

67.8.oldText: The first of these two clauses, it is clear, only provides a mode for appointing such officers, "whose appointments are NOT OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution, and which SHALL BE ESTABLISHED BY LAW." Of course it cannot extend to the appointments of senators, whose appointments are OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution, and who are ESTABLISHED BY THE CONSTITUTION, and will not require a future establishment by law. This position will hardly be contested.

67.9.oldText: The last of these two clauses, it is equally clear, cannot be understood to comprehend the power of filling vacancies in the Senate, for the following reasons. First. The relation in which that clause stands to the other, which declares the general mode of appointing officers of the United States, denotes it to be nothing more than a supplement to the other, for the purpose of establishing an auxiliary method of appointment, in cases to which the general method was inadequate. The ordinary power of appointment is confined to the President and Senate JOINTLY, and can therefore only be exercised during the session of the Senate. But since it would have been improper to oblige this body to be continually in session for the appointment of officers, and since vacancies might happen IN THEIR RECESS which it might be necessary for the public service to fill without delay, the succeeding clause is evidently intended to authorize the President, SINGLY, to make temporary appointments "during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session." Second. If this clause is to be considered as supplementary to the one which precedes, the VACANCIES of which it speaks must be construed to relate to the "officers" described in the preceding one. This, we have seen, excludes from its description the members of the Senate. Third. The time within which the power is to operate, "during the recess of the Senate," and the duration of the appointments, "to the end of the next session" of that body, conspire to elucidate the sense of the provision. If it had been intended to comprehend senators, it would naturally have referred the temporary power of filling vacancies to the recess of the State legislatures, who are to make the permanent appointments, and not to the recess of the national Senate, who are to have no concern in those appointments. It would have extended the duration in office of the temporary senators to the next session of the legislature of the State, in whose representation the vacancies had happened, instead of making it expire at the end of the ensuing session of the national Senate. The circumstances of the body authorized to make the permanent appointments would, of course, have governed the modification of a power which related to the temporary appointments. Since the national Senate is the body whose situation is alone contemplated in the clause upon which the suggestion under examination has been founded, the vacancies to which it alludes can only be deemed to respect those officers in whose appointment that body has a concurrent agency with the President. But last, the first and second clauses of the third section of the first article not only obviate all possibility of doubt, but destroy the pretext of misconception. The former provides that "the Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, chosen BY THE LEGISLATURE THEREOF for six years." The latter directs that "if vacancies in that body should happen by resignation or otherwise, DURING THE RECESS OF THE LEGISLATURE OF ANY STATE, the Executive THEREOF may make temporary appointments until the NEXT MEETING OF THE LEGISLATURE, which shall then fill such vacancies." Here is an express power given, in clear and unambiguous terms, to the State Executives, to fill casual vacancies in the Senate, by temporary appointments. This not only invalidates the supposition that the clause before considered could have been intended to confer that power upon the President of the United States, but proves that this supposition, destitute as it is even of the merit of plausibility, must have originated in an intention to deceive the people, too palpable to be obscured by sophistry, too atrocious to be palliated by hypocrisy.

67.10.oldText: I have taken the pains to select this instance of misrepresentation, and to place it in a clear and strong light, as an unequivocal proof of the unwarrantable arts which are practiced to prevent a fair and impartial judgment of the real merits of the Constitution submitted to the consideration of the people. Nor have I scrupled, in so flagrant a case, to allow myself a severity of animadversion little congenial with the general spirit of these papers. I hesitate not to submit it to the decision of any candid and honest adversary of the proposed government, whether language can furnish epithets of too much asperity, for so shameless and so prostitute an attempt to impose on the citizens of America.

68.0.oldText: The mode of appointment of the Chief Magistrate of the United States is almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents. The most plausible of these, who has appeared in print, has even deigned to admit that the election of the President is pretty well guarded. I venture somewhat further, and hesitate not to affirm, that if the manner of it is not perfect, it is at least excellent. It unites in an eminent degree all the advantages, the union of which was to be wished for.

68.1.oldText: It was desirable that the sense of the people should operate in the choice of the person to whom so important a trust was to be confided. This end will be answered by committing the right of making it, not to any preestablished body, but to men chosen by the people for the special purpose, and at the particular conjuncture.

68.2.oldText: It was equally desirable that the immediate election should be made by men most capable of analyzing the qualities adapted to the station, and acting under circumstances favorable to deliberation, and to a judicious combination of all the reasons and inducements which were proper to govern their choice. A small number of persons, selected by their fellow-citizens from the general mass, will be most likely to possess the information and discernment requisite to such complicated investigations.

68.3.oldText: It was also peculiarly desirable to afford as little opportunity as possible to tumult and disorder. This evil was not least to be dreaded in the election of a magistrate who was to have so important an agency in the administration of the government as the President of the United States. But the precautions which have been so happily concerted in the system under consideration promise an effective security against this mischief. The choice of SEVERAL, to form an intermediate body of electors, will be much less apt to convulse the community with any extraordinary or violent movements, than the choice of ONE who was himself to be the final object of the public wishes. Since the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments, which might be communicated from them to the people, than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.

68.4.oldText: Nothing was more to be desired than that every practicable obstacle should be opposed to cabal, intrigue, and corruption. These most deadly adversaries of republican government might naturally have been expected to make their approaches from more than one quarter, but chiefly from the desire in foreign powers to gain an improper ascendant in our councils. How could they better gratify this, than by raising a creature of their own to the chief magistracy of the Union? But the convention have guarded against all danger of this sort, with the most provident and judicious attention. They have not made the appointment of the President to depend on any preexisting bodies of men, who might be tampered with beforehand to prostitute their votes. They have referred it in the first instance to an immediate act of the people of America, to be exerted in the choice of persons for the temporary and sole purpose of making the appointment. They have excluded from eligibility to this trust all those who from situation might be suspected of too great devotion to the President in office. No senator, representative, or other person holding a place of trust or profit under the United States, can be of the numbers of the electors. Thus without corrupting the body of the people, the immediate agents in the election will at least enter upon the task free from any sinister bias. Their transient existence, and their detached situation, already noticed, afford a satisfactory prospect of their continuing so, to the conclusion of it. The business of corruption, when it is to embrace so considerable a number of men, requires time as well as means. Nor would it be found easy suddenly to embark them, dispersed as they would be over thirteen States, in any combinations founded upon motives, which though they could not properly be denominated corrupt, might yet be of a nature to mislead them from their duty.

68.5.oldText: Another and no less important desideratum was that the Executive should be independent for his continuance in office on all but the people themselves. He might otherwise be tempted to sacrifice his duty to his complaisance for those whose favor was necessary to the duration of his official consequence. This advantage will also be secured, by making his re-election depend on a special body of representatives, deputed by the society for the single purpose of making the important choice.

68.6.oldText: All these advantages will happily combine in the plan devised by the convention. The plan is that the people of each State shall choose a number of persons as electors, equal to the number of senators and representatives of such State in the national government, who shall assemble within the State, and vote for some fit person as President. Their votes, thus given, are to be transmitted to the seat of the national government, and the person who may happen to have a majority of the whole number of votes will be the President. But since a majority of the votes might not always happen to center in one man, and since it might be unsafe to permit less than a majority to be conclusive, it is provided that, in such a contingency, the House of Representatives shall select out of the candidates who shall have the five highest number of votes, the man who in their opinion may be best qualified for the office.

68.7.oldText: The process of election affords a moral certainty that the office of President will never fall to the lot of any man who is not in an eminent degree endowed with the requisite qualifications. Talents for low intrigue, and the little arts of popularity, may alone suffice to elevate a man to the first honors in a single State. But it will require other talents, and a different kind of merit, to establish him in the esteem and confidence of the whole Union, or of so considerable a portion of it as would be necessary to make him a successful candidate for the distinguished office of President of the United States. It will not be too strong to say that there will be a constant probability of seeing the station filled by characters pre-eminent for ability and virtue. This will be thought no inconsiderable recommendation of the Constitution, by those who are able to estimate the share which the executive in every government must necessarily have in its good or ill administration. Though we cannot acquiesce in the political heresy of the poet who says:

68.8.oldText: "For forms of government let fools contest — That which is best administered is best," — yet we may safely pronounce that the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration.

68.9.oldText: The Vice-President is to be chosen in the same manner as the President, with this difference: the Senate is to do, with respect to the former, what is to be done by the House of Representatives, with respect to the latter.

68.10.oldText: The appointment of an extraordinary person, as Vice-President, has been objected to as superfluous, if not mischievous. It has been alleged that it would have been preferable to have authorized the Senate to elect out of their own body an officer answering that description. But two considerations seem to justify the ideas of the convention in this respect. One is that, to secure at all times the possibility of a definite resolution of the body, it is necessary that the President should have only a casting vote. To take the senator of any State from his seat as senator, to place him in that of President of the Senate, would be to exchange, with regard to the State from which he came, a constant for a contingent vote. The other consideration is that, since the Vice-President may occasionally become a substitute for the President, in the supreme executive magistracy, all the reasons which recommend the mode of election prescribed for the one, apply with great if not with equal force to the manner of appointing the other. It is remarkable that in this, as in most other instances, the objection which is made would lie against the constitution of this State. We have a Lieutenant-Governor, chosen by the people at large, who presides in the Senate, and is the constitutional substitute for the Governor, in casualties similar to those which would authorize the Vice-President to exercise the authorities and discharge the duties of the President.

69.0.oldText: I now proceed to trace the real character of the proposed Executive as outlined in the convention's plan. This will help expose the unfairness of the criticisms that have been made against it.

69.1.oldText: The first thing that strikes us is that executive authority, with few exceptions, will be vested in a single magistrate. This, however, is hardly a point on which any meaningful comparison can be built. If there is a resemblance to the king of Great Britain in this respect, there is just as much resemblance to the Grand Seignior, the khan of Tartary, the Man of the Seven Mountains, or the governor of New York.

69.2.oldText: This magistrate will be elected for four years, and may be re-elected as often as the people of the United States judge him worthy of their trust. In these circumstances, he is entirely unlike a king of Great Britain, who is a hereditary monarch holding the crown as an inheritance passed down to his heirs forever. But he closely resembles a governor of New York, who is elected for three years and may be re-elected without limit. If we consider how much less time it would take to build a dangerous level of influence in a single state than across the whole United States, we must conclude that a four-year term for the Chief Magistrate of the Union is far less to be feared than a three-year term for the corresponding office in a single state.

69.3.oldText: The President of the United States could be impeached, tried, and, upon conviction of treason, bribery, or other high crimes or misdemeanors, removed from office. He would then be subject to prosecution and punishment under ordinary law. The person of the king of Great Britain is sacred and inviolable. There is no constitutional tribunal he can be brought before, and no punishment he can suffer without provoking a national revolution. On this critical matter of personal accountability, the President of Confederated America stands on no better footing than a governor of New York, and on worse footing than the governors of Maryland and Delaware.

69.4.oldText: The President of the United States will have power to return a bill, after it has passed both branches of the legislature, for reconsideration. The bill so returned becomes law if, on reconsideration, two-thirds of both houses approve it. The king of Great Britain, by contrast, has an absolute veto over the acts of both houses of Parliament. The disuse of that power for a long time does not affect its real existence. It is to be explained entirely by the fact that the crown has found ways to substitute influence for authority — gaining a majority in one or the other house, rather than exercising a prerogative that could rarely be used without risking some national upheaval. The President's qualified veto differs widely from this absolute veto of the British sovereign. It corresponds exactly to the revisionary authority of this state's council of revision, of which the governor is part. In this respect the President's power would exceed that of the governor of New York. The President would hold alone what the governor shares with the chancellor and judges. But it would be precisely the same as the power of the governor of Massachusetts, whose constitution on this point seems to have been the model the convention copied.

69.5.oldText: The President is to be the "commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States, when called into the actual service of the United States. He is to have power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment; to recommend to Congress such measures as he judges necessary and expedient; to convene, on extraordinary occasions, both houses of the legislature, or either of them, and, in case of disagreement between them about adjournment, to adjourn them to such time as he thinks proper; to take care that the laws are faithfully executed; and to commission all officers of the United States." In most of these particulars, the President's power resembles equally that of the king of Great Britain and that of the governor of New York. The most important differences are these: First. The President will only have occasional command of those parts of the militia called into actual service of the Union by legislative provision. The king of Great Britain and the governor of New York have at all times complete command of all militia within their jurisdictions. On this point, the President's power would be inferior to either the monarch's or the governor's. Second. The President is to be commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States. In this respect his authority is nominally the same as the king of Great Britain's, but in substance much weaker. It amounts only to the supreme command and direction of the military and naval forces, as first General and admiral of the Confederacy. The British king's authority extends to declaring war and to raising and regulating fleets and armies — all of which, under the proposed Constitution, would belong to the legislature.(1) The governor of New York, in contrast, is given by the state constitution only command of its militia and navy. But several state constitutions explicitly declare their governors to be commanders-in-chief of both army and navy. It may well be a question whether those of New Hampshire and Massachusetts, in particular, do not in this respect grant their governors larger powers than could be claimed by a President of the United States. Third. The President's power of pardon would extend to all cases except impeachment. The governor of New York may pardon in all cases, even impeachment, except for treason and murder. On this point, considering political consequences, is the governor's power not greater than the President's? All conspiracies and plots against the government, before they ripen into actual treason, could be shielded from any punishment by the prerogative of pardon. If a governor of New York were the head of such a conspiracy, he could, until the design ripened into open hostilities, guarantee complete impunity to his accomplices and supporters. A President of the Union, by contrast, even if he could pardon treason when prosecuted under ordinary law, could not shield any offender from impeachment and conviction. Would not the prospect of total immunity for all preliminary steps be a greater temptation to undertake and persist in a plot against public liberty than the mere prospect of escaping death and confiscation if the final scheme, on actual recourse to arms, should fail? Would this last expectation carry any weight at all, when one considers the probability that the very person granting the exemption might himself be entangled in the consequences and rendered incapable of granting it? To judge this matter properly, we must remember that under the proposed Constitution, treason is limited "to levying war upon the United States, and adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort"; and that under New York law it is similarly bounded. Fourth. The President can adjourn the national legislature only when there is disagreement about the time of adjournment. The British monarch may prorogue or even dissolve Parliament. The governor of New York may also prorogue this state's legislature for a limited time — a power that, in certain situations, may serve very important purposes.

69.6.oldText: The President is to have power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two-thirds of the senators present concur. The king of Great Britain is the sole and absolute representative of the nation in all foreign matters. He can on his own authority make treaties of peace, commerce, alliance, and every other kind. It has been suggested that his authority in this respect is not final, and that his agreements with foreign powers must be revised and ratified by Parliament. But I believe this doctrine was never heard of until it was raised on the present occasion. Every jurist(2) of that kingdom, and every other person familiar with its Constitution, knows as established fact that the prerogative of making treaties rests in the crown in its fullest extent. The agreements made under royal authority have complete legal validity and force without any other approval. Parliament, it is true, sometimes alters existing laws to bring them into conformity with the terms of a new treaty. This may have given rise to the impression that its cooperation was needed for the treaty's binding force. But this parliamentary action arises from a different cause: the necessity of adjusting an artificial and intricate system of revenue and commercial laws to the changes the treaty creates, and of adapting new provisions and safeguards to the new state of affairs, to keep the machine from falling into disorder. So in this respect there is no comparison between the proposed power of the President and the actual power of the British sovereign. The one can do alone what the other can do only with the agreement of a branch of the legislature. It must be admitted that on this point the federal Executive's power would exceed that of any state Executive. But this follows naturally from the sovereign authority that pertains to treaties. If the Confederacy were to dissolve, it would become a question whether the Executives of the several states would not be solely vested with this delicate and important prerogative.

69.7.oldText: The President is also authorized to receive ambassadors and other public ministers. This, though it has been a rich subject for declamation, is more a matter of dignity than of authority. It is a circumstance with no real consequence in the administration of government. It was far more convenient to arrange it this way than to require the legislature, or one of its branches, to convene whenever a foreign minister arrived — even merely to replace a departed predecessor.

69.8.oldText: The President is to nominate, and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, appoint ambassadors and other public ministers, judges of the Supreme Court, and generally all officers of the United States established by law whose appointments are not otherwise provided for by the Constitution. The king of Great Britain is emphatically and truly called the fountain of honor. He not only fills all offices but can create offices. He can confer titles of nobility at his pleasure, and has the disposal of an immense number of church appointments. The President's power in this respect is plainly far inferior to the British king's, and is not equal even to that of the governor of New York, if we interpret this state's constitution by the practice that has prevailed under it. Among us, the appointing power lies with a council made up of the governor and four senators chosen by the Assembly. The governor claims, and has often exercised, the right of nomination, and is entitled to a tie-breaking vote in the appointment. If he really has the right of nomination, his authority equals the President's on this point, and exceeds it in the matter of the tie-breaking vote. In the national government, if the Senate is divided, no appointment can be made. In the New York government, if the council is divided, the governor can tip the scale and confirm his own nomination.(3) If we compare the publicity that must surround appointment by the President and an entire branch of the national legislature with the secrecy of appointment by the governor of New York — closeted in a private room with at most four people, and often with only two — and if we also consider how much easier it must be to influence the small number on a council of appointment than the much larger number on the national Senate, we cannot hesitate to conclude that the chief magistrate of this state, in disposing of offices, must in practice hold far greater power than the Chief Magistrate of the Union.

69.9.oldText: Thus it appears that, except for the President's shared authority over treaties, it would be hard to say whether that magistrate would, on the whole, have more or less power than the Governor of New York. And it appears even more clearly that there is no basis for the parallel that has been attempted between him and the king of Great Britain. But to make the contrast even more striking, it may help to bring the main points of difference into a tighter group.

69.10.oldText: The President of the United States would be an officer elected by the people for four years; the king of Great Britain is a perpetual and hereditary prince. The one would be subject to personal punishment and disgrace; the person of the other is sacred and inviolable. The one would have a qualified veto on legislative acts; the other has an absolute veto. The one would have the right to command the military and naval forces of the nation; the other, in addition, possesses the right of declaring war and of raising and regulating fleets and armies on his own authority. The one would have a concurrent power with a branch of the legislature in making treaties; the other is the sole possessor of the treaty-making power. The one would have similar concurrent authority in appointing to offices; the other is the sole author of all appointments. The one can confer no privileges whatever; the other can naturalize aliens, ennoble commoners, and erect corporations with all the rights belonging to corporate bodies. The one can prescribe no rules concerning the nation's commerce or currency; the other is in several respects the arbiter of commerce, and in that capacity can establish markets and fairs, regulate weights and measures, lay embargoes for a limited time, coin money, and authorize or prohibit the circulation of foreign coin. The one has no scrap of spiritual jurisdiction; the other is the supreme head and governor of the national church! What answer shall we give to those who try to persuade us that things so unlike resemble each other? The same answer we should give to those who tell us that a government whose entire power is in the hands of the elective and periodic servants of the people is an aristocracy, a monarchy, and a despotism.

69.11.oldText: 1. A writer in a Pennsylvania paper, under the signature of TAMONY, has claimed that the king of Great Britain owes his prerogative as commander-in-chief to an annual mutiny bill. The truth is the opposite: his prerogative in this respect is immemorial, and was only disputed, "contrary to all reason and precedent," as Blackstone (vol. i, p. 262) puts it, by the Long Parliament of Charles I. By the statute 13 Charles II, chap. 6, it was declared to be in the king alone, for the sole supreme government and command of the militia within his Majesty's realms and dominions, and of all forces by sea and land, and of all forts and places of strength, EVER WAS AND IS the undoubted right of his Majesty and his royal predecessors, kings and queens of England, and that neither house of Parliament can or ought to claim the same.

69.12.oldText: 2. See Blackstone's Commentaries, Vol. I, p. 257.

69.13.oldText: 3. Candor, however, requires me to admit that I do not think the governor's claim to a right of nomination is well founded. Still, it is always legitimate to reason from the actual practice of a government until its propriety has been constitutionally questioned. And even setting aside this claim, when we take into account the other considerations and follow them through all their consequences, we will be inclined to draw much the same conclusion.

70.0.oldText: There is an idea, not without its supporters, that a vigorous Executive is inconsistent with the spirit of republican government. Enlightened well-wishers of this form of government must at least hope that this assumption has no foundation. They can never admit its truth without simultaneously condemning their own principles. Energy in the Executive is a defining feature of good government. It is essential to protecting the community against foreign attacks. It is no less essential to the steady administration of the laws; to protecting property against those irregular and high-handed combinations that sometimes interrupt the ordinary course of justice; to securing liberty against the schemes and assaults of ambition, faction, and anarchy. Anyone the least familiar with Roman history knows how often that republic had to take refuge in the absolute power of a single man, under the formidable title of Dictator. This was needed against the intrigues of ambitious individuals who aimed at tyranny, against the seditions of whole classes whose conduct threatened the existence of all government, and against external enemies who menaced Rome with conquest and destruction.

70.1.oldText: There is no need, however, to multiply arguments or examples on this point. A feeble Executive implies a feeble execution of the government. A feeble execution is just another phrase for bad execution. And a government badly executed, whatever it may be in theory, must in practice be a bad government.

70.2.oldText: Taking it for granted, then, that all sensible people will agree on the necessity of an energetic Executive, the only remaining question is: what are the ingredients that constitute this energy? How far can they be combined with the other ingredients that constitute safety in the republican sense? And how far does the convention's reported plan show this combination?

70.3.oldText: The ingredients that constitute energy in the Executive are: first, unity; second, duration; third, adequate provision for its support; fourth, competent powers.

70.4.oldText: The ingredients that constitute safety in the republican sense are: first, due dependence on the people; second, due responsibility.

70.5.oldText: The politicians and statesmen most celebrated for the soundness of their principles and the justice of their views have come down in favor of a single Executive and a numerous legislature. They have rightly considered energy as the most necessary qualification of the former, and have regarded this as most applicable to power in a single hand. They have, with equal correctness, considered the latter as best suited to deliberation and wisdom, and best calculated to win the confidence of the people and secure their privileges and interests.

70.6.oldText: That unity contributes to energy will not be disputed. Decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch will generally mark the proceedings of one man much more than those of any larger number. As the number is increased, these qualities will diminish.

70.7.oldText: This unity may be destroyed in two ways: either by vesting power in two or more magistrates of equal dignity and authority, or by vesting it nominally in one man who is in whole or in part subject to the control and cooperation of others acting as his counselors. For the first, the two Consuls of Rome serve as an example. For the second, we find examples in the constitutions of several states. New York and New Jersey, if I remember correctly, are the only states that have entrusted executive authority entirely to single men.(1) Both methods of destroying the unity of the Executive have their advocates, but supporters of an executive council are more numerous. Both are open, if not to equal, then to similar objections, and may in most respects be examined together.

70.8.oldText: The experience of other nations offers little instruction on this point. As far as it teaches anything, it teaches us not to be enamored of plurality in the Executive. We have seen that the Achaeans, after experimenting with two Praetors, were led to abolish one. Roman history records many instances of harm to the republic from disagreements between the Consuls, and between the military Tribunes who were sometimes substituted for the Consuls. But it offers no example of any particular advantage gained by the state from the plurality of those magistrates. That the disagreements between them were not more frequent or more disastrous is astonishing — until we consider the unique position the republic was almost continually in, and the prudent policy, suggested by the state's circumstances and pursued by the Consuls, of dividing the government between them. The patricians were engaged in a perpetual struggle with the plebeians for the preservation of their ancient authorities and dignities. The Consuls, generally chosen from the patrician body, were commonly united by their personal interest in defending the privileges of their order. In addition to this motive for union, after the republic's arms had greatly expanded its empire, it became established custom for the Consuls to divide the administration between themselves by lot — one remained at Rome to govern the city and its surroundings, while the other took command in the more distant provinces. This arrangement must have had great influence in preventing the collisions and rivalries that might otherwise have disturbed the peace of the republic.

70.9.oldText: But leaving the dim light of historical research and turning purely to the dictates of reason and good sense, we shall find far more cause to reject than to approve the idea of plurality in the Executive, in any form whatever.

70.10.oldText: Wherever two or more persons are engaged in any common enterprise or pursuit, there is always a danger of difference of opinion. If they are clothed with equal dignity and authority in a public trust or office, there is special danger of personal rivalry and even animosity. From any of these causes, and especially from all of them combined, the most bitter dissensions tend to arise. When they happen, they reduce the respectability, weaken the authority, and disrupt the plans and operations of those they divide. If such dissensions should unfortunately strike the supreme executive magistracy of a country composed of multiple persons, they could obstruct or frustrate the most important measures of government in the state's most critical emergencies. And what is even worse, they could split the community into the most violent and irreconcilable factions, each adhering to a different individual on the magistracy.

70.11.oldText: People often oppose a thing simply because they had no hand in planning it, or because it may have been planned by those they dislike. But if they have been consulted and have happened to disapprove, opposition then becomes, in their view, an indispensable duty of self-love. They seem to think themselves bound by honor and by every motive of personal infallibility to defeat what has been resolved upon contrary to their views. People of upright, benevolent temperaments have too many opportunities to observe with horror how desperate this disposition can become. They see how often the great interests of society are sacrificed to the vanity, conceit, and obstinacy of individuals who have enough credit to make their passions and caprices matter to the rest of mankind. Perhaps the question now before the public will, in its consequences, provide melancholy proof of the effects of this contemptible weakness — or rather detestable vice — in the human character.

70.12.oldText: On the principles of a free government, the inconveniences from the source just mentioned must necessarily be accepted in the formation of the legislature. But it is unnecessary, and therefore unwise, to introduce them into the constitution of the Executive. It is here, too, that they may be most harmful. In the legislature, promptness of decision is more often an evil than a benefit. Differences of opinion and clashes of parties in that branch, though they may sometimes obstruct beneficial plans, often promote deliberation and caution and serve to check excesses by the majority. And once a resolution is taken, opposition must end. That resolution is law, and resistance to it is punishable. But no favorable circumstances mitigate or atone for the disadvantages of dissension in the executive department. Here, they are pure and unmixed. There is no point at which they cease to operate. They serve to embarrass and weaken the execution of any plan or measure they touch, from the first step to its final conclusion. They constantly counteract the qualities most necessary in the Executive — vigor and dispatch — and do so without any compensating good. In the conduct of war, where the energy of the Executive is the bulwark of national security, everything would be at risk from its plurality.

70.13.oldText: It must be admitted that these observations apply with chief weight to the first case supposed — a plurality of magistrates with equal dignity and authority — a scheme whose advocates are unlikely to form a numerous group. But they apply, though with less force, with considerable weight to the proposal of a council whose concurrence is constitutionally required for the operations of the nominal Executive. A skillful cabal in such a council could distract and weaken the entire system of administration. Even if no such cabal existed, mere diversity of views and opinions would be enough to color the exercise of executive authority with a spirit of habitual feebleness and delay.

70.14.oldText: (But one of the weightiest objections to a plurality in the Executive — applying as much to the second plan as to the first — is that it tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility. Responsibility is of two kinds: to censure and to punishment. The first is the more important of the two, especially in an elective office. A man in public trust will far more often act in ways that make him unworthy of further trust than in ways that make him liable to legal punishment. But multiplying the Executive adds to the difficulty of detection in either case. Amid mutual accusations, it often becomes impossible to determine on whom the blame or punishment for a harmful measure, or series of harmful measures, ought really to fall. It is shifted from one to another with such dexterity, and under such plausible appearances, that public opinion is left in suspense about the real author. The circumstances that may have led to any national failure or misfortune are sometimes so complicated that, where there are several actors who may have had different degrees and kinds of involvement, we may clearly see overall that there has been mismanagement — yet it may be impossible to say to whose account the harm should truly be charged.)(E1)

70.15.oldText: (But one of the weightiest objections to a plurality in the Executive — applying as much to the second plan as to the first — is that it tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility.

The circumstances that may have led to any national failure or misfortune are sometimes so complicated that, where there are several actors who may have had different degrees and kinds of involvement, we may clearly see overall that there has been mismanagement — yet it may be impossible to say to whose account the harm should truly be charged.)(E1)

70.17.oldText: "I was overruled by my council. The council were so divided in their opinions that no better resolution on the point could be obtained." These and similar pretexts are constantly at hand, whether true or false. And who will take the trouble, or risk the unpopularity, of strict scrutiny into the secret springs of the transaction? Even if a citizen zealous enough to undertake this thankless task were found, if collusion exists between the parties involved, how easy it is to dress the circumstances in such ambiguity that the precise conduct of any of the parties remains uncertain.

70.18.oldText: In the single instance where the governor of this state is paired with a council — that is, in appointing to offices — we have seen the harm of such an arrangement in exactly the way now under consideration. Scandalous appointments to important offices have been made. Some cases have been so flagrant that ALL PARTIES have agreed on the impropriety. When inquiry was made, the blame was laid by the governor on the members of the council, who in turn pinned it on his nomination. The people remain entirely at a loss to determine by whose influence their interests have been committed to hands so unqualified and so plainly improper. Out of consideration for individuals, I refrain from going into particulars.

70.19.oldText: It is clear from these considerations that plurality of the Executive tends to deprive the people of the two greatest securities they can have for the faithful exercise of any delegated power. First, the restraints of public opinion, which lose their effect both because the censure for bad measures is divided among many, and because of the uncertainty about on whom it should fall. Second, the opportunity to detect, easily and clearly, the misconduct of the persons they trust, so they may either be removed from office or actually punished where the case allows.

70.20.oldText: In England, the king is a perpetual magistrate. By a maxim adopted for the sake of public peace, he is unaccountable for his administration and his person is sacred. Nothing, therefore, can be wiser in that kingdom than to attach to the king a constitutional council that may be answerable to the nation for the advice it gives. Without this, there would be no responsibility whatever in the executive department — an idea inadmissible in a free government. But even there the king is not bound by the resolutions of his council, though they are answerable for the advice they give. He is the absolute master of his own conduct in the exercise of his office and may observe or disregard the counsel given him entirely at his discretion.

70.21.oldText: But in a republic, where every magistrate ought to be personally responsible for his conduct in office, the reason that in the British Constitution recommends a council not only no longer applies but actually argues against the institution. In the monarchy of Great Britain, the council provides a substitute for the chief magistrate's prohibited responsibility, serving in some degree as a hostage to national justice for his good behavior. In the American republic, it would serve to destroy, or greatly diminish, the intended and necessary responsibility of the Chief Magistrate himself.

70.22.oldText: The idea of a council to the Executive, so widespread in the state constitutions, was derived from that maxim of republican jealousy which considers power safer in the hands of a number of men than in those of a single man. Even if the maxim were granted to apply here, I would contend that the advantage on that side would not outweigh the numerous disadvantages on the other. But I do not think the rule applies at all to the executive power. On this point I clearly agree with a writer whom the celebrated Junius pronounces "deep, solid, and ingenious" — that "the executive power is more easily confined when it is ONE";(2) that it is far safer to have a single object for the jealousy and watchfulness of the people; and, in a word, that all multiplication of the Executive is more dangerous than helpful to liberty.

70.23.oldText: A little reflection will convince us that the kind of security sought in multiplying the Executive cannot be achieved. Numbers must be so great as to make combination difficult, or they are a source of danger rather than security. The combined credit and influence of several individuals must be more formidable to liberty than the credit and influence of any one of them separately. When power, therefore, is placed in the hands of so small a number that their interests and views can easily be combined in a common enterprise by a skillful leader, it becomes more liable to abuse, and more dangerous when abused, than if it were lodged in the hands of one man. The single individual, by the very fact of being alone, will be more closely watched and more readily suspected, and cannot unite as much influence as when he is joined with others. The Decemvirs of Rome, whose name denotes their number,(3) were more to be feared in their usurpation than any ONE of them would have been. No one would propose an Executive much more numerous than that body; six to twelve have been suggested as the size of the council. Even the upper end of these numbers is not too large for easy combination, and from such a combination America would have more to fear than from the ambition of any single individual. A council to a magistrate who is himself responsible for what he does is generally nothing better than a drag on his good intentions, is often the instrument and accomplice of his bad ones, and is almost always a cloak for his faults.

70.24.oldText: I refrain from dwelling on the subject of expense, though it is plain that if the council were numerous enough to answer the main end of the institution, the salaries of members — who would have to be drawn from their homes to reside at the seat of government — would be too serious an item in the catalog of public expenditures to incur for an object of doubtful utility. I will only add that before the Constitution appeared, I rarely met an intelligent man from any of the states who did not admit, as the result of experience, that the UNITY of the executive of this state was one of the best distinguishing features of our constitution.

70.25.oldText: 1. New York has no council except for the single purpose of appointing to offices. New Jersey has a council whom the governor may consult. But I think, from the terms of the constitution, their resolutions do not bind him.

71.0.oldText: Duration in office has been mentioned as the second requirement for energy in the Executive authority. This has to do with two objects: the personal firmness of the executive magistrate in exercising his constitutional powers, and the stability of the system of administration adopted under his leadership. As to the first, it must be evident that the longer the term in office, the greater the chance of securing this important advantage. It is a general principle of human nature that a man's interest in what he holds is proportional to how firm or precarious his hold is. He will be less attached to what he holds by a momentary or uncertain title than to what he enjoys by a durable or certain one. He will, of course, be willing to risk more for the sake of the latter than the former. This observation applies just as much to a political privilege, honor, or trust as to any ordinary piece of property. The conclusion is that a man acting as chief magistrate, conscious that in a very short time he MUST leave office, will likely feel too little interested in it to risk any serious censure or trouble by an independent exercise of his powers, or by confronting the ill humors — however brief — that may prevail in a considerable part of society itself, or even in a dominant faction of the legislature. If the case is only that he MIGHT leave it unless continued by a new election, and if he wishes to be continued, his hopes — combined with his fears — would tend even more powerfully to corrupt his integrity or weaken his courage. In either case, feebleness and irresolution must mark the office.

71.1.oldText: There are some who would be inclined to view the servile pliancy of the Executive to a prevailing current — either in the community or in the legislature — as its chief recommendation. But such people hold very crude notions both of the purposes for which government was instituted and of the true means by which public happiness can be promoted. The republican principle requires that the deliberate sense of the community should govern the conduct of those entrusted with managing its affairs. But it does not require unqualified compliance with every sudden gust of passion, or every transient impulse the people may receive from the arts of those who flatter their prejudices in order to betray their interests. It is a fair observation that the people commonly INTEND the PUBLIC GOOD. This often applies even to their errors. But their good sense would scorn the flatterer who pretended that they always REASON RIGHT about the MEANS of promoting it. They know from experience that they sometimes err. The wonder is that they err so seldom, surrounded as they continually are by the wiles of parasites and sycophants, by the snares of the ambitious, the avaricious, the desperate, by the tricks of men who have their confidence more than they deserve it, and of those who seek to possess rather than deserve it. When occasions arise in which the interests of the people clash with their inclinations, it is the duty of the persons appointed to be the guardians of those interests to withstand the temporary delusion — to give the people time and opportunity for cooler and more sedate reflection. Instances could be cited in which conduct of this kind has saved the people from very fatal consequences of their own mistakes, and has earned lasting monuments of their gratitude toward the men who had courage and magnanimity enough to serve them at the risk of their displeasure.

71.2.oldText: But however inclined we might be to insist on unbounded compliance by the Executive with the inclinations of the people, we cannot reasonably argue for similar compliance with the moods of the legislature. The legislature may sometimes stand in opposition to the people, and at other times the people may be entirely neutral. In either case, it is surely desirable that the Executive be in a position to dare to act on his own opinion with vigor and decision.

71.3.oldText: The same rule that teaches the propriety of partitioning the various branches of power also teaches that this partition ought to be designed so that each is independent of the other. What is the point of separating the executive or the judiciary from the legislature, if both the executive and the judiciary are so constituted as to be entirely at the legislature's mercy? Such a separation must be merely nominal, and incapable of achieving its purpose. It is one thing to be subordinate to the laws, and another to be dependent on the legislative body. The first agrees with, the second violates, the fundamental principles of good government. Whatever the forms of the Constitution, the second arrangement unites all power in the same hands. The tendency of the legislative authority to absorb every other has been fully displayed and illustrated by examples in some preceding numbers. In purely republican governments, this tendency is almost irresistible. The representatives of the people in a popular assembly sometimes seem to imagine that they are the people themselves, and they betray strong symptoms of impatience and disgust at the slightest sign of opposition from any other quarter — as if the exercise of its rights by either the executive or the judiciary were a breach of their privilege and an outrage to their dignity. They often appear disposed to exert imperious control over the other departments. And as they commonly have the people on their side, they always act with such momentum that it becomes very difficult for the other branches of the government to maintain the balance of the Constitution.

71.4.oldText: It may be asked how the shortness of duration in office can affect the Executive's independence of the legislature, unless one had the power of appointing or removing the other. One answer to this question can be drawn from the principle already noted: the slight interest a man tends to take in a short-lived advantage, and the small inducement it gives him to expose himself, on its account, to any considerable inconvenience or risk. Another answer, perhaps more obvious though not more conclusive, will arise from considering the legislative body's influence over the people. That influence might be used to prevent the re-election of a man who, by upright resistance to some sinister project of the legislature, has made himself obnoxious to its resentment.

71.5.oldText: It may also be asked whether a duration of four years would answer the proposed end. And if it would not, whether a shorter period — which would at least be recommended by greater security against ambitious designs — would not, for that reason, be preferable to a longer period that was at the same time still too short to inspire the desired firmness and independence in the magistrate.

71.6.oldText: It cannot be claimed that a duration of four years, or any other limited term, would completely achieve the proposed end. But it would contribute toward it to a degree that would materially shape the spirit and character of the government. Between the start and end of such a period there would always be a considerable interval in which the prospect of leaving office would be remote enough not to have an improper effect on the conduct of a man with even a moderate share of fortitude. He might reasonably promise himself that there would be time enough before that moment arrived to make the community appreciate the soundness of the measures he was inclined to pursue. Though it is probable that, as he approached the moment when the public would, by a new election, signify their judgment of his conduct, his confidence — and with it his firmness — would decline, both would still draw support from the opportunities his prior continuance in office had given him to establish himself in the esteem and good will of his constituents. He could then take risks with safety, in proportion to the proofs he had given of his wisdom and integrity, and to the claim he had acquired to the respect and attachment of his fellow citizens. On the one hand, a four-year term will contribute to the firmness of the Executive enough to make it a very valuable ingredient in its composition. On the other, it is not enough to justify any alarm for public liberty. If a British House of Commons, from the most feeble beginnings — FROM THE MERE POWER OF ASSENTING TO OR DISAGREEING WITH THE IMPOSITION OF A NEW TAX — has, by rapid strides, reduced the prerogatives of the crown and the privileges of the nobility within limits they considered compatible with the principles of free government, while raising itself to the rank and consequence of a coequal branch of the legislature; if it has been able in one instance to abolish both the royalty and the aristocracy, and to overturn all the ancient establishments, as well in Church as in State; if it has been able, on a recent occasion, to make the monarch tremble at the prospect of an innovation(1) attempted by it — what is to be feared from an elective magistrate of four years' duration, with the limited authorities of a President of the United States? What, except that he might be unequal to the task the Constitution assigns him? I will only add that if his term is so short as to leave doubt about his firmness, that doubt is inconsistent with a jealousy of his encroachments.

71.7.oldText: 1. This was the case with respect to Mr. Fox's India bill, which was carried in the House of Commons and rejected in the House of Lords, to the entire satisfaction, it is said, of the people.

72.0.oldText: The administration of government, in its broadest sense, includes all the operations of the body politic — legislative, executive, or judicial. But in its more usual and perhaps more precise meaning, it is limited to executive details and falls particularly within the province of the executive department. The actual conduct of foreign negotiations; the preliminary plans of finance; the application and disbursement of public moneys in conformity with the legislature's general appropriations; the arrangement of the army and navy; the directions of war operations — these and similar matters constitute what seems most properly understood as the administration of government. The persons to whose immediate management these various matters are committed should therefore be considered the assistants or deputies of the chief magistrate. On this account, they ought to derive their offices from his appointment — at least from his nomination — and ought to be subject to his supervision. This view of the subject at once suggests the close connection between the duration of the executive magistrate in office and the stability of the system of administration. To reverse and undo what has been done by a predecessor is very often considered by a successor as the best proof he can give of his own ability and merit. Beyond this propensity, where the change has been the result of public choice, the successor is justified in supposing that the dismissal of his predecessor came from a dislike of his measures, and that the less he resembles him, the more he will recommend himself to the favor of his constituents. These considerations, together with the influence of personal confidences and attachments, would likely lead every new President to promote a change of personnel in subordinate positions. These causes together could not fail to produce a disgraceful and ruinous instability in the administration of the government.

72.1.oldText: With a positive duration of considerable length, I link the matter of re-eligibility. The first is necessary to give the officer himself the inclination and resolve to play his part well, and to give the community the time and leisure to observe the tendency of his measures and form an experimental judgment of their merits. The second is necessary to enable the people, when they see reason to approve of his conduct, to continue him in his post — to prolong the usefulness of his talents and virtues, and to secure for the government the advantage of permanence in a wise system of administration.

72.2.oldText: Nothing seems more plausible at first sight, nor more ill-founded on close inspection, than the scheme that, on this point, has had some respectable advocates — that of continuing the chief magistrate in office for a certain time and then excluding him from it, either for a limited period or forever after. This exclusion, whether temporary or perpetual, would have nearly the same effects, and these effects would for the most part be harmful rather than beneficial.

72.3.oldText: One ill effect of the exclusion would be a diminution of the inducements to good behavior. There are few men who would not feel much less zeal in the discharge of duty when they were conscious that the advantages of the office tied to it must be relinquished at a fixed point, than when they were allowed to entertain the hope of obtaining, by merit, the continuance of those advantages. This claim will not be disputed so long as it is admitted that desire of reward is one of the strongest incentives of human conduct, or that the best security for the fidelity of mankind is to make their interest coincide with their duty. Even the love of fame — the ruling passion of the noblest minds, which would prompt a man to plan and undertake extensive and arduous enterprises for the public benefit, requiring considerable time to mature and perfect — if he could flatter himself with the prospect of being allowed to finish what he had begun, would, on the contrary, deter him from the undertaking when he foresaw that he must quit the scene before he could complete the work, and must commit it, along with his own reputation, to hands that might be unequal or unfriendly to the task. The most that can be expected from most men in such a situation is the negative merit of doing no harm, instead of the positive merit of doing good.

72.4.oldText: Another ill effect of the exclusion would be the temptation to sordid views, to embezzlement, and in some cases to usurpation. An avaricious man who happened to fill the office, looking ahead to a time when he must in any case give up the income he enjoyed, would feel a temptation — not easily resisted by such a man — to make the best use of the opportunity while it lasted. He might not scruple to resort to the most corrupt expedients to make the harvest as abundant as it was brief. Yet the same man, with a different prospect, might content himself with the regular perquisites of his post, and might even be unwilling to risk the consequences of an abuse of his opportunities. His avarice might be a guard upon his avarice. Add to this that the same man might be vain or ambitious as well as avaricious. If he could expect to prolong his honors by good conduct, he might hesitate to sacrifice his appetite for honors to his appetite for gain. But with the prospect of inevitable removal before him, his avarice would be likely to win out over his caution, his vanity, or his ambition.

72.5.oldText: An ambitious man, too, when he found himself seated at the summit of his country's honors and looked ahead to the time when he must step down from that exalted height forever, and reflected that no exertion of merit could save him from this unwelcome reversal — such a man, in such a situation, would be far more violently tempted to seize a favorable moment to attempt the prolongation of his power, at every personal hazard, than if he had the probability of achieving the same end by doing his duty.

72.6.oldText: Would it promote the peace of the community, or the stability of the government, to have half a dozen men who had had credit enough to be raised to the seat of the supreme magistracy wandering among the people like discontented ghosts, sighing for a place they were destined never to hold again?

72.7.oldText: A third ill effect of the exclusion would be depriving the community of the experience gained by the chief magistrate in exercising his office. That experience is the parent of wisdom is an adage whose truth is recognized by the wisest as well as the simplest among mankind. What is more desirable or more essential than this quality in the governors of nations? Where more desirable or essential than in the first magistrate of a nation? Can it be wise to put this desirable and essential quality under the ban of the Constitution, and to declare that the moment it is acquired, its possessor must abandon the station in which it was acquired, and to which it is suited? Yet this is the precise meaning of all those regulations that prevent men from serving their country, by the choice of their fellow citizens, after they have, by a course of service, qualified themselves to do it with greater usefulness.

72.8.oldText: A fourth ill effect of the exclusion would be banishing men from posts in which, in certain emergencies of the state, their presence might be of the utmost importance to the public interest or safety. There is no nation that has not, at one time or another, experienced an absolute necessity for the services of particular men in particular situations — perhaps it would not be too strong to say, for the preservation of its political existence. How unwise, then, must be every such self-denying ordinance that prohibits a nation from using its own citizens in the way best suited to its needs and circumstances! Even without assuming the personal essentiality of the man, it is plain that changing the chief magistrate at the outbreak of war, or at any similar crisis, for another — even of equal merit — would always be harmful to the community. It would substitute inexperience for experience and would tend to unhinge and set adrift the already settled course of administration.

72.9.oldText: A fifth ill effect of the exclusion would be that it would operate as a constitutional ban on stability in administration. By forcing a change of men in the nation's highest office, it would force a change of measures. It is not generally to be expected that the men will change and the measures stay the same. The opposite is the usual course of things. And we need not fear that there will be too much stability while the option of change exists. Nor need we want to prohibit the people from continuing their trust where they think it can be safely placed — and where, by their constancy, they may avoid the fatal inconveniences of fluctuating councils and shifting policy.

72.10.oldText: These are some of the disadvantages that would flow from the principle of exclusion. They apply most forcefully to the scheme of perpetual exclusion. But when we consider that even a partial exclusion would always make the readmission of the person a remote and uncertain prospect, the observations made apply nearly as fully to one case as to the other.

72.11.oldText: What are the advantages claimed to counterbalance these disadvantages? They are said to be: first, greater independence in the magistrate; second, greater security to the people. Unless the exclusion is perpetual, there is no basis for inferring the first advantage. But even in that case, may he not have an aim beyond his present station for which he might sacrifice his independence? May he not have connections, friends, for whom he might sacrifice it? May he not be less willing, by firm conduct, to make personal enemies, when he is acting under the impression that a time is fast approaching when he not only MAY but MUST be exposed to their resentments, on an equal — perhaps inferior — footing? It is not an easy question whether his independence would be more promoted or impaired by such an arrangement.

72.12.oldText: As to the second supposed advantage, there is still greater reason to doubt it. If the exclusion were perpetual, a man of irregular ambition — the only kind of man we ever have reason to fear — would, with infinite reluctance, yield to the necessity of taking permanent leave of a post in which his passion for power and pre-eminence had acquired the force of habit. And if he had been fortunate or skillful enough to win the goodwill of the people, he might lead them to view as a very odious and unjustifiable restraint upon themselves a provision designed to bar them from giving fresh proof of their attachment to a favorite.
