We can imagine circumstances in which this discontent of the people, joining the thwarted ambition of such a favorite, could pose greater danger to liberty than could ever reasonably be feared from the possibility of his continuance in office, by the voluntary votes of the community exercising a constitutional privilege.

72.13.oldText: There is an excess of refinement in the idea of disabling the people from continuing in office men who, in their opinion, have earned approval and trust. The advantages of such a restriction are at best speculative and equivocal, and are outweighed by disadvantages far more certain and decisive.

73.0.oldText: The third ingredient toward constituting the vigor of the executive authority is an adequate provision for its support. It is plain that without proper attention to this point, the separation of the executive from the legislative department would be merely nominal and meaningless. The legislature, with discretionary power over the salary and emoluments of the Chief Magistrate, could render him as obsequious to its will as it pleased. In most cases, it could either reduce him by hunger or tempt him by lavish gifts to surrender his judgment to its inclinations. These expressions, taken in their full breadth, would no doubt convey more than is intended. There are men who could be neither distressed nor seduced into sacrificing their duty. But this stern virtue grows in few soils. In the main, it will be found that power over a man's support is power over his will. If it were necessary to confirm so plain a truth by facts, examples would not be lacking, even in this country, of the intimidation or seduction of the Executive by the threats or allurements of the legislative body's pecuniary arrangements.

73.1.oldText: It is not easy, therefore, to commend too highly the judicious attention paid to this subject in the proposed Constitution. It provides that "The President of the United States shall, at stated times, receive for his services a compensation which shall neither be increased nor diminished during the period for which he shall have been elected; and he shall not receive within that period any other emolument from the United States, or any of them." It is impossible to imagine any provision more eligible than this. The legislature, on the appointment of a President, is once and for all to declare what the compensation for his services shall be during the term for which he has been elected. Once this is done, it has no power to alter it, either by increase or diminution, until a new period of service begins by a new election. It can neither weaken his fortitude by acting on his needs, nor corrupt his integrity by appealing to his avarice. Neither the Union nor any of its members will be free to give, nor will he be free to receive, any other emolument than what was determined by the first act. He can thus have no pecuniary inducement to renounce or desert the independence the Constitution intended for him.

73.2.oldText: The last of the requirements for energy listed are competent powers. Let us proceed to consider those proposed to be vested in the President of the United States.

73.3.oldText: The first thing that strikes our notice is the President's qualified veto over the acts or resolutions of the two houses of the legislature. In other words, his power to return all bills with objections, with the effect of preventing them from becoming laws unless they are afterwards ratified by two-thirds of each house.

73.4.oldText: The tendency of the legislative department to intrude on the rights, and to absorb the powers, of the other departments has already been noted and repeated. The insufficiency of a mere parchment outline of the boundaries of each has also been remarked upon. The necessity of furnishing each with constitutional weapons for its own defense has been inferred and proved. From these clear and indisputable principles follows the propriety of a veto, either absolute or qualified, in the Executive over the acts of the legislative branches. Without one or the other, the Executive would be absolutely unable to defend himself against the encroachments of the legislature. He could be gradually stripped of his authorities by successive resolutions, or destroyed by a single vote. In one way or the other, the legislative and executive powers might quickly come to be combined in the same hands. Even if no tendency had ever shown itself in the legislative body to invade the rights of the Executive, the rules of just reasoning and theoretical propriety would themselves teach us that one ought not to be left to the mercy of the other, but ought to possess a constitutional and effective power of self-defense.

73.5.oldText: But the power in question has a further use. It serves not only as a shield to the Executive but also as an additional security against the enactment of improper laws. It establishes a beneficial check on the legislative body, designed to guard the community against the effects of faction, hastiness, or any impulse unfriendly to the public good that may happen to influence a majority of that body.

73.6.oldText: The propriety of a veto has on some occasions been opposed by the observation that we cannot presume one man would have more virtue and wisdom than a number of men, and that unless we make this presumption, it would be improper to give the executive magistrate any kind of control over the legislative body.

73.7.oldText: But this observation, when examined, will appear specious rather than solid. The propriety of the thing does not turn on supposing superior wisdom or virtue in the Executive, but on supposing that the legislature will not be infallible — that the love of power may sometimes betray it into a disposition to encroach on the rights of other branches of government; that a spirit of faction may sometimes pervert its deliberations; that impressions of the moment may sometimes hurry it into measures that, on more mature reflection, it would itself condemn. The chief inducement for conferring this power on the Executive is to enable him to defend himself; the secondary inducement is to increase the chances for the community against the passing of bad laws through haste, inadvertence, or design. The more often a measure is brought under examination, and the greater the diversity of situations among those examining it, the less the danger of errors flowing from lack of due deliberation, or of missteps coming from the contagion of a common passion or interest. It is far less probable that culpable views of any kind should infect every part of the government at the same moment, and concerning the same object, than that they should govern and mislead each in turn.

73.8.oldText: It may perhaps be said that the power to prevent bad laws also includes the power to prevent good ones, and may be used for one as well as the other. But this objection will carry little weight with those who can rightly estimate the harm of the inconstancy and instability of laws — which is the greatest blemish on the character and spirit of our governments. They will consider every institution designed to restrain the excess of lawmaking, and to keep things as they are at any given period, as much more likely to do good than harm. It is favorable to greater stability in the system of legislation. The injury possibly done by defeating a few good laws will be amply compensated by the advantage of preventing many bad ones.

73.9.oldText: Nor is this all. The superior weight and influence of the legislative body in a free government, and the risk to the Executive in a contest of strength with that body, provide a satisfactory security that the veto would generally be used with great caution. There would more often be room for a charge of timidity than of rashness in its use. A king of Great Britain, with all his train of sovereign attributes and all the influence he draws from a thousand sources, would today hesitate to veto the joint resolutions of the two houses of Parliament. He would not fail to exert the utmost of his influence to strangle a measure disagreeable to him on its way to the throne, to avoid the dilemma of either permitting it to take effect or risking the displeasure of the nation by opposing the sense of the legislative body. Nor is it likely that he would finally venture to exert his prerogatives except in a case of manifest propriety or extreme necessity. All well-informed men in that kingdom will agree to the justice of this remark. A very considerable period has passed since the crown's veto has been exercised.

73.10.oldText: If a magistrate so powerful and so well fortified as a British monarch would have qualms about exercising the power in question, how much greater caution may reasonably be expected in a President of the United States, clothed for the short period of four years with the executive authority of a government wholly and purely republican?

73.11.oldText: It is plain that there would be greater danger of his not using his power when necessary than of his using it too often, or too much. Indeed, an argument against its expediency has been drawn from this very source. It has been represented as a power odious in appearance and useless in practice. But it does not follow that because it might rarely be exercised, it would never be exercised. In the case for which it is chiefly designed — an immediate attack on the constitutional rights of the Executive, or one in which the public good was plainly and palpably sacrificed — a man of tolerable firmness would use his constitutional means of defense and would heed the admonitions of duty and responsibility. In the first case, his fortitude would be stimulated by his immediate interest in the power of his office; in the second, by the probable approval of his constituents, who, although they would naturally lean toward the legislative body in a doubtful case, would hardly let their partiality mislead them in a very plain one. I speak here of a magistrate with only an ordinary share of firmness. There are men who, under any circumstances, will have the courage to do their duty at every risk.

73.12.oldText: But the convention has pursued a middle course in this business, one that will both facilitate the exercise of the power vested in the executive magistrate and make its efficacy depend on the sense of a considerable part of the legislative body. Instead of an absolute veto, it is proposed to give the Executive the qualified veto already described. This is a power that would be much more readily exercised than the other. A man who might be afraid to defeat a law by his single VETO might not hesitate to return it for reconsideration, subject to being finally rejected only if more than one-third of each house concurred in the sufficiency of his objections. He would be encouraged by the thought that if his opposition prevailed, it would carry with it a very respectable portion of the legislative body, whose influence would join his in supporting the propriety of his conduct in the public eye. A direct and categorical veto has something in its appearance more harsh, and more apt to irritate, than the mere offering of argumentative objections to be approved or disapproved by those to whom they are addressed. To the extent it would be less apt to offend, it would be more apt to be exercised; and for this very reason, it may in practice prove more effective. It is to be hoped that it will not often happen that improper views will govern so large a proportion as two-thirds of both branches of the legislature at the same time — and this, too, in spite of the counterweight of the Executive. It is in any case far less probable that this should be the case than that such views should taint the resolutions and conduct of a bare majority. A power of this kind in the Executive will often have a silent and unnoticed, though forceful, effect. When men engaged in unjustifiable pursuits know that obstructions may come from a quarter they cannot control, they will often be restrained by the mere apprehension of opposition from doing what they would otherwise eagerly rush into.

73.13.oldText: This qualified veto, as remarked elsewhere, is in this state vested in a council consisting of the governor, with the chancellor and judges of the Supreme Court, or any two of them. It has been freely used on a variety of occasions, and frequently with success. Its utility has become so apparent that persons who, when the Constitution was being compiled, were violent opposers of it, have from experience become its declared admirers.(1)

73.14.oldText: I have remarked elsewhere that the convention, in framing this part of their plan, departed from the model of this state's constitution in favor of that of Massachusetts. Two strong reasons may be imagined for this preference. One is that the judges, who are to be the interpreters of the law, might receive an improper bias from having previously given an opinion in their revisionary capacity. The other is that by being often associated with the Executive, they might be drawn too far into the political views of that magistrate, so that a dangerous combination might gradually form between the executive and judiciary departments. It is impossible to keep the judges too distinct from every other occupation than that of expounding the laws. It is especially dangerous to put them in a position to be either corrupted or influenced by the Executive.

73.15.oldText: 1. Mr. Abraham Yates, a warm opponent of the plan of the convention, is of this number.

74.0.oldText: The President of the United States is to be "commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States when called into the actual service of the United States." The propriety of this provision is so evident in itself, and so much in line with the precedents of the state constitutions in general, that little need be said to explain or defend it. Even those state constitutions that, in other respects, pair the chief magistrate with a council have for the most part concentrated military authority in him alone. Of all the concerns of government, the direction of war most particularly demands the qualities that distinguish the exercise of power by a single hand. The direction of war implies the direction of the common strength, and the power of directing and employing the common strength forms a usual and essential part of the definition of executive authority.

74.1.oldText: "The President may require the opinion, in writing, of the principal officer in each of the executive departments, upon any subject relating to the duties of their respective offices." I consider this a mere redundancy in the plan, since the right it provides for would follow naturally from the office itself.

74.2.oldText: He is also authorized to grant "reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment." Humanity and good policy together dictate that the benign prerogative of pardon should be as little fettered or embarrassed as possible. The criminal code of every country has so much necessary severity that without easy access to exceptions in favor of unfortunate guilt, justice would wear a countenance too bloody and cruel. Since the sense of responsibility is always strongest in proportion as it is undivided, it may be inferred that a single man would be most ready to attend to the force of those motives that might plead for mitigating the rigor of the law, and least apt to yield to considerations calculated to shelter a fit object of its vengeance. The thought that the fate of a fellow human being depended on his sole decision would naturally inspire scrupulousness and caution. The dread of being accused of weakness or connivance would breed equal circumspection, though of a different kind. On the other hand, since men generally draw confidence from their numbers, they might often encourage each other in an act of obstinacy, and might be less sensitive to the threat of suspicion or censure for injudicious or affected clemency. For these reasons, one man appears to be a more suitable dispenser of the mercy of government than a body of men.

74.3.oldText: The expediency of vesting the power of pardon in the President has, if I am not mistaken, been contested only in relation to the crime of treason. It has been urged that this should have depended on the assent of one or both branches of the legislative body. I shall not deny that strong reasons can be given for requiring on this point the concurrence of that body, or part of it. Since treason is a crime aimed at the very being of society, once the laws have ascertained the guilt of the offender, there seems a fitness in referring the expediency of an act of mercy toward him to the judgment of the legislature. And this should be the case all the more because the supposition of the Chief Magistrate's connivance ought not to be entirely excluded. But there are also strong objections to such a plan. It cannot be doubted that a single man of prudence and good sense is better fitted, in delicate situations, to weigh the motives that may plead for and against the remission of punishment than any numerous body whatever. It deserves particular attention that treason will often be connected with seditions involving a large proportion of the community — as recently happened in Massachusetts. In every such case, we might expect to see the representation of the people tainted with the same spirit that gave birth to the offense. And when parties were fairly evenly matched, the secret sympathy of the condemned person's friends and supporters, taking advantage of the good nature and weakness of others, might frequently grant impunity where the terror of an example was necessary. On the other hand, when the sedition had arisen from causes that had inflamed the resentments of the majority party, they might often be obstinate and inexorable, when policy required forbearance and clemency. But the chief argument for placing the pardon power, in this case, in the Chief Magistrate is this: in seasons of insurrection or rebellion, there are often critical moments when a well-timed offer of pardon to the insurgents or rebels may restore the tranquility of the commonwealth — moments which, if allowed to pass unused, may never be recalled afterwards. The slow process of convening the legislature, or one of its branches, to obtain its sanction for the measure would frequently mean letting the golden opportunity slip. The loss of a week, a day, an hour, may sometimes be fatal. If it is suggested that a discretionary power, with such contingencies in view, might occasionally be conferred on the President, the answer is, first, that it is questionable whether, in a limited Constitution, such power could be delegated by law; and second, that it would generally be impolitic to take any step beforehand that might hold out the prospect of impunity. Such a proceeding, outside the usual course, would likely be construed as an argument of timidity or weakness and would tend to embolden guilt.

75.0.oldText: The President is to have power, "by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur." Though this provision has been attacked, on different grounds, with no small vehemence, I do not hesitate to declare my firm conviction that it is one of the best digested and most unobjectionable parts of the plan. One ground of objection is the trite topic of the intermixture of powers. Some contend that the President alone should hold the power of making treaties, while others say it should have been deposited exclusively in the Senate. Another source of objection is drawn from the small number of persons by whom a treaty may be made. Of those who hold this objection, some think the House of Representatives should have been associated in the business, while others seem to think that nothing more was needed than to substitute two-thirds of all the members of the Senate for two-thirds of the members present. As I flatter myself that the observations made in a preceding number on this part of the plan must have been enough to place it in a very favorable light to a discerning eye, I shall here content myself with offering only some supplementary remarks, mainly aimed at the objections just stated.

75.1.oldText: Regarding the intermixture of powers, I shall rely on the explanations already given elsewhere of the true sense of the rule on which that objection is founded. I shall take it for granted, as an inference from them, that the union of the Executive with the Senate in the matter of treaties is no infringement of that rule. I venture to add that the particular nature of the treaty-making power suggests a special propriety in that union. Though several writers on government place that power in the class of executive authorities, this is plainly an arbitrary classification. If we attend carefully to its operation, it will be found to partake more of the legislative than of the executive character, though it does not strictly fall within the definition of either. The essence of legislative authority is to enact laws — to prescribe rules for regulating society. Executing the laws and employing the common strength, either for that purpose or for the common defense, seem to comprise all the functions of the executive magistrate. The power to make treaties is plainly neither of these. It does not relate to the execution of existing laws, nor to the enactment of new ones, and still less to an exertion of the common strength. Its objects are CONTRACTS with foreign nations, which have the force of law but derive it from the obligations of good faith. They are not rules prescribed by the sovereign to the subject, but agreements between sovereign and sovereign. The power in question therefore seems to form a distinct department, properly belonging neither to the legislative nor to the executive. The qualities described elsewhere as indispensable in the management of foreign negotiations point to the Executive as the most fit agent in those transactions, while the vast importance of the trust, and the operation of treaties as laws, plead strongly for the participation of all or part of the legislative body in the making of them.

75.2.oldText: However proper or safe it may be in governments where the executive magistrate is a hereditary monarch to commit to him the entire treaty-making power, it would be wholly unsafe and improper to entrust that power to an elective magistrate of four years' duration. It has been observed elsewhere, and the observation is unquestionably just, that a hereditary monarch — though often the oppressor of his people — has personally too much stake in the government to be in any serious danger of being corrupted by foreign powers. But a man raised from the station of a private citizen to the rank of chief magistrate, possessing a moderate or slender fortune, and looking forward to a not very distant time when he may probably have to return to the station from which he was taken, might sometimes be under temptations to sacrifice his duty to his interest that would require superlative virtue to resist. An avaricious man might be tempted to betray the interests of the state for the acquisition of wealth. An ambitious man might make his own aggrandizement, with the aid of a foreign power, the price of his treachery to his constituents. The history of human conduct does not warrant the exalted opinion of human virtue that would make it wise in a nation to commit interests so delicate and momentous as those concerning its dealings with the rest of the world to the sole disposal of a magistrate situated as a President of the United States would be.

75.3.oldText: To have entrusted the treaty-making power to the Senate alone would have been to give up the benefits of the constitutional involvement of the President in the conduct of foreign negotiations. It is true that the Senate would in that case have the option of employing him in this capacity. But it would also have the option of leaving him out, and pique or cabal might lead to the latter rather than the former. Besides this, the ministerial servant of the Senate could not be expected to enjoy the confidence and respect of foreign powers to the same degree as the constitutional representative of the nation, and so would not be able to act with equal weight or effectiveness. While the Union would, for this reason, lose a considerable advantage in managing its external concerns, the people would lose the additional security that would result from the cooperation of the Executive. Though it would be imprudent to confide such an important trust to him alone, it cannot be doubted that his participation would materially add to the safety of society. It must indeed be clear to a demonstration that joint possession of this power by the President and Senate would offer greater prospects of security than separate possession by either of them. And whoever has carefully weighed the circumstances that must come together in the appointment of a President will be satisfied that the office will always be likely to be filled by men of such character as to make their concurrence in the formation of treaties especially desirable, both on the score of wisdom and of integrity.

75.4.oldText: The remarks made in a former number, alluded to in another part of this paper, will apply with conclusive force against admitting the House of Representatives to a share in the formation of treaties. The fluctuating composition of that body, and — taking its future increase into account — its very large size, forbid us to expect in it the qualities essential to the proper execution of such a trust. Accurate and comprehensive knowledge of foreign politics; steady and systematic adherence to the same views; a delicate and uniform sensibility to national character; decision, secrecy, and dispatch — these are incompatible with the spirit of a body so variable and so numerous. The very complexity of the business, by requiring the concurrence of so many different bodies, would itself form a solid objection. The greater frequency of calls on the House of Representatives, and the greater length of time it would often be necessary to keep them together when convened, to obtain their approval at progressive stages of a treaty, would be a source of such great inconvenience and expense as alone ought to condemn the proposal.

75.5.oldText: The only objection that remains to be examined is the one that would substitute two-thirds of all the members of the Senate for two-thirds of the members present. It has been shown, under the second head of our inquiries, that all provisions requiring more than a majority of any body for its resolutions have a direct tendency to embarrass the operations of government, and an indirect one to subject the sense of the majority to that of the minority. This consideration seems enough to settle our opinion that the convention has gone as far as could be reconciled with the activity of the public councils or with a reasonable regard for the majority sense of the community in trying to secure the advantage of numbers in the formation of treaties. If two-thirds of the whole number of members had been required, it would, in many cases — because of the non-attendance of some — amount in practice to a necessity of unanimity. And the history of every political establishment where this principle has prevailed is a history of impotence, perplexity, and disorder. Proofs of this could be drawn from the examples of the Roman Tribuneship, the Polish Diet, and the States-General of the Netherlands — were it not that an example at home renders foreign precedents unnecessary.

75.6.oldText: Requiring a fixed proportion of the whole body would not, in all probability, contribute to the advantages of a numerous body any better than merely requiring a proportion of the attending members. The first, by always requiring a determinate number for a resolution, lessens the motives for punctual attendance. The second, by making the capacity of the body depend on a proportion that may vary with the absence or presence of a single member, has the opposite effect. And since, by promoting punctuality, it tends to keep the body complete, there is great likelihood that its resolutions would generally be dictated by as large a number in the latter case as in the former, while there would be far fewer occasions of delay. It ought not to be forgotten that under the existing Confederation, two members may, and usually do, represent a state. As a result, Congress — which is now solely invested with all the powers of the Union — rarely consists of a greater number of persons than would compose the proposed Senate. If we add that the members vote by states, and that where only a single member from a state is present, his vote is lost, it justifies the supposition that the active votes in the Senate, where members are to vote individually, would rarely fall short in number of the active votes in the present Congress. When, in addition to these considerations, we take into view the cooperation of the President, we shall not hesitate to infer that the people of America would have greater security against an improper use of the treaty-making power under the new Constitution than they now enjoy under the Confederation. And when we go a step further and look forward to the probable enlargement of the Senate by the erection of new states, we shall not only see ample ground for confidence in the sufficiency of those to whom that power is entrusted, but we shall probably be led to conclude that a body more numerous than the Senate is likely to become would be very little fit for the proper discharge of the trust.

76.0.oldText: The President is "to nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other officers of the United States whose appointments are not otherwise provided for in the Constitution. But the Congress may by law vest the appointment of such inferior officers as they think proper, in the President alone, in the courts of law, or in the heads of departments. The President shall have power to fill up all vacancies which may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session."

76.1.oldText: It has been observed in a former paper that "the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration." If the justness of this observation is admitted, the mode of appointing the officers of the United States contained in the foregoing clauses must, when examined, be entitled to particular commendation. It is not easy to conceive a plan better calculated than this to promote a judicious choice of men for filling the offices of the Union. And it needs no proof that the character of its administration must essentially depend on this point.

76.2.oldText: It will be agreed on all hands that the appointing power, in ordinary cases, ought to be modified in one of three ways. It ought to be vested either in a single man, in a select assembly of moderate size, or in a single man with the concurrence of such an assembly. Its exercise by the people at large will readily be admitted impracticable; setting every other consideration aside, it would leave them little time to do anything else. So when mention is made in the following reasoning of an assembly or body of men, it must be understood to refer to a select body or assembly as already described. The people collectively, by their numbers and their dispersed location, cannot be governed in their movements by that systematic spirit of cabal and intrigue that will be urged as the chief objection to placing this power in a body of men.

76.3.oldText: Those who have themselves reflected on the subject, or who have attended to the observations made in other parts of these papers concerning the appointment of the President, will, I presume, agree to the proposition that there would always be a great probability of having the place filled by a man of abilities at least respectable. Granting this, I proceed to lay it down as a rule that one man of discernment is better fitted to analyze and assess the particular qualities suited to particular offices than a body of men of equal or perhaps even superior discernment.

76.4.oldText: The sole and undivided responsibility of one man will naturally produce a livelier sense of duty and a more exact regard to reputation. He will, on this account, feel under stronger obligations and more interested in carefully investigating the qualities required for the stations to be filled, and in impartially preferring the persons who have the fairest claims. He will have fewer personal attachments to gratify than a body of men who may each be supposed to have an equal number, and so much the less liable to be misled by sentiments of friendship and affection. A single, well-directed mind cannot be distracted and warped by that diversity of views, feelings, and interests that frequently distracts and warps the resolutions of a collective body. Nothing is so apt to stir the passions of mankind as personal considerations — whether they relate to ourselves or to others who are to be the objects of our choice or preference. Hence, in every exercise of the appointing power by an assembly of men, we must expect to see a full display of all the private and party likings and dislikes, partialities and antipathies, attachments and animosities felt by those composing the assembly. The choice that may at any time be made under such circumstances will of course be the result either of a victory by one party over the other, or of a compromise between the parties. In either case, the intrinsic merit of the candidate will too often be out of sight. In the first, the qualifications best suited to uniting the votes of the party will be more considered than those that fit the person for the station. In the second, the coalition will commonly turn on some interested equivalent: "Give us the man we want for this office, and you shall have the one you want for that." This will be the usual condition of the bargain. And it will rarely happen that advancing the public service is the primary object of either party victories or party negotiations.

76.5.oldText: The truth of the principles here advanced seems to have been felt by the most intelligent of those who have found fault with the provision the convention has made on this subject. They contend that the President alone should have been authorized to make appointments under the federal government. But it is easy to show that every advantage to be expected from such an arrangement would, in substance, be derived from the power of nomination, which is proposed to be conferred on him, while several disadvantages that might attend an absolute appointing power in his hands would be avoided. In the act of nomination, his judgment alone would be exercised. And since it would be his sole duty to point out the man who, with the Senate's approval, should fill an office, his responsibility would be as complete as if he made the final appointment. In this view, there can be no difference between nominating and appointing. The same motives that would lead to a proper discharge of his duty in one case would exist in the other. And since no man could be appointed except on his previous nomination, every man who might be appointed would in fact be his choice.

76.6.oldText: But might not his nomination be overruled? I grant it might. Yet this could only be to make room for another nomination by him. The person ultimately appointed must still be the object of his preference, though perhaps not the first. Nor is it very probable that his nomination would often be overruled. The Senate could not be tempted, by a preference they might feel for someone else, to reject the one proposed, because they could not be sure that the person they wished for would be brought forward by a second or any subsequent nomination. They could not even be certain that a future nomination would present a candidate any more acceptable to them. And since their dissent might cast a kind of stigma on the individual rejected and might appear to be a reflection on the judgment of the chief magistrate, it is unlikely that their sanction would often be refused without special and strong reasons for refusal.

76.7.oldText: To what purpose, then, require the cooperation of the Senate? I answer that the necessity of their concurrence would have a powerful, though generally silent, effect. It would be an excellent check on a spirit of favoritism in the President, and would tend greatly to prevent the appointment of unfit characters from state prejudice, family connection, personal attachment, or a view to popularity. In addition, it would be an effective source of stability in the administration.

76.8.oldText: It will be easily understood that a man who had sole control over offices would be governed far more by his private inclinations and interests than when he was bound to submit the propriety of his choice to the discussion and decision of a different and independent body — and that body an entire branch of the legislature. The possibility of rejection would be a strong motive for care in proposing. The danger to his own reputation — and, in the case of an elective magistrate, to his political existence — from betraying a spirit of favoritism, or an unbecoming pursuit of popularity, before the observation of a body whose opinion would carry great weight in forming public opinion, could not fail to act as a barrier against both. He would be both ashamed and afraid to bring forward, for the most distinguished or lucrative stations, candidates whose only merit was that of coming from the same state to which he particularly belonged, of being personally allied to him in some way, or of possessing the necessary insignificance and pliancy to render them the obsequious instruments of his pleasure.

76.9.oldText: To this reasoning it has been objected that the President, by the influence of the power of nomination, may secure the compliance of the Senate to his views. This supposition of universal venality in human nature is little less an error in political reasoning than the supposition of universal rectitude. The institution of delegated power implies that there is a portion of virtue and honor among mankind that may be a reasonable foundation of confidence — and experience justifies the theory. It has been found to exist in the most corrupt periods of the most corrupt governments. The venality of the British House of Commons has long been a topic of accusation against that body, both in the country to which they belong and here. It cannot be doubted that the charge is, to a considerable extent, well founded. But it is as little to be doubted that there is always a large proportion of the body consisting of independent and public-spirited men who carry influential weight in the councils of the nation. It is for this reason (the present reign not excepted) that the sense of that body is often seen to control the inclinations of the monarch, both as to men and as to measures. Though it might therefore be allowable to suppose that the Executive could occasionally influence some individuals in the Senate, the supposition that he could in general purchase the integrity of the whole body would be strained and improbable. A man disposed to view human nature as it is, without either flattering its virtues or exaggerating its vices, will see sufficient ground of confidence in the probity of the Senate to rest satisfied not only that it will be impracticable for the Executive to corrupt or seduce a majority of its members, but that the necessity of its cooperation in the business of appointments will be a considerable and beneficial restraint on the conduct of that magistrate. Nor is the integrity of the Senate the only safeguard. The Constitution has provided some important guards against the danger of executive influence on the legislative body. It declares that "No senator or representative shall during the time for which he was elected, be appointed to any civil office under the United States, which shall have been created, or the emoluments whereof shall have been increased, during such time; and no person, holding any office under the United States, shall be a member of either house during his continuance in office."

77.0.oldText: It has been mentioned as one of the advantages to be expected from the cooperation of the Senate in the business of appointments that it would contribute to the stability of the administration. The consent of that body would be necessary to remove as well as to appoint. A change of Chief Magistrate, therefore, would not produce so violent or general a revolution in the officers of the government as might be expected if he were the sole disposer of offices. Where a man in any post had given satisfactory evidence of his fitness, a new President would be restrained from attempting a change in favor of someone more agreeable to him by the apprehension that the disapproval of the Senate might frustrate the attempt and bring some discredit upon himself. Those who can best estimate the value of a steady administration will be most disposed to prize a provision that ties the official existence of public men to the approval or disapproval of that body — which, owing to the greater permanency of its own composition, will in all probability be less subject to inconstancy than any other branch of the government.

77.1.oldText: On the union of the Senate with the President in the matter of appointments, it has in some cases been suggested that this would give the President an undue influence over the Senate, and in others that it would have the opposite effect — strong proof that neither suggestion is true.

77.2.oldText: To state the first in its proper form is to refute it. It amounts to this: the President would have an improper influence over the Senate, because the Senate would have the power of restraining him. This is an absurdity in terms. It cannot be doubted that the entire power of appointment would enable him much more effectively to establish a dangerous empire over that body than a mere power of nomination subject to their control.

77.3.oldText: Let us consider the converse of the proposition: "the Senate would influence the Executive." As I have had occasion to remark in several other instances, the vagueness of the objection forbids a precise answer. In what manner is this influence to be exerted? Concerning what objects? The power of influencing a person, in the sense used here, must imply the power of conferring a benefit on him. How could the Senate confer a benefit on the President by how it used its right of veto over his nominations? If it is said they might sometimes gratify him by acquiescing in a favorite choice, when public motives might dictate different conduct, I answer that the instances in which the President could be personally interested in the result would be too few for him to be materially affected by the Senate's compliance. The POWER that can originate the disposition of honors and emoluments is more likely to attract than to be attracted by the POWER that can merely obstruct their course. If by influencing the President is meant restraining him, this is precisely what was intended. And it has been shown that the restraint would be salutary, and at the same time would not destroy a single advantage to be looked for from the unrestrained agency of that magistrate. The right of nomination would produce all the (good, without the ill.)(E1) (good of the appointing power, and would in great measure avoid its evils.)(E1)

77.4.oldText: Comparing the plan for appointing officers of the proposed government with that established by the constitution of this state, a decided preference must be given to the former. In that plan the power of nomination is unequivocally vested in the Executive. And since each nomination must be submitted to the judgment of an entire branch of the legislature, the circumstances surrounding an appointment, from the mode of conducting it, would naturally become matters of public knowledge. The public would be at no loss to determine what part each actor played. The blame for a bad nomination would fall on the President alone and absolutely. The censure for rejecting a good one would lie entirely at the door of the Senate, aggravated by the consideration that they had counteracted the good intentions of the Executive. If a bad appointment were made, the Executive for nominating, and the Senate for approving, would share, though in different degrees, in the opprobrium and disgrace.

77.5.oldText: The opposite of all this characterizes the manner of appointment in this state. The council of appointment consists of three to five persons, of whom the governor is always one. This small body, shut up in a private apartment impenetrable to the public eye, proceeds to execute the trust committed to them. It is known that the governor claims the right of nomination on the strength of some ambiguous expressions in the constitution. But it is not known to what extent, or in what manner, he exercises it, nor on what occasions he is contradicted or opposed. The censure of a bad appointment, owing to the uncertainty of its author and the lack of a determinate target, has neither poignancy nor duration. And while an unbounded field for cabal and intrigue lies open, all idea of responsibility is lost. The most the public can know is that the governor claims the right of nomination; that two out of the inconsiderable number of four men can too often be managed without much difficulty; that if some members of a particular council should happen to be uncomplying, it is frequently possible to get rid of their opposition by setting the times of meeting in a way that makes their attendance inconvenient; and that, for whatever cause, a great number of very improper appointments are made from time to time. Whether a governor of this state uses the ascendancy he must necessarily have in this delicate and important part of the administration to prefer to offices men best qualified for them, or whether he prostitutes that advantage to the advancement of persons whose chief merit is their implicit devotion to his will and the support of a despicable and dangerous system of personal influence, are questions that — unfortunately for the community — can only be subjects of speculation and conjecture.

77.6.oldText: Every council of appointment, however constituted, will be a conclave in which cabal and intrigue will have full scope. Their number, without an unwarrantable increase of expense, cannot be large enough to prevent easy combination. And since each member will have his friends and connections to provide for, the desire for mutual gratification will breed a scandalous bartering of votes and bargaining for places. The private attachments of one man might easily be satisfied. But to satisfy the private attachments of a dozen or twenty men would result in a monopoly of all the principal posts of government in a few families, and would lead more directly to an aristocracy or oligarchy than any measure that could be contrived. If, to avoid an accumulation of offices, there were to be frequent change in the persons composing the council, this would involve the harms of a mutable administration in their full extent. Such a council would also be more liable to executive influence than the Senate, because they would be fewer in number and would act less immediately under public inspection. Such a council, in short, as a substitute for the plan of the convention, would produce an increase of expense, a multiplication of the evils that spring from favoritism and intrigue in the distribution of public honors, a decrease of stability in the administration of the government, and a diminution of security against undue influence by the Executive. And yet such a council has been warmly contended for as an essential amendment in the proposed Constitution.

77.7.oldText: I could not properly conclude my observations on the subject of appointments without taking notice of a scheme for which some — though few — advocates have appeared. I mean that of joining the House of Representatives in the power of making them. I shall, however, do little more than mention it, since I cannot imagine it is likely to gain the support of any considerable part of the community. A body so fluctuating and at the same time so numerous can never be deemed fit to exercise that power. Its unfitness will be plain to all when it is remembered that within half a century it may consist of three or four hundred persons. All the advantages of stability — both of the Executive and the Senate — would be defeated by this union, and infinite delays and embarrassments would be caused. The example of most of the states in their local constitutions encourages us to reject the idea.

77.8.oldText: The only remaining powers of the Executive are: giving information to Congress of the state of the Union; recommending to their consideration such measures as he judges expedient; convening them, or either branch, on extraordinary occasions; adjourning them when they cannot themselves agree on the time of adjournment; receiving ambassadors and other public ministers; faithfully executing the laws; and commissioning all the officers of the United States.

77.9.oldText: Except for some cavils about the power of convening either house of the legislature and the power of receiving ambassadors, no objection has been made to this class of authorities — nor could they possibly admit of any. It required, indeed, an insatiable appetite for censure to invent exceptions to the parts that have been excepted to. As to the power of convening either house of the legislature, I shall merely remark that for the Senate at least, we can readily see a good reason for it. Since this body shares power with the Executive in the matter of treaties, it might often be necessary to call it together for that purpose when it would be unnecessary and improper to convene the House of Representatives. As to the reception of ambassadors, what I have said in a former paper will provide a sufficient answer.

77.10.oldText: We have now completed a survey of the structure and powers of the executive department, which, I have tried to show, combines, as far as republican principles will admit, all the requisites for energy. The remaining inquiry is: does it also combine the requisites for safety in a republican sense — a due dependence on the people, a due responsibility? The answer to this question has been anticipated in the investigation of its other features, and is satisfactorily deducible from these circumstances: the election of the President once every four years by persons immediately chosen by the people for that purpose; and his being at all times liable to impeachment, trial, dismissal from office, disqualification from any other office, and to forfeiture of life and estate by subsequent prosecution in the ordinary course of law. But these precautions, great as they are, are not the only ones the plan of the convention has provided for the public security. In the only instances in which abuse of executive authority was materially to be feared, the Chief Magistrate of the United States would, under that plan, be subjected to the control of a branch of the legislative body. What more could be desired by an enlightened and reasonable people?

78.0.oldText: We now proceed to an examination of the judiciary department of the proposed government.

78.1.oldText: In setting out the defects of the existing Confederation, the utility and necessity of a federal judiciary have been clearly demonstrated. There is less need to repeat the considerations urged there, since the propriety of the institution in the abstract is not disputed. The only questions raised concern the manner of constituting it and its extent. Our observations shall therefore be confined to these points.

78.2.oldText: The manner of constituting it seems to involve these several objects: First, the mode of appointing the judges. Second, the tenure by which they are to hold their places. Third, the partition of the judiciary authority between different courts and their relations to each other.

78.3.oldText: First. As to the mode of appointing the judges: this is the same as that of appointing officers of the Union in general, and has been so fully discussed in the last two numbers that nothing could be said here without useless repetition.

78.4.oldText: Second. As to the tenure by which the judges are to hold their places: this chiefly concerns their duration in office, the provisions for their support, and the precautions for their responsibility.

78.5.oldText: According to the plan of the convention, all judges appointed by the United States are to hold their offices during good behavior. This conforms to the most approved of the state constitutions, and among the rest, to that of this state. The fact that its propriety has been called into question by the adversaries of the plan is no slight symptom of the rage for objection that disorders their imaginations and judgments. The standard of good behavior for the continuance in office of the judicial magistracy is certainly one of the most valuable modern improvements in the practice of government. In a monarchy it is an excellent barrier to the despotism of the prince. In a republic it is no less an excellent barrier to the encroachments and oppressions of the representative body. And it is the best expedient that can be devised in any government to secure a steady, upright, and impartial administration of the laws.

78.6.oldText: Whoever attentively considers the different departments of power must perceive that, in a government where they are separated from each other, the judiciary, by the nature of its functions, will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution, because it will be least able to harm or injure them. The Executive not only dispenses the honors but holds the sword of the community. The legislature not only commands the purse but prescribes the rules by which the duties and rights of every citizen are to be regulated. The judiciary, on the contrary, has no influence over either the sword or the purse. It directs neither the strength nor the wealth of society, and can take no active resolution whatever. It may truly be said to have neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment, and must ultimately depend on the aid of the executive arm even to give effect to its judgments.

78.7.oldText: This simple view of the matter suggests several important consequences. It proves incontestably that the judiciary is beyond comparison the weakest of the three departments of power(1); that it can never successfully attack either of the other two; and that all possible care is required to enable it to defend itself against their attacks. It equally proves that, though individual oppression may now and then proceed from the courts of justice, the general liberty of the people can never be endangered from that quarter — I mean so long as the judiciary remains truly distinct from both the legislature and the Executive. For I agree that "there is no liberty, if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers."(2) And it proves, finally, that since liberty has nothing to fear from the judiciary alone but would have everything to fear from its union with either of the other departments; since all the effects of such a union must follow from a dependence of the former on the latter, despite a nominal and apparent separation; since, from the natural feebleness of the judiciary, it is in continual jeopardy of being overpowered, awed, or influenced by its coordinate branches; and since nothing can contribute so much to its firmness and independence as permanency in office — this quality may therefore justly be regarded as an indispensable ingredient in its constitution, and, in great measure, as the citadel of public justice and public security.

78.8.oldText: The complete independence of the courts of justice is especially essential in a limited Constitution. By a limited Constitution, I mean one that contains certain specified exceptions to the legislative authority — for example, that it shall pass no bills of attainder, no ex post facto laws, and the like. Limitations of this kind can be preserved in practice in no other way than through the medium of courts of justice, whose duty must be to declare void all acts contrary to the manifest tenor of the Constitution. Without this, all reservations of particular rights or privileges would amount to nothing.

78.9.oldText: Some perplexity over the right of the courts to pronounce legislative acts void because contrary to the Constitution has arisen from a notion that the doctrine would imply a superiority of the judiciary to the legislative power. It is urged that the authority that can declare the acts of another void must necessarily be superior to the one whose acts may be declared void. As this doctrine is of great importance in all the American constitutions, a brief discussion of the ground on which it rests cannot be unwelcome.

78.10.oldText: There is no position that depends on clearer principles than this: that every act of a delegated authority contrary to the tenor of the commission under which it is exercised is void. No legislative act, therefore, contrary to the Constitution, can be valid. To deny this would be to affirm that the deputy is greater than his principal; that the servant is above his master; that the representatives of the people are superior to the people themselves; that men acting by virtue of powers may do not only what their powers do not authorize, but what they forbid.

78.11.oldText: If it is said that the legislative body is itself the constitutional judge of its own powers, and that the construction it puts on them is conclusive on the other departments, the answer is that this cannot be the natural presumption where it is not to be gathered from any particular provisions in the Constitution. It is not otherwise to be supposed that the Constitution could have intended to enable the representatives of the people to substitute their will for that of their constituents. It is far more rational to suppose that the courts were designed to be an intermediate body between the people and the legislature, in order, among other things, to keep the latter within the limits assigned to their authority. The interpretation of the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts. A constitution is, in fact, and must be regarded by the judges as, a fundamental law. It therefore belongs to them to ascertain its meaning, as well as the meaning of any particular act proceeding from the legislative body. If there should happen to be an irreconcilable conflict between the two, the one with the superior obligation and validity ought, of course, to be preferred — or, in other words, the Constitution ought to be preferred to the statute, the intention of the people to the intention of their agents.

78.12.oldText: Nor does this conclusion in any way imply a superiority of the judicial to the legislative power. It only supposes that the power of the people is superior to both, and that where the will of the legislature, declared in its statutes, stands in opposition to that of the people, declared in the Constitution, the judges ought to be governed by the latter rather than the former. They ought to regulate their decisions by the fundamental laws, rather than by those that are not fundamental.

78.13.oldText: This exercise of judicial discretion in deciding between two contradictory laws is illustrated in a familiar instance. It not uncommonly happens that two statutes exist at the same time, clashing in whole or in part with each other, and neither contains any repealing clause or expression. In such a case, it is the province of the courts to settle and fix their meaning and operation. Insofar as they can, by any fair construction, be reconciled, reason and law join in dictating that this should be done. Where this is impracticable, it becomes a matter of necessity to give effect to one and exclude the other. The rule that has prevailed in the courts for determining their relative validity is that the last in order of time shall be preferred to the first. But this is a mere rule of construction, not derived from any positive law but from the nature and reason of the thing. It is a rule not imposed on the courts by legislative provision, but adopted by themselves as consonant with truth and propriety, for the direction of their conduct as interpreters of the law. They thought it reasonable that, between the conflicting acts of an EQUAL authority, the one that was the last indication of its will should have the preference.

78.14.oldText: But concerning conflicting acts of a superior and a subordinate authority, of an original and a derivative power, the nature and reason of the thing point to the converse of that rule as proper to be followed. They teach us that the prior act of a superior ought to be preferred to the subsequent act of an inferior and subordinate authority. Accordingly, whenever a particular statute contravenes the Constitution, it will be the duty of the judicial tribunals to adhere to the Constitution and disregard the statute.

78.15.oldText: It can carry no weight to say that the courts, on the pretense of a conflict, may substitute their own pleasure for the constitutional intentions of the legislature. This might just as well happen in the case of two contradictory statutes, or in every adjudication on any single statute. The courts must declare the sense of the law. And if they should be disposed to exercise WILL instead of JUDGMENT, the consequence would equally be the substitution of their pleasure for that of the legislative body. The observation, if it proves anything, would prove that there ought to be no judges distinct from that body.

78.16.oldText: If, then, the courts of justice are to be considered as the bulwarks of a limited Constitution against legislative encroachments, this consideration provides a strong argument for the permanent tenure of judicial offices. Nothing will contribute so much as this to that independent spirit in the judges which must be essential to the faithful performance of so arduous a duty.

78.17.oldText: This independence of the judges is equally needed to guard the Constitution and the rights of individuals from the effects of those ill humors that the arts of designing men, or the influence of particular conjunctures, sometimes spread among the people themselves. Such humors, though they speedily give way to better information and more deliberate reflection, tend in the meantime to occasion dangerous innovations in the government and serious oppressions of the minority in the community. Though I trust the friends of the proposed Constitution will never join with its enemies(3) in questioning that fundamental principle of republican government which admits the right of the people to alter or abolish the established Constitution whenever they find it inconsistent with their happiness, it is not to be inferred from this principle that the representatives of the people, whenever a momentary inclination happens to seize a majority of their constituents that is incompatible with the provisions in the existing Constitution, would on that account be justified in violating those provisions; or that the courts would be under a greater obligation to connive at infractions in this form than when those infractions had proceeded wholly from the cabals of the representative body. Until the people have, by some solemn and authoritative act, annulled or changed the established form, it is binding upon themselves collectively as well as individually. No presumption — or even knowledge — of their sentiments can warrant their representatives in departing from it before such an act. But it is easy to see that it would require an uncommon portion of fortitude in the judges to do their duty as faithful guardians of the Constitution, where legislative invasions of it had been instigated by the majority voice of the community.

78.18.oldText: But it is not with a view to infractions of the Constitution only that the independence of the judges may be an essential safeguard against the effects of occasional ill humors in society. These sometimes extend no further than to the injury of the private rights of particular classes of citizens, by unjust and partial laws. Here too the firmness of the judicial magistracy is of vast importance in moderating the severity of such laws and confining their operation. It serves not only to moderate the immediate harms of laws that may have been passed, but operates as a check on the legislative body in passing them. The legislature, perceiving that obstacles to the success of iniquitous intentions are to be expected from the scruples of the courts, are in a manner compelled, by the very motives of the injustice they contemplate, to qualify their attempts. This is a circumstance calculated to have more influence on the character of our governments than few may realize. The benefits of the integrity and moderation of the judiciary have already been felt in more states than one. Though they may have displeased those whose sinister expectations they have disappointed, they must have commanded the esteem and applause of all the virtuous and disinterested. Considerate men of every description ought to prize whatever will tend to beget or fortify that temper in the courts. No man can be sure that he may not tomorrow be the victim of a spirit of injustice by which he may be a gainer today. And every man must now feel that the inevitable tendency of such a spirit is to sap the foundations of public and private confidence and to introduce universal distrust and distress in its stead.

78.19.oldText: That inflexible and uniform adherence to the rights of the Constitution, and of individuals, which we see to be indispensable in the courts of justice, certainly cannot be expected from judges who hold their offices by a temporary commission. Periodic appointments, however regulated, or by whomever made, would in some way or other be fatal to their necessary independence. If the power of making them were committed to the Executive or to the legislature, there would be danger of improper compliance with the branch holding it. If to both, there would be an unwillingness to risk the displeasure of either. If to the people, or to persons chosen by them for the special purpose, there would be too great a disposition to consult popularity, to justify a reliance that nothing would be consulted but the Constitution and the laws.

78.20.oldText: There is yet a further and weightier reason for the permanency of the judicial offices, drawn from the nature of the qualifications they require. It has been frequently remarked, with great propriety, that a voluminous code of laws is one of the inconveniences necessarily connected with the advantages of a free government. To avoid an arbitrary discretion in the courts, it is indispensable that they be bound down by strict rules and precedents, which serve to define and point out their duty in every particular case that comes before them. From the variety of controversies that grow out of the folly and wickedness of mankind, it will be readily seen that the records of those precedents must unavoidably swell to a very considerable bulk, and must demand long and laborious study to acquire a competent knowledge of them. Hence there can be but few men in society with sufficient skill in the laws to qualify them for the stations of judges. And making the proper deductions for the ordinary depravity of human nature, the number must be still smaller of those who combine the requisite integrity with the requisite knowledge. These considerations make it clear that the government can have no great choice among fit characters, and that a temporary duration in office, which would naturally discourage such men from leaving a lucrative line of practice to accept a seat on the bench, would tend to throw the administration of justice into hands less able and less well qualified to conduct it with utility and dignity. In the present circumstances of this country, and in those it is likely to be in for a long time to come, the disadvantages on this score would be greater than they may at first appear. But it must be admitted that they are far inferior to those that present themselves under the other aspects of the subject.

78.21.oldText: On the whole, there can be no room to doubt that the convention acted wisely in copying from the models of those constitutions that have established good behavior as the tenure of their judicial offices, in point of duration. Far from being blamable on this account, their plan would have been inexcusably defective if it had lacked this important feature of good government. The experience of Great Britain offers an illustrious comment on the excellence of the institution.

78.22.oldText: 1. The celebrated Montesquieu, speaking of them, says: "Of the three powers above mentioned, the judiciary is next to nothing." — Spirit of Laws, Vol. I, page 186.

78.24.oldText: 3. See Protest of the Minority of the Convention of Pennsylvania, Martin's Speech, etc.

79.0.oldText: Next to permanency in office, nothing can contribute more to the independence of the judges than a fixed provision for their support. The remark made about the President applies equally here. In the general course of human nature, power over a man's subsistence amounts to power over his will. We can never hope to see, in practice, the complete separation of the judicial from the legislative power in any system that leaves the former dependent for financial resources on the occasional grants of the latter. The enlightened friends of good government in every state have had cause to lament the lack of precise and explicit precautions in the state constitutions on this point. Some have indeed declared that permanent(1) salaries should be established for the judges. But experience has in some cases shown that such expressions are not sufficiently definite to preclude legislative evasions. Something still more positive and unequivocal has been shown to be needed. The plan of the convention has accordingly provided that the judges of the United States "shall at stated times receive for their services a compensation which shall not be diminished during their continuance in office."

79.1.oldText: All circumstances considered, this is the most eligible provision that could have been devised. It will be readily understood that fluctuations in the value of money and in the state of society made a fixed rate of compensation in the Constitution inadmissible. What might be extravagant today might in half a century become miserly and inadequate. It was therefore necessary to leave it to the discretion of the legislature to vary its provisions in conformity to changing circumstances, but under such restrictions as to put it out of the power of that body to change the condition of the individual for the worse. A man may then be sure of the ground on which he stands, and can never be deterred from his duty by the apprehension of being placed in a less favorable situation. The clause quoted combines both advantages. The salaries of judicial officers may from time to time be altered as occasion requires, yet never so as to lessen the allowance with which any particular judge comes into office, with respect to him. It will be noted that a difference has been made by the convention between the compensation of the President and of the judges. That of the former can neither be increased nor diminished; that of the latter can only not be diminished. This probably arose from the difference in the duration of the respective offices. Since the President is to be elected for no more than four years, it can rarely happen that an adequate salary, fixed at the start of that period, will not continue to be adequate at its end. But with the judges, who, if they behave properly, are secured in their places for life, it may well happen — especially in the early stages of the government — that a stipend very sufficient at their first appointment becomes too small as their service progresses.

79.2.oldText: This provision for the support of the judges bears every mark of prudence and efficacy. It may be safely affirmed that, together with the permanent tenure of their offices, it offers a better prospect for their independence than is found in the constitutions of any of the states regarding their own judges.

79.3.oldText: The precautions for their responsibility are contained in the article regarding impeachments. They are liable to be impeached for misconduct by the House of Representatives and tried by the Senate. If convicted, they may be dismissed from office and disqualified from holding any other. This is the only provision on the point that is consistent with the necessary independence of the judicial character, and the only one we find in our own Constitution regarding our own judges.

79.4.oldText: The lack of a provision for removing judges on account of inability has been a subject of complaint. But all considerate men will see that such a provision would either not be acted on or would be more liable to abuse than calculated to serve any good purpose. The measurement of the faculties of the mind has, I believe, no place in the catalog of known arts. An attempt to fix the boundary between the regions of ability and inability would much more often give scope to personal and party attachments and enmities than advance the interests of justice or the public good. The result, except in the case of insanity, must for the most part be arbitrary. And insanity, without any formal or express provision, may be safely pronounced a virtual disqualification.

79.5.oldText: The constitution of New York, to avoid investigations that must always be vague and dangerous, has taken a particular age as the criterion of inability. No man can be a judge beyond sixty. I believe few at present approve of this provision. There is no station to which it is less proper than that of a judge. The deliberating and comparing faculties generally preserve their strength much beyond that period in men who survive it. And when, in addition, we consider how few there are who outlive the season of intellectual vigor, and how improbable it is that any considerable portion of the bench, whether more or less numerous, should be in such a state at the same time, we shall be ready to conclude that limitations of this sort have little to recommend them. In a republic, where fortunes are not affluent and pensions not expedient, the dismissal of men from stations in which they have served their country long and usefully — and on which they depend for subsistence, and from which it will be too late to turn to any other occupation for a livelihood — ought to have some better justification to humanity than is found in the imaginary danger of a superannuated bench.

80.0.oldText: To judge accurately the proper extent of the federal judiciary, we must first consider what its proper objects are.

80.1.oldText: It seems hardly to admit of controversy that the judicial authority of the Union ought to extend to these several kinds of cases: first, to all that arise out of the laws of the United States, passed in pursuance of their just and constitutional powers of legislation; second, to all that concern the execution of the provisions expressly contained in the articles of Union; third, to all in which the United States are a party; fourth, to all that involve the PEACE of the CONFEDERACY, whether they relate to the dealings between the United States and foreign nations, or to those between the states themselves; fifth, to all that originate on the high seas, and are of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction; and finally, to all in which the state tribunals cannot be supposed to be impartial and unbiased.

80.2.oldText: The first point depends on this obvious consideration: that there ought always to be a constitutional method of giving effect to constitutional provisions. What, for instance, would restrictions on the authority of state legislatures be worth, without some constitutional way of enforcing their observance? The states, by the plan of the convention, are forbidden to do a variety of things, some of which are incompatible with the interests of the Union, and others with the principles of good government. Imposing duties on imported articles, and emitting paper money, are examples of each kind. No man of sense will believe that such prohibitions would be scrupulously observed without some effective power in the government to restrain or correct violations of them. This power must either be a direct veto on state laws, or an authority in the federal courts to overrule those that are in manifest violation of the articles of Union. There is no third course I can imagine. The latter appears to have been thought by the convention preferable to the former, and, I presume, will be most agreeable to the states.

80.3.oldText: On the second point, it is impossible by any argument or comment to make the matter clearer than it is in itself. If there are such things as political axioms, the propriety of having a government's judicial power coextensive with its legislative power may be ranked among them. The mere necessity of uniformity in the interpretation of the national laws decides the question. Thirteen independent courts of final jurisdiction over the same causes, arising upon the same laws, is a hydra in government, from which nothing but contradiction and confusion can come.

80.4.oldText: Still less need be said about the third point. Controversies between the nation and its members or citizens can only properly be referred to the national tribunals. Any other plan would be contrary to reason, to precedent, and to decorum.

80.5.oldText: The fourth point rests on this plain proposition: that the peace of the WHOLE ought not to be left at the disposal of a PART. The Union will undoubtedly be answerable to foreign powers for the conduct of its members. And the responsibility for an injury ought always to be paired with the power to prevent it. Since the denial or perversion of justice by court sentences, as well as by other means, is reasonably classed among the just causes of war, it follows that the federal judiciary ought to have cognizance of all causes in which the citizens of other countries are concerned. This is no less essential to preserving the public faith than to securing public tranquility. A distinction may perhaps be imagined between cases arising under treaties and the law of nations, and those that rest merely on municipal law. The former might be supposed proper for the federal jurisdiction, the latter for the states.
